Featured characters: Stan Marsh, Kyle Broflovski, Eric Cartman, Kenny McCormick, the Chinpokomon creators, the toy-shop owner, Randy and Sharon Marsh, the parents of South Park.

Locations: the toy store, the bus stop, Cartman's house, Chinpokomon Camp, City Hall, the airfield.

Key events & continuity: the fad-cycle satire — the craze dies the moment adults embrace it; Kenny's seizure builds all story until the rats finish him; the 'large penis' flattery trick works on every adult man, including the president.

Liane buys Cartman a present to help him win the school spelling bee: Hooked on Monkey Fonics, a drum-playing monkey that teaches spelling from a cassette. At the bee, Cartman crashes out immediately on the word 'chair' — the monkey is too busy masturbating to help. Kyle and two homeschooled siblings, Mark and Rebecca Cotswolds, reach the finals; Kyle chokes on a brutal word and the Cotswolds win, enraging Jimbo, who bet on Kyle. Kyle develops a crush on Rebecca, and the boys grill Mark about homeschooling; Cartman, seeing a life of bed-and-TV, gets himself homeschooled too. Mark attends public school sealed in a protective hamster ball, answers everything in class, and gets duct-taped to a bench by the boys for his trouble — twice, once in the cafeteria. Mr. Cotswolds, fretting over Mark's bullying and Kyle's pursuit of Rebecca, takes his complaints to the town bar, admits he prefers wine coolers to beer, and gets duct-taped to a bench himself. Kyle serenades Rebecca (she thinks he's busking and tips him), introduces her to kissing, and she agrees to the Bay of Pigs Memorial Dance — then reinvents herself as boy-crazy, flirting with everyone. Mark beats Kyle up for it and is suddenly the coolest kid in school. At the dance, Mark explains to his father what sheltering has done: kids kept from socializing go wild the moment they taste freedom, as Rebecca just proved. The Cotswolds relent and enroll Mark in public school; the crowd forgets its duct-tape plans and embraces him while Dio plays 'Holy Diver' — though Mr. Cotswolds still ends up taped to the flagpole. Meanwhile the starved Fonics Monkey goes berserk from lack of food and beats Kenny to death.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman, Kyle Broflovski, Stan Marsh, Kenny McCormick, Mark and Rebecca Cotswolds, Mr. and Mrs. Cotswolds, Jimbo Kern, the Fonics Monkey.

Locations: South Park Elementary (spelling bee, cafeteria), the Cotswolds home, Cartman's bedroom, the Bay of Pigs Memorial Dance.

Key events & continuity: Mark Cotswolds joins the orbit of the school after his parents relent; Rebecca's instant transformation satirizes sheltered upbringing; the Fonics Monkey's rampage is one of Kenny's most absurd ends; Cartman's homeschooling era is pure laziness.

An alien of the Marklar people lands its ship on Earth and is promptly killed by lions. Nearby, Starvin' Marvin is enduring a Christian mission where Sister Hollis makes the starving Ethiopians worship Christ and take Christian names under the false promise of food. Marvin walks out, finds the alien craft, climbs in, and accidentally launches it — straight through a wormhole to the planet Marklar. The FBI spots the launch and recruits the four American boys who knew Marvin before; two CIA agents pull them from class, and under torture-by-balloon-scraping Cartman finally explains who Marvin is. The ship crash-lands into Cartman's house, drags the boys through the wormhole, and strands them on Marklar — a world where every noun, verb, and person is called 'Marklar.' Back on Earth, the CIA bribes the now-Hutt-like Sally Struthers with Kenny's body, and the missionaries realize Marklar is virgin territory for conversion, raising starship funds over cable TV. The boys (minus Kenny) escape with Marvin and race to claim Marklar as a new homeland for the starving Ethiopians — but the Marklars won't agree, because nobody can speak their language. Kyle saves the day with his trademark big speech delivered entirely in the word 'marklar,' and the Marklars, moved, grant the Ethiopians sanctuary. The pursuing missionaries and CIA agents are dragged away. Cartman, meanwhile, neutralizes Sally Struthers by appealing to her vanity, convincing her the missionaries are just copying her own 'generosity.' The boys promise to visit again — 'when Jesse Jackson is President,' Cartman adds.

Featured characters: Starvin' Marvin, Stan Marsh, Kyle Broflovski, Eric Cartman, Kenny McCormick, the Marklars, Sally Struthers, Sister Hollis, the CIA agents, the missionaries.

Locations: Ethiopia, the alien crash site, Cartman's house, the planet Marklar.

Key events & continuity: Starvin' Marvin returns and secures a homeworld for his people; the Marklar language gag (everything is 'Marklar') becomes iconic; Sally Struthers is now a Jabba-like Hutt; Kenny is traded to Struthers as a bribe and dies off-screen.

entries.n: S03E14 — The Red Badge of Gayness
entries.t:
The boys rehearse their fife-and-drum routine for the annual Civil War reenactment of the Battle of Tamarack Hill, directed by Grandpa Marsh. Cartman, cast as a drummer, keeps messing around until Kyle demands he switch instruments; Cartman refuses, Stan backs Kyle, and Cartman smashes the drum and storms off. At the reenactment, Cartman appears dressed as Confederate General Robert E. Lee and proposes a wager: if the South wins the war, Stan and Kyle become his slaves; if the South loses, he's theirs. He then tells Jimbo the Southern reenactors are tired of being teased for losing every year — and, all of them drunk on the event's sponsor beer, S'more Schnapps, the men agree to let the South win this time. It works too well: the drunken Union reenactors join the Confederates, and the whole mob marches out of town to conquer America, raiding town after town for more S'more Schnapps. Kenny is killed somewhere on the march; Cartman informs Mrs. McCormick by mail. Stan, Kyle, and Grandpa Marsh realize the only cure is sobriety, so they steal every drop of S'more Schnapps from the rebel camp — but Cartman just calls the company, which delivers a fresh truck of beer plus a S'more Schnapps spokeswoman, and the crusade resumes. With President Clinton about to sign a surrender to the South, Stan and Kyle take desperate measures: posing as Jefferson Davis and Abraham Lincoln on the White House lawn, they stage a formal Southern surrender. The troops, recognizing Davis as Lee's superior, stand down and march home. Cartman protests that surrender abolishes slavery — meaning he can't claim Stan and Kyle — and Clinton himself affirms the loophole. Stan and Kyle walk off insulting the president.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman (as Robert E. Lee), Stan Marsh, Kyle Broflovski, Kenny McCormick, Grandpa Marsh, Jimbo Kern, the S'more Schnapps army, President Clinton.

Locations: the reenactment field (Battle of Tamarack Hill), the rebel camp, Topeka (targeted), the White House lawn.

Key events & continuity: Cartman's slave bet backfires via his own surrender; the S'more Schnapps-fueled march parodies drunken revisionism; Grandpa Marsh directs the reenactment; Kenny's off-screen march death is reported by post.

Mr. Hankey hosts a fireside Christmas songbook from his sewer home, introducing a parade of holiday musical numbers performed South Park-style. The mailman opens with 'Mr. Hankey, the Christmas Poo' backed by a children's chorus. Kyle tries to teach Ike the dreidel game and sings 'Dreidel, Dreidel, Dreidel,' with Stan, Cartman, Sheila, and Gerald each adding verses — Gerald's confessing his love for Courteney Cox — before all five sing together. In Hell, Adolf Hitler kneels by an empty tree stand, weeping through 'O Tannenbaum' for all his lost Christmases, until Satan takes pity and leads nearly the whole underworld in 'Christmas Time in Hell.' Mr. Mackey, dressed as a bell, performs all four parts of 'Carol of the Bells' by himself. Cartman, in formal wear in Bethlehem, sings 'O Holy Night' with rewritten lyrics about how much he loves getting presents and sweets. Mr. Garrison teaches the class about countries that don't celebrate Christmas — the Middle East, India, Japan — and sings 'Merry Fucking Christmas,' explaining he visits each one yearly to force the holiday on them. Shelly performs 'I Saw Three Ships' at the piano while Stan and Kyle mock her behind her back; warned repeatedly, she finally drops the entire piano on them and walks away calmly. Santa Claus and Jesus share a stage for a Christmas medley, each trying to hijack it into songs about himself. The show closes with Mr. Hankey and the full cast singing 'Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas,' and the news anchor is later seen fighting the frizzies while the dreidel song plays.

Featured characters: Mr. Hankey, Kyle and Ike Broflovski, Stan Marsh, Eric Cartman, Sheila and Gerald Broflovski, Adolf Hitler, Satan, Mr. Mackey, Mr. Garrison, Shelly Marsh, Santa Claus, Jesus, the mailman.

Locations: Mr. Hankey's sewer home, the Broflovski home, Hell, the school classroom, the Christmas medley stage, Bethlehem (Cartman's number).

Key events & continuity: the all-musical format makes it a franchise outlier; Hitler and Satan's Hell caroling becomes a fan-favorite bit; Gerald's Courteney Cox verse is pure character; Shelly's piano-drop is her signature retaliation.

entries.n: S03E16 — Are You There God? It's Me, Jesus
entries.t:
With the new millennium approaching, crowds and media gather outside Jesus's house demanding to know what miracle he'll perform for the year 2000 — they want to see God. Jesus visits Heaven to ask, but God refuses to appear. Scrambling, Jesus books a comeback concert for Rod Stewart in Las Vegas instead. Meanwhile Cartman announces he's finally gotten his period — he's bleeding from his backside — and the boys, consulting a girl, mistakenly believe him. Kenny discovers the same bleeding and thinks he's maturing too; Kyle, after checking with Ike, simply lies that he's had his. Stan, the odd one out, is shut out of the 'mature people only' club and spirals. Chef assumes Stan is pining over a girl and sings him an irrelevant love song. Stan then lies to Dr. Mephesto that his father never went through puberty, pockets the hormone pills, and swallows the whole bottle — growing facial hair, breasts, and a deep voice, though Cartman still won't admit him. A news report reveals the truth: a colon infection is spreading through town, and nobody's having a period at all. At their club the boys insert tampons rectally; Kenny dies from it. Jesus lands Rod Stewart — wheelchair-bound, diapered, nurse-dependent — but the concert bombs; Stewart soils himself on stage, the crowd demands God, and they're ready to crucify Jesus again. Sulking with Stan, Jesus hears the boy's troubles and suddenly understands God's message: God can't solve everyone's problems, or there'd be no point in living — Jesus has to make himself matter on his own. A beam of light splits the stage and God appears: a short-legged chimera of squirrel, elephant, cat, and hippopotamus with an extendable reptilian tongue. He'll answer exactly one question before returning in the year 4000. Stan seizes it and asks why he never got his period. God's answer: boys don't get periods — Cartman and Kenny have the colon infection, and Kyle lied. The crowd, furious that Stan wasted the one question, attacks him as he tries to calm them by singing 'Auld Lang Syne' in his new deep voice.

Featured characters: Stan Marsh, Kyle Broflovski, Eric Cartman, Kenny McCormick, Jesus, God, Rod Stewart, Chef, Dr. Mephesto, Ike Broflovski.

Locations: Jesus's house, Heaven, Las Vegas (the Rod Stewart concert), the Marsh and McCormick bathrooms, the boys' 'mature' club.

Key events & continuity: God's first full appearance establishes his bizarre chimera form and his one-question-per-two-millennia policy; Jesus's arc resolves into self-reliance; Stan's hormone-bottle stunt gives him a deep voice and facial hair; Kenny's tampon death is one of his most ignominious.
k: are you there god? it's me, jesus

entries.t:
Mr. Garrison's class is rehearsing for the Four Million Child Blow 2000, the first worldwide recorder concert — relocated from flood-stricken Oklahoma to Arkansas. Garrison panics: his parents live in Arkansas. When Mackey gently asks whether Garrison suffered childhood abuse, Garrison bursts into tears and flees; on the bus, Mackey theorizes Garrison is hiding behind Mr. Hat, the puppet insults him ('Monkeys make better counselors!'), and the two brawl in the aisle until the puppet wins. On the road, Cartman hunts for the legendary 'brown noise' — a tone tested in World War II that supposedly makes anyone who hears it lose bowel control — using Kenny as his test subject. Stan and Kyle are preoccupied with revenge on some New York third-graders who mocked them as rednecks and 'queefs'; their counter-prank word, 'mung,' backfires when the New Yorkers reveal it's a real word. Garrison visits his parents and tearfully confesses the truth: his father never molested him — he's upset precisely because he wasn't abused, and doesn't know how far a parent should go for a child. His father, at a loss, asks bar buddies for advice and gets only jokes. That night someone slips into Garrison's bedroom and sleeps with him; he assumes it was his father and leaves happy — it was actually Kenny G, secretly hired by Garrison Senior. Meanwhile Cartman finds the brown noise and proves it on Kenny, who soils himself. The boys slip the note into the New Yorkers' sheet music, but an organizer mistakes it for a Yoko Ono revision and distributes it to all four million players. At the concert the boys watch in horror as the entire world plays the brown note at once — the planet suffers a simultaneous bowel catastrophe, and Kenny dies from defecating too hard. Only the New Yorkers learn the truth, and they admit the boys are pretty cool after all. On the bus home, Mackey finally explains what 'queef' means as Garrison gives Ms. Crabtree directions.

Featured characters: Stan Marsh, Kyle Broflovski, Eric Cartman, Kenny McCormick, Mr. Garrison and Mr. Hat, Mr. Mackey, Garrison Senior, Yoko Ono, Kenny G, the New York third-graders.

Locations: South Park Elementary, the bus to Arkansas, the hotel, the Garrison family home, the recorder concert stadium.

Key events & continuity: the brown noise becomes one of the show's most infamous gags; Garrison's abuse-that-never-happened is played as genuine anguish; Kenny G's secret gig is the episode's quiet punchline; the New Yorkers' respect is hard-won.

The Tooth Fairy leaves Cartman two dollars for a lost tooth, and he unveils his master plan: pool everyone's lost teeth, cash in big, and buy a Sega Dreamcast. Stan and Kyle are out of baby teeth, but Kenny isn't — and Butters has a loose one he's saving. Cartman tries having Timmy yank a tooth from Kenny with a string tied to his wheelchair, then simply steals Butters's tooth while disguised as the Tooth Fairy and plants it under his own pillow. Liane, alarmed by the tooth count, calls the dentist and finally confesses there's no Tooth Fairy; Kyle spirals into questioning his own existence while Stan decides the Dreamcast scheme can still work. They plant a tooth under a rich kid's pillow and walk straight into a professional tooth-stealing ring, whose boss — a kid kingpin named Loogie — runs a full black-market operation: crews plant teeth under pillows, leave notes for parents, then circle back to collect the cash. The boys' options are a two-percent cut or having their penises cut off; they take the two percent. The American Dental Association notices the missing teeth and money; its leader, Dr. Roberts, concludes the culprit is a giant half-chicken, half-squirrel building a nest for its genetically superior offspring — a creature with at least a mild grasp of algebra. Only Tom Foley suspects a black-market tooth racket, citing a Montreal precedent; the others laugh that Montreal is fictional. Foley sets a trap with a fake news report about a sick boy named Billy Circlovich who lost a tooth; Cartman and Loogie walk into it and are caught. Meanwhile Kyle, mid-existential-crisis, vanishes and reappears able to warp reality, terrifying the police, the dentists, and Loogie's gang into retreat. Loogie declares the fall of his empire a blessing and shuts the racket down; the real Billy finds Tooth Fairy money under his pillow after all. Cartman, greedy to the end, tries to break Kenny out of a shallow river Loogie dumped him in — and Kenny hops his way into a deep spot and drowns as Timmy rolls by on the bridge.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman, Stan Marsh, Kyle Broflovski, Kenny McCormick, Butters Stotch, Timmy, Loogie, Liane Cartman, Dr. Roberts, Tom Foley, Billy Circlovich.

Locations: Cartman's house, the rich kid's bedroom, Loogie's headquarters, the ADA meeting, the river.

Key events & continuity: Loogie's tooth empire rises and falls in one night; Kyle's reality-warping existential crisis is played straight; the half-chicken half-squirrel becomes ADA canon; Kenny's drowning is witnessed only by Timmy.

The boys challenge the girls to a sled race down Phil Collins Hill. When Tolkien teases Cartman about his weight one too many times, Cartman hurls a rock — Kyle ducks behind the insult ('fat ass'), the rock hits Tolkien, and Tolkien gets a black eye. Mackey assigns two weeks' detention, but two FBI agents intervene: because the victim is Black, the rock-throwing is automatically a hate crime. At the trial of the century, the media brands Cartman a monster; he's convicted and sentenced to Alamosa Maximum Security Juvenile Hall until age twenty-one, as a warning to racists everywhere. Cartman flees to Kenny's, and they attempt an escape to Mexico in Kenny's battery-powered Go-Go-Action Bronco — it crawls past a police barricade and dies at the border. In juvie, Cartman cells with Romper Stomper and strikes a deal: smuggled cigarettes for an escape plan. The boys, meanwhile, replace Cartman first with Clyde (the second-fattest kid, not heavy enough), then with a stack of bricks — which spins out and crushes Kenny. Their rescue plan (a nail file baked in a cake) fails because inmates can't take food to their cells; the cigarettes get through only via Cartman's rectum, which he then flushes by reflex, voiding the deal. Kyle and Stan visit Tolkien's father and learn only the governor can pardon Cartman, so the three boys prepare a presentation arguing hate-crime laws are hypocritical — all crimes are hate crimes, and harsher punishment for intergroup offenses is itself discrimination. The governor is persuaded and pardons him. Romper Stomper, moved by Cartman's tears, helps him escape anyway — for the chance to see Disneyland — but they're recaptured mid-flight, only to learn Cartman's already free. Romper Stomper gifts him his trademark yellow walking buckets. Cartman makes the sled race just in time, trips the girls' sled with the buckets (their sled goes off a cliff; Lizzy is carried off by a bear), and the boys win. They swear never to exploit Cartman's rear again; he swears never to take them for granted. Minutes later, Pip calls his backside fat, Cartman rocks him in the face — and walks free, because injuring British people doesn't count as a hate crime. He visits Romper Stomper and, off-screen, craps out Disneyland for him.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman, Stan Marsh, Kyle Broflovski, Kenny McCormick, Tolkien Black, Romper Stomper, Clyde, the governor, the FBI agents, Pip.

Locations: Phil Collins Hill, the courtroom, the Mexican border, Alamosa Juvenile Hall, Tolkien's house.

Key events & continuity: Cartman's hate-crime conviction and pardon satirize the whole legal concept; Romper Stomper's buckets win the sled race; Kenny is crushed by the brick-sled; the closing Pip loophole ('British doesn't count') is pure Cartman.

A new student joins the class: Timmy, a disabled boy in a wheelchair whose entire vocabulary is his own name, assorted noises, and 'LIVIN' A LIE!' Garrison and Principal Victoria ignore the obvious; Mackey suggests ADD, a doctor rubber-stamps the diagnosis in seconds, and Timmy is excused from all homework. Every other kid promptly claims ADD too, and the whole class is prescribed Ritalin. Freed from schoolwork, Timmy is discovered by Skyler's band, the Lords of the Underworld, and installed as lead singer; his antics make them an overnight sensation. Phil Collins — booked to headline the Lalapalalapaza festival with Timmy's band opening — is outraged at being upstaged by what he sees as exploitation, and when Timmy's band takes his headliner slot, he schemes to break them up. Meanwhile the Ritalin turns the other boys into placid zombies (Cartman hallucinates pink Christina Aguilera monsters), and soon the parents are all dosing themselves too; only Chef and the pharmacists remain undrugged. Collins plays on Skyler's ego, convincing him Timmy is stealing his spotlight; Skyler quits for a solo project, 'Reach for the Skyler,' the band is dropped from the festival, and Collins reclaims his slot. Chef tries to warn the parents about alternatives to medication, but they're too sedated to listen, so he confronts the doctor and pharmacists directly. Horrified to learn they're responsible for the town's Collins fandom, the adults cook up 'Ritalout' — an antidote mixed into free lemonade from Mr. Derp's stand at the festival. It works: the crowd sobers up, boos Collins off the stage, and chants for Timmy. The band reunites with Skyler, and Timmy himself announces them as 'Timmy and the Lords of the Underworld' — to Skyler's delight — while Timmy's parents, Richard and Helen Burch (who share his exact condition and vocabulary), groove in the crowd.

Featured characters: Timmy Burch, Stan Marsh, Kyle Broflovski, Eric Cartman, Kenny McCormick, Phil Collins, Skyler, Chef, Mr. Garrison, Mr. Derp, Richard and Helen Burch.

Locations: South Park Elementary, the Lalapalalapaza festival grounds, Mr. Derp's lemonade stand, the pharmacy.

Key events & continuity: Timmy's debut as a series regular; the Ritalin epidemic satirizes over-diagnosis; Phil Collins is established as Timmy's nemesis; the band's name becomes 'Timmy and the Lords of the Underworld' by Timmy's own declaration.

After watching the French-Canadian Cirque Du Cheville, the boys form their own circus, inspired by its stars: five contorting eight-year-old quintuplets from Romania. The quintuplets, fleeing the Romanian government with their grandmother, turn up at the Marsh house begging for shelter. That night, Grandpa Marvin Marsh and the quintuplets' grandmother get together — and she dies in the act. Randy breaks the news, and Stan, Cartman, and Kyle persuade him to let the girls stay so they can build the circus around them, planning a contortion act performed in underpants. They set out to sell the girls on America's greatness while the Romanian government enlists Janet Reno to retrieve them. Kenny, meanwhile, decides he needs opera training in Romania: he busks Verdi's 'La donna è mobile' for travel money, becomes a sensation in Romania, and — once his mother realizes their few American dollars make them rich there — stays for good. Back home, protesters surround the Marsh house demanding the quintuplets stay; in a parody of the Elián González case, Reno storms in dressed as the Easter Bunny, gun drawn, and seizes the girls. The boys rally the protesters, a street battle erupts with government troops — and the quintuplets themselves stop it, lecturing every faction: America only wants them for money, Reno for publicity, Romania for prestige, their father (who abandoned them five years ago) for show, and the boys for their ignorant circus and cultural arrogance. They leave South Park for Oprah and a press tour. In the mirror-image ending, Romanian protesters demand Kenny stay, American soldiers raid the house to bring him home, and Kenny is accidentally killed by his own government.

Featured characters: Stan Marsh, Kyle Broflovski, Eric Cartman, Kenny McCormick, the Romanian quintuplets, Grandpa Marvin Marsh, Randy Marsh, Janet Reno, Carol McCormick.

Locations: the Marsh home, the circus practice space, Romania, the protest line, the Oprah-bound road.

Key events & continuity: the Elián González parody structures the whole custody battle; Kenny's Romanian opera fame is his most glamorous arc — ended by friendly fire; the quintuplets' lecture indicts every side equally; Kenny's mother chooses to stay in Romania.

Convinced he's too mature for Stan, Kyle, and Kenny, Cartman goes online seeking older male friends and wanders into a chat room for 'Men Who Like Young Boys,' oblivious to what that means. He's flooded with replies from eager predators; the first, 'Tony316,' gives him candy and backrubs at a meeting and is promptly arrested. Cartman assumes Stan and Kyle are sabotaging him. His next contact, 'Mr. Hammerhead,' turns out to be Mr. Garrison — also arrested on the spot. At the police station, the North American Man/Boy Love Association tries to spring the prisoners, claiming there's nothing wrong with loving young boys; Barbrady throws them out. Dr. Mephesto can't genetically engineer adult friends for Cartman, but suggests an organization called NAMBLA that might suit him. Cartman shows up at the South Park Inn, is welcomed as their poster child, and poses for photos in a red thong. Told a banquet will be held in his honor, he's instructed to invite every boy in town — pointedly excluding Stan and Kyle out of spite, which only makes them want in. Meanwhile Kenny is waging his own war: learning his mother is pregnant again, he tries to end it — hurling a ball into his father's groin, spiking Carol's drink with birth-control pills and vodka (Stuart drinks it instead), dragging his parents onto the banned-for-pregnant-women 'John Denver Experience' ride (Carol is fine; Stuart's nose breaks and he empties himself into a trash can), and finally chasing his mother through town with a plunger. The police raid what they think is the predators' meeting — but it's the other NAMBLA, the North American Marlon Brando Look-Alikes, who've been fighting the pedophiles for the name. Both NAMBLAs and the cops converge on the banquet; the boys realize what's happening and flee through hotel rooms, with Cartman volunteering Butters as a sacrificial distraction (Butters wanders into an empty room and escapes). Stuart, searching for Kenny, walks into the wrong room and is mistaken for a boy. It ends with Stuart hospitalized, the predators arrested, their leader's rights-speech shouted down by Stan and Kyle, and Cartman apologizing to his friends — mature enough, he decides, to wait until they grow up. The ambulance carrying Stuart runs Kenny over; Carol gives birth to a baby identical to Kenny, parka and all. Stuart swears it's the fiftieth time this has happened. Carol says it's the fifty-second.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman, Stan Marsh, Kyle Broflovski, Kenny McCormick, Butters Stotch, Stuart and Carol McCormick, Mr. Garrison, Dr. Mephesto, Officer Barbrady, Tony316, both NAMBLA chapters.

Locations: the internet chat room, the docks, the police station, the South Park Inn, North Park Funland, the hospital.

Key events & continuity: the dual-NAMBLA mix-up drives the farce; Kenny dies by ambulance and is immediately 'reborn' as an identical baby — with Stuart and Carol disagreeing on how many times this has happened (50 vs 52); Butters's narrow escape foreshadows his future as the group's victim-in-residence.

With Mr. Garrison fired for soliciting a minor, a substitute takes the class; Stan, Cartman, and Kenny spend the lesson impersonating each other, and Cartman laughs so hard he squirts milk from his nose without drinking any. Kyle is absent — he's in kidney failure. Kyle has had diabetes all along, his kidneys are shutting down, and Sheila is terrified of surgery; Sharon steers her toward the town's new mystic healer, Miss Information, who blames 'mysterious toxins' and prescribes herbal nostrums that only make Kyle worse — while convincing everyone the invisible healing is working. Soon the whole town is buying her remedies, including 'Cherokee hair tampons' sold by two supposed Native Americans who look and sound more Mexican (they're modeled on Cheech and Chong). Meanwhile Garrison reinvents himself as a romance novelist; his novel The Valley of Penises uses the word 'penis' 6,083 times, and he bullies a Harlequin-style publisher into a deal by insisting his audience is women. Stan, distrusting the mystic, consults Dr. Doctor: Kyle needs a transplant, and the only AB-negative match in South Park is Eric Cartman. Cartman names his price: ten million dollars. That night Stan, Kenny, Butters, and Timmy break into Cartman's bedroom to take the kidney themselves — but Cartman, paranoid, is wearing a 'Kidney Blocker 2000,' and Butters steps on the cat Fluffy, blowing their cover. The next day Sheila drags the skeletal, unresponsive Kyle to the 'Native Americans' for a personal appointment; one look at the dying boy cracks them — they confess they're actually Mexican, hired to play Indians because, as Miss Information put it, nobody would buy medicine from Mexicans. The town realizes Miss Information is a con artist and beats her to death on the spot. Stan tells Sheila not to worry about the kidney: he has a plan. Cartman wakes to find his Kidney Blocker removed and his sheets soaked in red liquid; he storms to Stan's, demands his kidney back, and marches on the hospital insisting the doctor reimplant it. The doctor agrees — after Cartman signs a release form. In recovery, Kyle is himself again, Cartman wakes furious at being tricked into saving Kyle's life — until Kyle laughs and squirts milk from his nose, exactly like Cartman. Satisfied, Cartman declares: 'Oh, good. You got the crappy kidney.' The twist: Liane opened the Kidney Blocker herself, and the red liquid was ketchup Stan planted — the whole thing was a ruse to get Cartman's signature.

Featured characters: Kyle Broflovski, Stan Marsh, Eric Cartman, Kenny McCormick, Butters Stotch, Timmy, Sheila and Gerald Broflovski, Sharon Marsh, Miss Information, the fake medicine men, Mr. Garrison, Dr. Doctor, Liane Cartman, Fluffy.

Locations: South Park Elementary, Miss Information's shop, Cartman's bedroom, the hospital.

Key events & continuity: Kyle's diabetes and kidney transplant become permanent canon; Cartman is tricked into donating via the ketchup ruse; Miss Information is beaten to death by her own customers; Garrison's 6,083-penis novel launches his writing career; Kyle inheriting Cartman's milk-squirt is the final insult.

Chef and Jimbo are shouting at each other in the mayor's office over the South Park town flag — and when the mayor unfurls it, Chef's fury is clear: it depicts four white figures hanging a black figure from a gallows, cheering. Jimbo insists it's historic and must stay. The third-grade class is assigned the flag debate: Stan, Kyle, and Kenny research the keep side with Jimbo, while Wendy, Bebe, Clyde, and Butters join Chef's change side. At lunch, Stan and Kyle discover Chef has converted to Islam and renamed himself Abdul Mohammed Jabar Rauf Kareem Ali; when they say they're arguing to keep the flag, he erupts. Wendy's team is making progress in the library until Cartman hijacks their strategy: forget arguments, dig up dirt on Stan and Kyle and win with ad hominem attacks. Then the local Ku Klux Klan chapter endorses the keep side as a symbol of white power — horrifying Jimbo, Ned, and the other keepers, who want nothing to do with them. Jimbo and Ned infiltrate a Klan meeting in disguise and persuade the leader to switch sides to the change camp, reasoning the keep side will collapse rather than stand with the Klan; slipping out, they're spotted in their robes by Chef, who walks away without a word. The mayor tries a compromise — the hanged man is redrawn smiling serenely — but Chef storms out anyway, and the mayor dumps the whole decision on the kids. Meanwhile Wendy develops a genuine, tormenting crush on Cartman; Bebe diagnoses sexual tension and advises her to kiss him and get it over with. Mid-speech, Wendy does — Stan looks on appalled — then argues that society must change with the times. The twist: Stan and Kyle's side never noticed the race angle at all; they thought the debate was about capital punishment. Moved, the town reaches a compromise: the flag now shows people of all races — including another black man — happily hanging the black figure together, holding hands. Chef closes with the moral: his anti-racism nearly turned him racist, and seeing everything through race only breeds more racism. Wendy tells Cartman her feelings are gone and runs back to Stan, leaving Cartman alone and dejected — he was starting to feel it too.

Featured characters: Chef, Jimbo Kern, Ned Gerblansky, Stan Marsh, Kyle Broflovski, Kenny McCormick, Wendy Testaburger, Eric Cartman, Bebe Stevens, Mayor McDaniels, the Ku Klux Klan.

Locations: the mayor's office, South Park Elementary (library), the Klan meeting, City Hall.

Key events & continuity: the flag is redesigned as a multiracial hanging; Chef's conversion and new name; Wendy and Cartman's brief, genuine mutual attraction — the only time it ever happens; Jimbo and Ned's Klan infiltration; the capital-punishment misunderstanding deflates the entire debate.

entries.n: S04E08 — Something You Can Do with Your Finger
entries.t:
Cartman wakes from a vivid dream in which he, Stan, Kyle and Kenny have become the biggest boy band in America, adored by screaming fans and rolling in ten million dollars. Convinced the dream was a message from God, he drafts the others into a group he names Fingerbang. Kyle points out that every major boy band has five members, so they hold auditions for a fifth singer. Butters tries out with a nursery rhyme about a bunny and gets rejected over his intonation; Ike's attempt ends with him flipping Cartman off. The standout is Wendy, whose audition song is startlingly explicit and clearly the best of the bunch. Cartman objects to a girl in a boy band on the grounds that everyone will notice her chest, but he is outvoted, and Wendy joins on the condition that she dress like a boy. Meanwhile Randy forbids Stan from participating, flying into an inexplicable rage at the mere mention of the band. The boys' big break comes when they land a gig performing at the South Park mall, and their signature move turns out to be giving the audience the finger — literally flipping everyone off in unison, which the crowd reads as the band's edgy trademark. Mid-show, Randy's strange behavior is explained: he was once in a boy band himself, and the whole fiasco stirs up old humiliations. The performance collapses the way only a Cartman-managed enterprise can, but the dream of the ten million dollars does not die — his pursuit of that fortune becomes a running scheme across the episodes that follow.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman, founder, manager and self-appointed star of Fingerbang, driven by the dream of $10 million and fame; Stan Marsh, Kyle Broflovski and Kenny McCormick, the reluctant bandmates; Wendy Testaburger, the fifth member, recruited for her voice and made to cross-dress; Randy Marsh, mysteriously hostile to the whole project; Butters Stotch and Ike Broflovski, the failed auditionees.

Locations: the audition space where the boys hold tryouts; the South Park mall, where Fingerbang performs its one show; the Marsh residence, scene of Randy's outburst.

Key events & continuity: Fingerbang is founded and plays its one disastrous mall show; Randy's past as a boy-band member is revealed, explaining his hostility; Cartman's $10 million dream becomes a recurring motivation in the episodes that follow.
k: something you can do with your finger

entries.n: S04E09 — Do the Handicapped Go to Hell?
entries.t:
After Father Maxi warns Stan, Cartman and Kenny that neglecting their faith will damn them, the boys start attending Sunday school with Sister Anne, where lessons on communion and confession leave them thoroughly confused — they walk away convinced Jesus was made of crackers and that snacking on wafers is a ticket out of Hell. During first confessions, Cartman swears that God's own arm reached out of the confessional and shook him; in reality it was Father Maxi, furious after learning which parishioner had tormented him in the past. The real crisis hits when the boys realize Kyle cannot confess because he is Jewish and Timmy cannot confess because his disability limits him to saying his own name. Father Maxi declares flatly that both boys are Hell-bound, which sends the gang into a panic. Their solution is to baptize Kyle, Ike and Timmy themselves. The plan derails when Cartman lets slip a swear word, prompting a frantic dash back to the confessional — and on the way across the street, Kenny is flattened by a bus bound for Mexico. In the fallout, Cartman reinvents himself as a fire-and-brimstone preacher to the town's children, building a congregation of terrified kids and launching the storyline that continues in the next episode.

Featured characters: Stan Marsh, Eric Cartman and Kenny McCormick, the frightened Sunday schoolers; Father Maxi, dispenser of damnation; Sister Anne, the Sunday school teacher; Kyle Broflovski, Ike Broflovski and Timmy Burch, the would-be damned.

Locations: the South Park church and its Sunday school classroom; the confessional; the street where Kenny meets the Mexico-bound bus.

Key events & continuity: Kenny is killed by the bus, and his soul's journey continues in 'Probably'; Cartman founds his own kid-sized ministry, setting up the two-part Hell saga; Father Maxi's hardline damnation theology is established, as is Timmy's limited speech as a plot driver.
k: do the handicapped go to hell?

entries.t:
The children of South Park have gone full revival: they have built Cartman a church, stopped going to school, avoid going home, and hang on every word of his televangelist-style sermons about sin. Parental countermeasures — guilt trips, bribes from Cartman's own mother — only feed his zeal. Meanwhile Kenny phones in from Ensenada, where the Mexico-bound bus dragged his body; convinced he has landed in Hell, he reports back his findings for Cartman's sermons: everyone speaks Spanish, the water makes you bleed from the rear for seven hours, and every trinket shop sells the same trinkets. In the actual Hell, Satan is tangled in a love triangle between the abusive Saddam Hussein and the gentle Chris, who keep murdering each other and popping right back. On the advice of JonBenet Ramsey, Satan takes his romantic dilemma to God — who resides in a Heaven populated entirely by Mormons — and gets told bluntly that his problem is codependency: he should spend time alone instead of bouncing between a cruel lover and a kind one. Back on Earth, Cartman finally reads the Bible closely enough to realize his own rap sheet damns him too, and the children's crusade collapses as everyone trudges home.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman, the child preacher; Stan Marsh and Kyle Broflovski; Kenny McCormick, reporting from 'Hell'; Satan, Saddam Hussein and Chris, the feuding love triangle; God; JonBenet Ramsey as a celestial advice columnist.

Locations: the children's makeshift church; Ensenada, Mexico; Hell; Heaven.

Key events & continuity: concludes the two-part Hell storyline begun in 'Do the Handicapped Go to Hell?'; Satan dumps both lovers on God's advice and resolves to be independent; Kenny's death is treated as semi-permanent, keeping him out of the cast for a stretch of season five; God is established as presiding over a Mormon-only Heaven.

The boys start fourth grade determined to dominate their new teacher, a woman from Denver they have never met. Stan's master plan: at 8:35 sharp, the whole class stands on their desks, drops their pants, and yells for the teacher to kiss their asses. Their teacher turns out to be Ms. Choksondik, a middle-aged woman with spectacularly saggy breasts she seems not to notice, whose name sounds exactly like 'chokes on dick' — a fact every adult hears but no child does; the kids invent their own nicknames like 'makes me sick' instead. When the moment comes, only Cartman follows through, mooning the class solo while the others freeze. Fourth grade proves miserable — harder work, a scarier teacher — and Cartman convinces the gang they took third grade's easiness for granted. Their fix: hire two Star Trek-obsessed nerds to build a time machine out of Timmy's wheelchair and go back a year. Meanwhile the teachers' lounge reveals the faculty cannot stand Choksondik either. The time-machine scheme fizzles — the nerds' contraption cannot actually send anyone into the past — and the boys are stuck accepting that fourth grade is their life now, with Choksondik as their permanent teacher.

Featured characters: Stan Marsh, Kyle Broflovski, Eric Cartman and Kenny McCormick; Ms. Choksondik, debuting as their new teacher; Timmy Burch, unwilling wheelchair donor; the two Star Trek nerds.

Locations: the South Park Elementary fourth-grade classroom; the teachers' lounge.

Key events & continuity: the boys permanently move into fourth grade and Choksondik becomes their teacher for the season; Timmy's wheelchair is established as endlessly repurposable technology; the class's failure to hear Choksondik's name becomes a running gag.

Kyle brings a Dawson's Creek Trapper Keeper to school and Cartman immediately one-ups him with the Dawson's Creek Trapper Keeper Ultra Keeper Futura S 2000, a binder so advanced it might as well be alien technology. A stranger calling himself Bill Cosby tries to steal it, gets caught by Officer Barbrady, and confesses the truth: he is BSM-471, a cyborg from the future, and Cartman's binder is destined to conquer the world and wipe out humanity. He destroys the binder — but Cartman simply buys another one, which by the rules of time travel is the actual world-ending unit, and Cartman refuses to let anyone destroy his property. The binder begins absorbing everything around it and fusing with Cartman into a growing technological monstrosity. Parallel to this, the demoted Mr. Garrison oversees a kindergarten class-president election between Ike and a boy named Filmore. The vote ties, the tiebreaker falls to an agonizingly indecisive girl named Flora, and the recounts spiral until Rosie O'Donnell shows up protesting on her nephew's behalf — a pint-sized parody of the 2000 Florida recount. In the end the keeper-blob is stopped and the election resolves, with Cartman learning nothing.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman and Kyle Broflovski, binder rivals; Stan Marsh and Kenny McCormick; BSM-471, the cyborg posing as 'Bill Cosby'; Officer Barbrady; Mr. Garrison; Ike Broflovski, Filmore and Flora; Rosie O'Donnell.

Locations: South Park Elementary; the kindergarten classroom; the town itself as the keeper-blob grows.

Key events & continuity: parodies the 2000 U.S. presidential election recount through the kindergarten vote; Garrison's demotion to kindergarten teacher continues; the Trapper Keeper becomes a world-threatening entity before being destroyed.

The fourth grade is staging a play about Helen Keller when Butters bursts in with alarming news: the kindergarteners' play is incredible, and the older kids will be humiliated unless they outdo the tiny tots. The class decides to juice up their show by replacing Keller's dog with a trick-performing turkey to make it more Thanksgiving-y. Cartman dispatches Kyle and Timmy to procure a turkey; they return with a crippled one — Gobbles — because Timmy adores him and the bird would otherwise have been shot. Cartman wants the defective turkey gone, and the hired animal trainer agrees, so Cartman rigs a spotlight to 'accidentally' crush the bird — and kills Kenny instead. The trainer then cons Timmy into releasing Gobbles into the wild with a lie about the shelter experimenting on him; the turkey is promptly shipped to a processing plant, where his handicap saves him — he cannot lift his head into the chopper — and he is dumped outside, where Jimbo and his hunting buddies spot him. On opening night the play goes on, Gobbles and all, with Timmy racing to save his bird and the fourth graders desperate to top the kindergarteners' show.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman, Kyle Broflovski, Timmy Burch and Butters Stotch; Kenny McCormick, the spotlight victim; Gobbles the crippled turkey; the turkey trainer; Jimbo Kern and Ned Gerblanski.

Locations: the school auditorium; the turkey farm and processing plant; the woods where Gobbles is spotted.

Key events & continuity: Kenny dies by rigged spotlight; Gobbles survives through sheer disability; the fourth-grade versus kindergarten rivalry drives the plot; Timmy's compassion for the crippled turkey mirrors his own experience.

Narrated by Malcolm McDowell as a tribute to English literature, this is the tale of Pip Pirrip, South Park's resident polite British kid, retold through Dickens' Great Expectations. Orphaned Pip visits his parents' graves and is ambushed by an escaped convict, whom he helps out of sheer kindness — sharing his sandwich and cutting the man's handcuffs. Back home, Joe reads aloud an advertisement: Miss Havisham seeks a boy to play with her daughter Estella. Pip goes, endures Estella's constant insults, and slowly wins her over until she treats him kindly and even lets him kiss her; he falls hard, convinced a commoner like him could never marry her. Then a mysterious benefactor offers to send Pip to London to be raised as a gentleman. Sure it is Miss Havisham, Pip accepts. In London his roommate Mr. Pocket tells him Havisham's history: a rich girl left at the altar who stopped every clock in her house and rotted in her wedding dress. The truth proves darker — Havisham has been grooming Estella to break men's hearts as revenge on the world, and Pip is her chosen victim. In the end it is the escaped convict — Pip's true secret benefactor, grateful for the long-ago sandwich — who helps Pip see through the scheme, and Pip walks away from the gilded trap toward an honest life.

Featured characters: Pip Pirrip; Miss Havisham; Estella Havisham; Joe; Mr. Pocket; the escaped convict.

Locations: Pip's village and home; Miss Havisham's decaying mansion; London.

Key events & continuity: a rare Pip-centric episode with the main boys entirely absent; Miss Havisham's heartbreak-revenge plot is exposed; the convict is revealed as Pip's true benefactor; Pip rejects the gentleman's life.

Cartman stays home from school claiming illness and walks straight into an intervention: his mother, family and friends have had it with his weight. His usual 'big-boned' defense collapses when his mom admits the stories about heavy relatives were lies — he is just fat — and he is shipped off to fat camp. At school, Ms. Choksondik's biology class is supposed to dissect frogs, but a mix-up delivers manatees instead while the frogs go to the aquarium. Kyle pays Kenny to eat a dead manatee's spleen; Kenny promptly vomits it back up, and then Stan, Butters, Tolkien and others start paying him to eat the vomit back up. The boys realize Kenny will ingest anything for cash and smell a business opportunity. Meanwhile Cartman keeps trying to break out of fat camp, but every escape attempt ends the same way: the ice-cream truck he flags down is actually the camp's escapee round-up truck, and he is hauled right back. Back home, Kenny's stomach-for-hire act snowballs toward reality-TV stardom, while Cartman schemes to keep eating junk food behind the counselors' backs and sabotages his own weight loss.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman; Kenny McCormick, the paid vomit-eater turned TV prospect; Stan Marsh, Kyle Broflovski, Butters Stotch and Tolkien Black; Liane Cartman; Ms. Choksondik; the fat-camp counselors.

Locations: the Cartman home, scene of the intervention; South Park Elementary, site of the manatee dissection; the fat camp; the ice-cream round-up truck.

Key events & continuity: Cartman's 'big-boned' myth is definitively debunked by his own mother; Kenny's willingness to eat anything for money becomes a business and a TV opportunity; Cartman undermines his own diet at every turn.

Cartman has four tickets to the Raging Pussies concert and the boys all want to go, but Kyle's parents forbid it as dangerous and vile. After relentless negotiating, Kyle's mom sarcastically says he can go if he cleans the garage, shovels the driveway and brings democracy to Cuba — all of which Kyle actually accomplishes. His parents still refuse. Furious, Kyle wishes he had no parents at all, and Cartman suggests a trick he once used on his mom's ex-boyfriend: call the police and claim his parents 'molestered' him with 'bad touch.' After rehearsing the accusation, Kyle makes the call and his parents are arrested. The boys hit the concert, Kyle throws a parent-free party and dances in his underwear — and seeing that freedom, every kid in town starts phoning the police on their parents and teachers. Soon South Park is entirely adult-free, and the children split into two rival city-states: one side builds a gleaming utopia while Cartman's faction descends into a feral, Mad Max-style wasteland. Even Shelly gets arrested after attacking Stan mid-celebration. When the kids finally tire of ruling themselves and the parents return, the town has to reckon with what the children did — and the parents, bizarrely, end up more traumatized than the kids.

Featured characters: Kyle Broflovski, whose false accusation starts it all; Eric Cartman, Stan Marsh and Kenny McCormick; Gerald and Sheila Broflovski; Shelly Marsh; the South Park police.

Locations: the Broflovski home; the Raging Pussies concert; the divided, adult-free South Park — Cartman's wasteland versus the other children's city.

Key events & continuity: the entire adult population of South Park is jailed, leaving the kids to split the town into two rival factions; Kyle's 'molestation' phone call becomes the episode's infamous inciting incident; order is restored by the end with the parents returning.

When Mr. Hankey fails to appear even for Hanukkah, Kyle leads Stan, Cartman and Kenny into the sewers to find him. They discover the Christmas Poo moping over family troubles: his dissatisfied wife Autumn and their three little nuggets — Cornwallis, Amber and Simon. Nobody in town seems to have Christmas spirit anymore, and the boys' attempt at sidewalk caroling is totally ignored. While lamenting the lack of presents, Cornwallis sinks into an existential depression about being a mere piece of poo. Watching a Peanuts Christmas special gives the boys an idea: they will make their own animated short with cut-out animation and screen it at the drive-in to revive the town's spirit, with Mayor McDaniels backing the project out of economic worry. Meanwhile Mr. Hankey comforts Cornwallis with 'Circle of Poo,' a parody of 'Circle of Life' explaining how poo is the lifeblood of the planet, climaxing with Hankey holding his son aloft over a cliff. The boys' crude cartoon premieres to the townspeople and actually works — Christmas spirit returns to South Park, and the Hankey family finds its footing.

Featured characters: Mr. Hankey; Kyle Broflovski, Stan Marsh, Eric Cartman and Kenny McCormick; Autumn, Cornwallis, Amber and Simon Hankey; Mayor McDaniels.

Locations: the South Park sewers, the Hankey family home; the town sidewalks; the drive-in theater.

Key events & continuity: Mr. Hankey's family is introduced — wife Autumn and children Cornwallis, Amber and Simon; Cornwallis's existential crisis is resolved through the 'Circle of Poo'; the boys' homemade cartoon saves Christmas, cementing their annual holiday-special tradition.

Cartman announces earth-shaking news at the bus stop: the word 'shit' is going to be said uncensored on the TV show Cop Drama tonight. The whole town tunes in, and when the word finally airs, South Park erupts in celebration — everyone except Kyle, who finds the hype idiotic and storms outside only to find it raining frogs. The next morning the news covers both the Cop Drama phenomenon and a mysterious virus making people vomit their intestines. At school the kids are taught the acceptable verbal forms of the word, and Cartman treats it as a thrilling new discovery while Kyle fumes that it is the same old word and vows to prove it via the encyclopedia. Mr. Garrison even teaches the kindergartners to say it and sing with it. The overuse of the word begins warping reality — plagues, dead wildlife, general calamity — until the town realizes the word has lost all meaning through repetition. Order is restored when everyone agrees the word is just a word, and the world goes back to normal, with the townspeople having learned nothing.

Featured characters: Stan Marsh, Kyle Broflovski, Eric Cartman and Kenny McCormick; Butters Stotch; Mr. Garrison; the Cop Drama cast.

Locations: the bus stop; the town's living rooms and the local bar, where everyone watches Cop Drama; South Park Elementary.

Key events & continuity: the word 'shit' is said uncensored 162 times, a broadcast milestone for the show; Kyle's encyclopedia crusade establishes him as the voice of reason against mass hysteria; reality itself destabilizes from the word's overuse, then resets.

The boys join the Mountain Scouts and discover their scoutmaster is Big Gay Al — which sends some parents into a panic over his homosexuality, and Al is promptly fired from the organization he has loved his whole life. The Scouts are branded a hate group in the media and celebrity supporters pull out. His replacement, Mr. Grazier, turns out to be an actual predator photographing the scouts and threatening them into silence. Meanwhile a new handicapped kid, Jimmy Valmer, arrives in town and joins the Scouts. Jimmy is a stand-up comedian who becomes instantly beloved, which drives Timmy wild with jealousy. Timmy tries to sabotage the new kid — even gifting him an orange parka to make him look like Kenny — but nothing works, and the parka fails to attract Kenny's usual fatal misfortune despite several near misses. The rivalry comes to a head in an epic, over-the-top brawl between Timmy and Jimmy. In the end the boys expose the real predator scoutmaster, Big Gay Al is vindicated, and Timmy and Jimmy settle into an uneasy coexistence as South Park's two disabled kids.

Featured characters: Timmy Burch and Jimmy Valmer, debuting Jimmy, in their jealousy-fueled rivalry; Big Gay Al; Stan Marsh, Eric Cartman and Kenny McCormick; Mr. Grazier, the predatory replacement scoutmaster.

Locations: the Mountain Scouts meeting hall; the South Park outdoors where the brawl erupts.

Key events & continuity: Jimmy Valmer debuts and becomes a permanent cast member; Timmy's jealousy of Jimmy establishes their long-running frenemy dynamic; Big Gay Al is fired and then vindicated when the true predator is exposed.

The street magician David Blaine comes to South Park, and his feats dazzle the boys into signing up for his $69.95 'camp' — which is actually a front for a cult, the Blaintologists, who worship Blaine as a messianic figure and call his tricks miracles. Stan joins but quickly gets creeped out and wants out; when Kyle refuses to leave and says they cannot be friends if Stan rejects his new religion, Stan walks away alone. After nearly being run over by cultists, Stan turns to the one higher power he knows personally: South Park's own resident messiah, Jesus. At Blaine's massive Denver show, packed with Blaintologists, Jesus shows up to challenge him, countering Blaine's illusions with the genuine miracle of the loaves and fishes. Stan calls upon the Super Best Friends — Jesus's superhero team of religious figures including Buddha, Moses, Joseph Smith, Krishna, Laozi, Muhammad and Sea Man — to stop Blaine's plan, which turns out to be a mass suicide pact. The team defeats Blaine, the cult collapses, and Stan and Kyle reconcile.

Featured characters: Stan Marsh and Kyle Broflovski; David Blaine, the cult-leading magician; Jesus Christ; the Super Best Friends — Buddha, Moses, Joseph Smith, Krishna, Laozi, Muhammad and Sea Man.

Locations: the streets of South Park where Blaine performs; the Blaintologist camp; the Denver arena hosting Blaine's big show.

Key events & continuity: the Super Best Friends debut as a team; David Blaine's cult and its mass suicide plot are thwarted; Stan and Kyle's friendship survives a religious split.

Cartman brags that he has hit puberty first — he has his first pubes. The catch: he bought them from the older bully Scott Tenorman for ten dollars. Once Stan and Kyle explain that real pubes are grown, not purchased, Cartman tries every angle to get his money back, but Scott outsmarts him at every turn — costing him another $6.12, ruining a movie outing, and sending him on a wild trip to Fort Collins for a nonexistent pube fair. Kyle advises him to accept defeat since Scott is simply smarter, but Cartman will not let it go. After Scott makes Cartman dance like a pig and then burns the money in front of him, Cartman snaps and vows revenge. His schemes escalate: he trains a pony to bite off Scott's penis, enlists Jimbo and Ned to exploit Scott's weaknesses, and finally hatches a master plan involving a chili cook-off. At the cook-off, Cartman reveals the truth: he had Scott's parents killed by a farmer, ground into chili, and fed to Scott — who weeps as Cartman licks his tears. It is Cartman's most depraved victory, and the moment he crosses a line from bully to monster.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman; Scott Tenorman, the red-haired ninth-grader; Stan Marsh and Kyle Broflovski; Jimbo Kern and Ned Gerblanski; Bill Denkins and his pony.

Locations: South Park and the surrounding county; the road to Fort Collins; the chili cook-off.

Key events & continuity: Cartman murders Scott Tenorman's parents and feeds them to him in chili — the single darkest act of his career and a permanent escalation of his villainy; Scott's weeping defeat becomes iconic; Kyle's warning that Scott is smarter goes unheeded until it is far too late.

entries.n: S05E05 — Terrance and Phillip: Behind the Blow
entries.t:
The boys are desperate to see Terrance and Phillip live at the Denver Coliseum, and Kyle scores tickets. At school, Ms. Choksondik announces that South Park has been chosen to host the national Earth Day Brainwashing Festival, and a trio of environmentalists harangues the class with heavy-handed propaganda. The boys beg off helping with the festival because of the concert, and when that fails, Kyle promises the environmentalists he will get Terrance and Phillip to perform at it — a promise he cannot keep. At the show the boys discover Terrance has gotten enormously fat and is performing with a stand-in who is neither Phillip nor funny. Determined to find the real Phillip, the boys dig into the duo's breakup and learn the split was over creative differences and ego. Through a chaotic series of misadventures the boys manage to reunite the real Terrance and Phillip just in time — and drag them to the Earth Day festival, where the duo's flatulent reunion act horrifies the earnest environmentalists and saves the boys from Kyle's impossible promise. Kyle's bluff works only because the environmentalists are desperate for celebrity star power, and the boys spend the episode scrambling to engineer the impossible reunion before the festival begins.

Featured characters: Stan Marsh, Kyle Broflovski, Eric Cartman and Kenny McCormick; Terrance and Phillip; Ms. Choksondik; the Earth Day environmentalists.

Locations: South Park Elementary; the Denver Coliseum; the Earth Day festival grounds.

Key events & continuity: Terrance and Phillip's breakup and reunion; Kyle's reckless promise to the environmentalists drives the plot; the duo's act remains the boys' cultural touchstone despite the behind-the-scenes mess.
k: terrance and phillip: behind the blow

entries.t:
Cartman's grandmother dies and leaves him one million dollars, and he immediately fulfills his lifelong dream: buying the North Park Funland amusement park and renaming it Cartmanland — a park where he never has to wait in line because no one else is allowed in, especially Stan and Kyle. Business analysts on TV hail the 'you can't come' technique as genius. Hearing of Cartman's fortune, Kyle develops a stress-induced hemorrhoid that grows increasingly sentient as Cartman's wealth grows. When Kyle and Stan try to sneak in over the fence, Kyle pops the hemorrhoid on the wire, the wound gets infected, and he lands in the hospital — where he renounces his faith entirely, and his parents' retelling of the trials of Job only convinces him God is petty. Meanwhile Cartmanland's success forces Cartman to hire a security guard, who refuses to work for free rides; to pay him Cartman must admit paying customers, then more staff, then deal with lawsuits and expenses — and his million evaporates. By the end Cartman has lost everything, Kyle's hemorrhoid bursts and heals, and Kyle's faith is restored by the sheer justice of Cartman's downfall.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman, the amusement park mogul; Kyle Broflovski and his sentient hemorrhoid; Stan Marsh; the Cartmanland security guard.

Locations: North Park Funland, rechristened Cartmanland; the hospital where Kyle wastes away; the TV studios of the business analysts.

Key events & continuity: Cartman inherits and loses a million dollars in one episode; Kyle's crisis of faith — triggered by Cartman's unearned fortune — resolves when that fortune collapses; the sentient hemorrhoid becomes one of the show's most infamous gags.

It starts with the boys' Jennifer Lopez playset and a magnifying glass, then Cartman demonstrates something he learned from the fifth graders: he masturbates Kenny's dog, which the boys mistake for 'milking' it in a game called Red Rocket. Stan, thinking it is cool, performs Red Rocket on his own dog Sparky in front of his parents' dinner guests — the Stotches, Blacks, Tweaks and Tuckers — and is grounded for ten months. His parents cannot explain sex to him, so the town decides the school should teach sex ed earlier. Mr. Mackey instructs the boys while Ms. Choksondik teaches the girls about the horrors of STDs and pregnancy — and both lessons misfire spectacularly. The terrified boys start wearing condoms at all times, even over their clothes, while the girls, convinced by Choksondik's scare tactics, refuse to ever kiss boys again. The gender war escalates until the kids' paranoia burns the school's seriousness down to absurdity, and the parents are forced to admit that outsourcing the talk to the school was the real failure. In the end the boys ditch the condoms and things return to a fragile normal.

Featured characters: Stan Marsh, Kyle Broflovski, Eric Cartman and Kenny McCormick; Mr. Mackey and Ms. Choksondik, the disastrous sex-ed teachers; Sparky and Kenny's dog; the boys' and girls' factions.

Locations: the Marsh home; South Park Elementary classrooms; the schoolyard where the condom panic plays out.

Key events & continuity: the 'Red Rocket' incident becomes a lasting gag; the boys' condom hysteria and the girls' kiss strike parody abstinence-only education; the parents' abdication of the talk is the episode's real target.

Cartman finds a used tampon in Stan's garbage, mistakes it for an aborted fetus, and to shut the kids up Stan's mom buys them the brand-new Okama GameSphere. The boys plan to play it all weekend without sleeping. A talking towel named Towelie keeps materializing to remind them to bring a towel — then asks if they want to get high, and wanders off when they decline. The boys fake sick to skip baseball practice and play through the weekend, but on Monday the GameSphere is gone — confiscated by the government, or so it seems. What follows is a spiraling conspiracy: the boys chase the console through a military operation, Towelie turns out to be a genetically engineered smart towel created by a corporation, and rival factions — the military and the towel's creators — battle over him while the boys just want their game back. Towelie, constantly losing his train of thought and lighting up, proves both useless and indispensable. In the end the boys recover the GameSphere, the conspiracy collapses into farce, and Towelie drifts off to get high, having taught everyone nothing about towels.

Featured characters: Towelie, the forgetful talking towel; Stan Marsh, Kyle Broflovski, Eric Cartman and Kenny McCormick; the military operatives and the corporate scientists fighting over Towelie.

Locations: Stan's house; the baseball field the boys dodge; the military base and corporate lab.

Key events & continuity: Towelie debuts and becomes a recurring character; his catchphrases — towel reminders and 'wanna get high?' — enter the show's permanent vocabulary; the GameSphere weekend establishes the boys' gaming obsession.

entries.n: S05E09 — Osama bin Laden Has Farty Pants
entries.t:
South Park is living in post-9/11 paranoia: gas masks everywhere, anthrax fears, and Stan's mom catatonic on the couch watching cable news for eight weeks straight. At school the kids each donate a dollar for Afghan children at the president's request; Stan, Kyle, Cartman and Kenny's money reaches four Afghan boys who mirror them exactly — Kenny's counterpart even wears a headscarf that muffles his speech. In return the Afghans mail the boys a goat. Unable to keep it, the boys try to send it back, but only military planes are flying — so they sneak the goat onto a base by passing it off as Stevie Nicks arriving for a USO show, and end up flown to Afghanistan themselves. They find their counterparts, who refuse the goat, and the two groups bicker until American soldiers arrive and a firefight breaks out. The boys are captured by Afghan fighters and meet Osama bin Laden himself, portrayed as a gibbering, incompetent loon. In the climax the boys help the Americans, bin Laden is defeated in slapstick fashion, and the Afghan kids — who turn out to like the same crude humor — wave goodbye as the boys fly home, the goat situation somehow resolved.

Featured characters: Stan Marsh, Kyle Broflovski, Eric Cartman and Kenny McCormick; their four Afghan counterparts; Osama bin Laden; the U.S. soldiers; Sharon Marsh.

Locations: paranoid South Park; the military base; Afghanistan.

Key events & continuity: the show's direct response to 9/11, aired less than two months later; the Afghan counterparts mirror the boys beat for beat; bin Laden is depicted as a bumbling coward rather than a mastermind.
k: osama bin laden has farty pants

entries.n: S05E10 — How to Eat with Your Butt
entries.t:
On school picture day, Kenny wears his parka upside down and stands on his head so his rear shows through the hood. Ms. Choksondik declares one boy ruined his picture — and it turns out to be Butters, not Kenny, because that is simply what Butters looks like; neither she nor his parents believe he was not making a face, and he is grounded. Cartman, delighted by the upside-down Kenny photo, takes it to a missing-children center and describes the child as having a 'winking brown eye,' blond hair and rosy cheeks. The photo lands on milk cartons nationwide — and impossibly, a couple named Martha and Stephen Thompson respond: they lost their son years ago and are convinced the butt-photo is him. The catch: the Thompsons suffer from a fictional condition that makes their buttocks appear where their faces should be, and vice versa. Cartman's prank spirals as the Thompsons arrive in South Park to claim Kenny, the media descends, and the whole town must untangle a joke that went national. In the end the real missing Thompson child is found, the Thompsons are reunited with their actual son, and Cartman's milk-carton scheme collapses — with Kenny, as always, surviving the indignity.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman, the prankster; Kenny McCormick, the butt-photo; Butters Stotch, grounded for his own face; Martha and Stephen Thompson; Ms. Choksondik.

Locations: South Park Elementary on picture day; the missing-children center; the Thompson home.

Key events & continuity: Cartman's milk-carton prank goes national; the Thompsons' reversed anatomy becomes a one-episode visual gag; Butters is punished for simply looking like himself, a classic Butters injustice.
k: how to eat with your butt

entries.t:
Kyle's cousin Kyle Schwartz arrives from Connecticut to live with the Broflovskis while his mother is ill, and he is a walking storm of exaggerated stereotypes — complaining about everything, hyper-sensitive to dry air, allergic to most meat, and pathologically frugal. Kyle is mortified and promises Cartman $40 not to mock his cousin; Cartman lasts about five minutes before a concentration-camp joke blows the deal. The boys try increasingly desperate measures to get rid of cousin Kyle — tying him to a bus back to Connecticut, tricking him onto a plane to Antarctica — but he keeps coming back. Meanwhile Mr. Garrison, fed up with airport lines and delays, invents his own transportation: the Entity, a vehicle he rides by sitting on a handlebar-like contraption in a deeply suggestive position. The Entity is a massive hit, drawing the wrath of the airline industry, which sends assassins after Garrison. In the end cousin Kyle's penny-pinching saves the day when his frugality exposes a scheme, the airlines are thwarted, and Kyle is stuck with his cousin — who, for all his annoyance, proves unexpectedly useful.

Featured characters: Kyle Broflovski and his cousin Kyle Schwartz; Eric Cartman; Mr. Garrison, inventor of the Entity; Stan Marsh and Kenny McCormick.

Locations: the Broflovski home; South Park Elementary; the airport; Garrison's workshop.

Key events & continuity: Kyle Schwartz debuts as Kyle's unbearably stereotypical cousin; Mr. Garrison's Entity — ridden in a compromising position — becomes a recurring invention; the airline industry's murderous response parodies corporate overreach.

Tolkien is sick of being both the only black kid and the only rich kid in South Park, mocked by everyone for his wealth. His solution: buy ad space in Forbes magazine and market South Park as the next Aspen. It works too well — a wave of wealthy black celebrities moves to town: Will Smith, Oprah, P. Diddy, Kobe Bryant, Snoop Dogg, Bill Cosby and more. Mr. Garrison leads the resentful locals, dubbing the newcomers 'richers,' and the town starts passing petty segregation laws — the rich cannot eat in certain restaurants or drink in certain bars. But Tolkien finds the rich kids just as alienating: they speak in snotty rich accents and play polo, and he fits in with them no better than with the poor kids. Defeated, he decides his only home is the South Park Zoo, with the lions. The town's class war escalates until the absurdity peaks and the rich families, unwelcome and unbothered, simply leave — restoring South Park to its comfortably poor status quo, with Tolkien back where he started: the odd one out.

Featured characters: Tolkien Black; Mr. Garrison; the celebrity 'richers' — Will Smith, Oprah Winfrey, P. Diddy, Kobe Bryant, Snoop Dogg, Bill Cosby and others; Stan, Kyle, Cartman and Kenny.

Locations: South Park, newly gentrified; the Forbes-advertised town; the South Park Zoo.

Key events & continuity: Tolkien's wealth and isolation take center stage; the town's anti-rich segregation laws parody historical discrimination; the celebrity influx reverses itself, leaving the status quo intact.

In an abortion clinic, a woman donates her fetus for stem-cell research — but the transport truck crashes, and Cartman, passing by, steals the cargo hoping to resell it for a fortune. His plan collapses when the government bans stem-cell research outright. Meanwhile the boys learn Kenny has been diagnosed with a terminal illness, implied to be muscular dystrophy. Everyone rallies around Kenny except Stan, who is too upset to even visit his dying friend. A researcher explains stem-cell science to Cartman, who realizes the research could cure Kenny — and, incidentally, duplicate a Shakey's Pizza. Cartman takes his stolen fetuses and his cause to Washington, delivering a genuinely moving speech before Congress begging them to lift the ban, all for Kenny's sake. The speech works — the ban is lifted — but it comes too late: Kenny dies in the hospital, with Stan finally at his side, having overcome his inability to face it. Cartman, ever Cartman, immediately pivots his stem-cell victory into a business scheme. It is the rare episode that plays Kenny's death straight, and Stan's grief is the emotional core.

Featured characters: Kenny McCormick, dying of a terminal disease; Eric Cartman, the unlikely stem-cell crusader; Stan Marsh, too heartbroken to visit; Kyle Broflovski; the stem-cell researcher.

Locations: the abortion clinic and the crashed transport truck; the hospital; the U.S. Congress.

Key events & continuity: Kenny dies 'permanently' — he stays dead through most of season six, the longest absence in the show's history; Cartman's congressional speech is played sincerely, a rarity; Stan's arc is about facing grief instead of running from it.

It starts like a wholesome sitcom: Butters is excited for his parents' anniversary dinner at his favorite restaurant, Bennigan's. His mom asks him to spy on his dad to discover his anniversary gift. Butters tails his father — straight into a gay adult theater, then into a gay bathhouse called the White Swallow, where his dad has casual sex with men. Butters, innocent to the point of absurdity, reports back cheerfully that his dad saw a sad movie and did some 'wrestling,' complete with photos. His mother snaps: she spends the next day in a dissociative fugue, painting the walls coat after coat. Butters, oblivious, keeps trying to get his dad home in time for the anniversary dinner, trekking through bathhouses and adult theaters, even bumping into Mr. Garrison in a steam room. The truth detonates the Stotch marriage on screen: Linda tries to kill Butters and then herself, fails at both, and the episode ends with the family broken — Chris moving out, Linda shattered — while Butters, still sunny, just wants his Bennigan's dinner. It is the show's bleakest family portrait, played as a parody of saccharine 80s sitcoms.

Featured characters: Butters Stotch; Chris and Linda Stotch; Mr. Garrison, encountered in the bathhouse.

Locations: the Stotch home; the adult theater and the White Swallow bathhouse; Bennigan's, the unreachable anniversary dinner.

Key events & continuity: Butters gets his first solo spotlight episode; his parents' marriage implodes — Chris's double life is exposed and Linda's breakdown turns violent; the Stotch family dysfunction becomes a permanent fixture.

Jared Fogle, the Subway spokesman, comes to South Park preaching that losing weight is easy with sub sandwiches. When Stan, Cartman, Butters and Kyle corner him, he admits the truth: his transformation came from a personal trainer and a dietitian — his 'aides.' Cartman smells a sponsorship opportunity and pitches the same scheme to City Wok: Butters will gain fifty pounds, then lose it, crediting a strict City Wok diet. With Chef's help they start fattening Butters up. Meanwhile Jared decides to come clean about his 'aides' — and everyone hears 'AIDS.' His girlfriend thinks he is confessing to having the disease, Subway fires him, and the misunderstanding snowballs through the whole town in a relentless running gag. The boys' City Wok deal moves forward with the restaurant's proprietor, Tuong Lu Kim, until the whole fatten-then-thin scam collapses under its own absurdity and Butters is left heavier than he started. Jared, ruined by a homophone, slinks away while the town congratulates itself on missing the point entirely. Cartman's pitch to City Wok hinges on Butters as the before-and-after model, with Chef enlisted to supervise the force-feeding, while Jared's televised confession about his 'aides' keeps getting misheard in increasingly disastrous settings.

Featured characters: Jared Fogle; Butters Stotch, the would-be weight-loss poster boy; Stan Marsh, Kyle Broflovski and Eric Cartman; Chef; Tuong Lu Kim.

Locations: South Park, site of Jared's speech; City Wok; the fattening-up operation.

Key events & continuity: the 'aides' versus 'AIDS' misunderstanding drives the entire episode; Butters is force-fed toward a fifty-pound gain for a scam diet deal; Jared is fired by Subway over the confusion.

The Marshes, Broflovskis, Cartmans and Stotches take a family ski trip to Aspen, lured by a free two-day stay in exchange for sitting through a half-hour timeshare presentation. At the lodge, Cartman gives a sleeping Butters a 'Hitler' — a prank involving a finger and an upper lip — and coins the episode's title pun. On the bunny slope, the instructor Thumper teaches the kids to ski 'pizza' versus 'french fries,' while Ike crashes straight through the lodge wall. Then Tad Mikowski, the mountain's arrogant teen ski star, starts mocking Stan's surname and challenges him to a ski race. The parents, meanwhile, are trapped in the timeshare salesmen's endless pitch, which stretches from a half hour into an entire weekend of psychological warfare. Stan trains for the race, the showdown on the slopes goes disastrously — Stan wipes out spectacularly — but Tad's victory is hollow: the real contest was surviving the timeshare meeting, which the parents finally escape, vowing never again. The families drive home broke, exhausted, and still technically timeshare-free. Through it all the parents never get their promised half-hour meeting, only an endless sales pitch they cannot escape.

Featured characters: Stan Marsh; Tad Mikowski, the bully skier; Butters Stotch, victim of the 'Hitler'; the parents — Randy, Sharon, Gerald, Sheila, Liane, Chris and Linda; the timeshare salesmen Phil and Josh; Thumper the ski instructor.

Locations: Aspen, Colorado; the ski lodge and the bunny slope; the timeshare presentation room.

Key events & continuity: the families' Aspen vacation; Stan's ski-race humiliation at Tad's hands; the timeshare pitch becomes a weekend-long siege; Cartman's 'Hitler' prank on Butters.

After watching a talk show reward a deformed guest with prizes, Stan, Kyle, Cartman and Butters decide to get Butters on the Maury Povich show wearing fake testicles on his chin, built by the Star Trek nerds. Butters flies alone to New York, terrified. In the green room he meets the 'freak union' — genuinely deformed talk-show regulars who despise fakers, and he hears the cautionary tale of Lobster Boy, who turned out to be an actual lobster and was boiled alive. On air, Maury introduces Butters as 'Napoleon Bonaparte from South Park'; Butters rants about being teased, nearly blows his cover, and wins a trip to the world's largest miniature golf course. Meanwhile the boys back home exploit the system too, and the episode spirals into a satire of daytime TV's freak-show economy. Butters makes it home with his secret intact, the chin-balls removed, having survived national television by the skin of his teeth — and the talk-show circuit moves on to its next exploitable guest. The Star Trek nerds' prosthetics have to survive a plane flight and a national broadcast, and Butters spends the whole trip terrified the union will boil him like Lobster Boy.

Featured characters: Butters Stotch, the fake freak; Stan Marsh, Kyle Broflovski and Eric Cartman; Maury Povich; the freak union, including the Man with Foot on Head; the Star Trek nerds.
