Locations: South Park; the Maury Povich green room and studio in New York; the miniature golf course prize.

Key events & continuity: Butters goes on national TV with prosthetic chin testicles; the freak union and the Lobster Boy legend are introduced; the episode satirizes talk shows that reward deformity with prizes.

Ms. Choksondik's class visits a farm and the boys learn that veal is meat from baby calves. Everyone is horrified except Cartman, who finds it tender and scrumptious. Stan decides to rescue the calves, with Kyle and Butters backing him; Cartman agrees to help only if Kyle smells his farts. They break into the veal farm at night and smuggle the calves to Stan's house, though Cartman's 'cow-curling' game leaves a trail in the snow leading the police straight to the Marsh home. When the parents demand the calves back, Stan barricades himself in his room and the standoff becomes a full protest, with the parents unable to reason, bribe or force their way in. The siege drags on as the boys' conviction wavers — especially when they get hungry and the calves start looking like dinner. In the end the boys learn the calves were already destined for slaughter regardless, their rescue changes nothing, and they surrender the animals, having discovered that moral crusades are easier to start than to finish. Sharon refuses to lie to the boys about the calves' fate, Randy cannot get the barricaded door open without wrecking the house, and the parents are reduced to negotiating through a bedroom door.

Featured characters: Stan Marsh, the crusader; Kyle Broflovski, Butters Stotch and Eric Cartman; Randy and Sharon Marsh; Ms. Choksondik; the police.

Locations: the veal farm; Stan's house, under siege; the fourth-grade classroom.

Key events & continuity: the boys' animal-rights standoff ends in futility; Cartman's fart-smelling price for his help; the protest parodies activist sieges, with the kids' resolve crumbling at the smell of barbecue.

entries.n: S06E05 — The New Terrance and Phillip Movie Trailer
entries.t:
Stan, Kyle, Cartman and Butters camp out at Stan's house for one reason: the first trailer for the new Terrance and Phillip movie airs during a commercial break of 'Fightin' Around the World with Russell Crowe.' Everything conspires against them. Shelly hijacks the remote for her own show and extorts the boys into fetching her tampons — a job that falls to Butters. Cartman, declaring the TV's color 'saturated,' fiddles with a cable and blows the television up. The boys migrate to Kyle's house, only to be evicted by Gerald and Ike settling in for the news. Barred from Butters' and Cartman's homes, they end up at Chef's, then keep getting displaced — by parents, by programming, by sheer bad luck — chasing the broadcast from house to house across South Park. Every time they settle in front of a screen, something yanks them away before the trailer airs. The episode becomes a slapstick odyssey of missed television, ending with the boys having endured the entire night without ever seeing the trailer they waited for. Shelly's price for surrendering the remote is a tampon run that falls to Butters, and each new house offers a fresh humiliation before the boys are chased off again.

Featured characters: Stan Marsh, Kyle Broflovski, Eric Cartman and Butters Stotch; Shelly Marsh; Chef; Gerald Broflovski and Ike.

Locations: Stan's house; Kyle's house; Chef's house; various living rooms across South Park.

Key events & continuity: the boys' all-night quest to see a single movie trailer; Shelly's tampon extortion; Cartman destroys a television 'fixing' the color; the trailer remains unseen, the ultimate anticlimax.
k: the new terrance and phillip movie trailer

entries.t:
Still grieving Kenny's death months later, Stan, Kyle and Cartman decide Butters is no longer fit to be their friend — and fire him. Devastated, Butters goes home and unloads at his bedroom window, reciting everything he did for them: the tampons, the Maury Povich chin-balls, all of it. Done being the doormat, he builds a costume from aluminum foil and a cape and is reborn as Professor Chaos, sworn to wreak havoc on the unsuspecting populace — right after his mom sends him to bed. Meanwhile the boys hold a Bachelor-style contest to choose Kenny's replacement, parading candidates through town: Tweek, Craig, Tolkien, the kindergartners, even Towelie. Professor Chaos's reign of terror amounts to swapping restaurant orders and stealing erasers, but Butters commits to the bit with total sincerity. In the end the boys pick Tweek as their new fourth friend, and Professor Chaos vows that his evil has only begun — a promise he will keep, in his own tiny way, for seasons to come.

Featured characters: Butters Stotch, debuting as Professor Chaos; Stan Marsh, Kyle Broflovski and Eric Cartman; Tweek Tweak, the winning candidate; the parade of replacement hopefuls including Craig Tucker, Tolkien Black and Towelie.

Locations: Butters' bedroom, birthplace of Professor Chaos; the amusement park and town tour of the friend contest; Bennigan's, first target of Chaos.

Key events & continuity: Butters is fired as the boys' friend and creates his Professor Chaos alter ego, a permanent recurring identity; Tweek is chosen as Kenny's replacement, joining the core group; Kenny's absence continues to shape the season.

entries.n: S06E07 — The Simpsons Already Did It
entries.t:
Cartman talks everyone into chipping in for 'Sea People' from a magazine ad, imagining a race of mermaid-like beings who will carry him away from this miserable planet. What arrives is brine shrimp. To salvage the purchase, the boys dump the Sea People into Ms. Choksondik's coffee — and she drops dead. When the news reports semen found in the teacher's stomach, the boys conclude their 'sea men' killed her and raid the morgue to steal the evidence before anyone 'finds the women too.' Chef has to explain the difference between sea-men and semen, and that brine shrimp could not have killed anyone. Meanwhile Butters, as Professor Chaos, is thwarted at every turn: every evil scheme he dreams up — blocking the sun, rigging an election, unleashing a plague of frogs — has already been done on The Simpsons. His meltdown over this becomes the episode's thesis. In the end the Sea People, mixed with the recovered semen in Cartman's aquarium, evolve into a tiny civilization that builds its own society — which the boys then destroy. Choksondik's death, announced two months earlier, is now official, and the class faces a future without her.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman, Stan Marsh, Kyle Broflovski and Tweek Tweak; Butters Stotch as Professor Chaos; Ms. Choksondik; Chef; the Sea People civilization.

Locations: Cartman's bedroom aquarium; the school; the morgue.

Key events & continuity: Ms. Choksondik dies, leaving the fourth grade teacherless; Professor Chaos learns every plot has been done by The Simpsons; the Sea People evolve and are wiped out in miniature.

When Father Maxi announces a Young Men's Catholic Retreat, the parents of South Park refuse to send their kids — and then a counselor asks the boys point-blank whether the priest ever tried to put anything in their butts. Never having been molested, the boys are baffled, and Cartman has a 'brilliant' idea: if food goes in the mouth and out the rear, then eating through the rectum should make you defecate through the mouth. He bets Kyle $20 it works, and the experiment proceeds in all its horror. Meanwhile every parent in town converts to atheism in protest, and Father Maxi — genuinely appalled by the abuse scandal — travels to the Vatican to demand change, only to find priests worldwide committed to covering it up rather than stopping it. Maxi discovers the Church's hierarchy is rotten to the core, with the molestation treated as business as usual. Back home, Cartman's anatomical experiment fails exactly as physics demands, Kyle collects his $20, and the parents' atheism fizzles once the scandal cycle moves on. The counselor's blunt questioning leaves the boys genuinely confused about what molestation even is, which is exactly what gives Cartman his brainstorm.

Featured characters: Father Maxi; Eric Cartman and Kyle Broflovski, the $20 bet; Stan Marsh and Kenny McCormick; the Vatican priests; the South Park parents.

Locations: South Park; the Vatican; the boys' experimental grounds.

Key events & continuity: Father Maxi confronts the Church's abuse cover-up all the way to the Vatican; the town's mass conversion to atheism is pure protest theater; Cartman's reverse-digestion experiment fails and costs him $20.

The boys — with Tweek filling Kenny's spot — go see the re-re-re-release of The Empire Strikes Back, but the trailers horrify them first: E.T. with guns digitally replaced by walkie-talkies, Saving Private Ryan with 'Nazi' changed to 'persons with political differences,' and then Empire itself with 'Wookiee' redubbed 'hair-challenged animal' and the cast replaced by Ewoks. Outraged at directors 'improving' classics, they found an organization to save films from their directors, with Cartman scrawling 'Free Hat' on the poster to drum up members and Tweek tasked with making fifty paper hats. Their campaign draws the attention of Steven Spielberg and George Lucas themselves, who turn out to be the villains of the piece — literally melting down anyone who opposes their edits. The boys' movement grows into a full-blown crusade against revisionism, complete with chants and hats, until the directors are stopped and the films are restored. The episode ends with the boys victorious, their favorite movies safe from further 'enhancement.' Tweek's assignment is fifty handmade paper hats, and the boys' protest grows from a complaint into a full movement with chants, hats and a manifesto against directorial revisionism. Their slogan, misspelled on the poster and all, becomes the rallying cry of the whole campaign.

Featured characters: Stan Marsh, Kyle Broflovski, Eric Cartman and Tweek Tweak; Steven Spielberg and George Lucas, the revisionist villains.

Locations: the movie theater; the 'Free Hat' campaign headquarters; the directors' lair.

Key events & continuity: the boys' anti-revisionism crusade; Spielberg and Lucas appear as the episode's antagonists; the 'Free Hat' slogan and paper hats become the movement's uniform.

After two weeks off following Ms. Choksondik's death, the fourth grade returns with Mr. Mackey as substitute teacher — which Cartman protests by insisting on prolonging his grief indefinitely. Over the break, Bebe developed breasts. They are small — she first mistook them for mosquito bites — but every boy in class suddenly finds her brilliant and fascinating without understanding why. They invite her to throw rocks at cars, fawn over her essays, and bicker like apes competing for a mate, while Wendy and the other girls, jealous, start calling Bebe a slut. Bebe's mom explains it is just growing up: boys once thought she was dumb, then one day decided she was smart, so apparently intelligence runs in the family. Meanwhile Cartman tries to exploit the chaos, attempting to install Bebe in the group and eject Kyle, then Tweek, in a power play that backfires. By the end the boys' hormones settle into an uneasy truce, Bebe remains bemused by her new power, and Wendy's resentment simmers — the first crack in her relationship with Stan's world. Wendy, who has never once been invited to hang out with Stan's group, watches her social standing evaporate as the boys lose their minds over Bebe.

Featured characters: Bebe Stevens; Wendy Testaburger; Stan Marsh, Kyle Broflovski, Eric Cartman and Tweek Tweak; Mr. Mackey; Bebe's mom.

Locations: South Park Elementary; the rock-throwing spot after school; the Stevens home.

Key events & continuity: Bebe's development scrambles the boys' social order; Wendy's jealousy foreshadows her later breakup with Stan; Cartman's failed coup against Kyle and Tweek; Mr. Mackey subs following Choksondik's death.

entries.n: S06E11 — Child Abduction is Not Funny
entries.t:
Panicked by news reports of child abductions, Tweek's parents drill him to trust no one — then his own dad, posing as 'Officer Daniels,' proves the lesson by holding a gun to him through his bedroom door. Tweek becomes a wreck: he flees a movie theater over an unfamiliar cashier, refuses to speak to strangers, and even ignores a disabled man stuck on train tracks, who is run over while Tweek watches. That night the Ghost of Human Kindness visits Tweek and shows him a kinder world — volunteers with the elderly, adoptive parents, strangers helping strangers — to prove the media's terror is overblown. Meanwhile the town's parents, whipped into a frenzy, hire City Wok's owner to build a Great Wall around South Park to keep kidnappers out. The wall goes up, the town seals itself off, and the parents congratulate themselves — until the absurdity of walling in an entire town collapses the panic. Tweek learns the world is not as evil as the news claims, though his parents' paranoia is unlikely to fade. The Ghost's tour takes in a woman comforting lonely elders, adoptive parents with needy children, and strangers helping at a car wreck — ordinary kindness the news never shows.

Featured characters: Tweek Tweak; Richard and Mrs. Tweak; the Ghost of Human Kindness; Tuong Lu Kim, the wall builder; Stan, Kyle, Cartman and Kenny.

Locations: the Tweak home; the movie theater; the train tracks; the Great Wall of South Park.

Key events & continuity: the town builds a literal wall around South Park; the Ghost of Human Kindness counters media-driven fear; Tweek's stranger-danger trauma, including the man on the tracks, satirizes parental panic.

The boys win an all-you-can-grab candy prize from Lolly's Candy Factory — but they gave the winning ticket to Kenny to hold before he died. At the McCormick house they learn Kenny was cremated; stealing the urn, they expect a body and find ashes, which they mistake for chocolate milk mix. Cartman mixes the ashes with milk and drinks them. Their plan: build a ladder to Heaven, find Kenny, and get the ticket back. The adults, touched by what they think is grief, rally the whole town — and then the whole country — behind the project, with a weepy celebrity ballad milking the emotion. When the boys run out of building materials, the military arrives to construct a reinforced tower to beat the Japanese to Heaven. Suspicious photos of Heaven spark a media frenzy, the tower climbs into the clouds, and Cartman — with Kenny's ashes inside him — begins channeling Kenny's spirit. In the end the ladder goes nowhere, the candy prize is lost, but Cartman expels Kenny's soul, which ascends properly — setting the stage for Kenny's eventual return.

Featured characters: Stan Marsh, Kyle Broflovski and Eric Cartman; Kenny McCormick, as ashes and as a possessing spirit; the McCormick family; the military; the celebrity balladeer.

Locations: Lolly's Candy Factory; the McCormick home; the ladder/tower construction site reaching for the sky.

Key events & continuity: Kenny's ashes are drunk by Cartman, who becomes Kenny's vessel; the town builds a ladder to Heaven for the candy ticket; Kenny's soul is released at the end, paving the way for his return later in the season.

entries.n: S06E13 — The Return of the Fellowship of the Ring to the Two Towers
entries.t:
Randy sends the boys — deep in a Lord of the Rings roleplay — to return a rented copy of the movie to Butters' house. What Randy does not mention is that he also rented an adult film, and the tapes get mixed up: the Marshes end up watching the fantasy epic while the boys deliver the hottest porno ever made to the Stotches. Butters, home alone, watches the tape without realizing it is not Lord of the Rings, and becomes obsessed with its 'precious.' When Randy and Sharon realize the swap, they race to the Stotch house, ordering the boys to retrieve the tape under the cover story that it is cursed by dark powers. The boys — now fully in character as a fellowship — embark on a mythic quest across town to reclaim the tape from Butters, who has descended into a Gollum-like creature hissing about his 'precious.' Parents, video-store clerks and rival factions all converge in a parody of the film's battles. In the end the tape is recovered, Butters is pried away from his precious, and the whole town pretends none of it happened.

Featured characters: Stan Marsh, Kyle Broflovski, Eric Cartman and Kenny McCormick as the fellowship; Butters Stotch as Gollum; Randy and Sharon Marsh; Stephen and Linda Stotch.

Locations: the Marsh home; the Stotch residence; the video store; the streets of South Park as the quest route.

Key events & continuity: the infamous tape-swap — the boys deliver porn to Butters; Butters' transformation into a 'precious'-hissing Gollum; the episode parodies Lord of the Rings beat for beat while the parents scramble to cover up the mix-up.
k: the return of the fellowship of the ring to the two towers

entries.n: S06E14 — The Death Camp of Tolerance
entries.t:
Mr. Garrison is promoted back to fourth-grade teacher — and, realizing he could get rich suing the school if fired for being gay, he sets out to be as outrageously inappropriate as possible, with his S&M partner Mr. Slave in tow. The fourth graders are horrified, but when they complain, their parents mistake it for bigotry and ship them to the Museum of Tolerance as punishment — where the tour ends with the guide and the parents viciously berating a smoker, tolerance forgotten. Garrison escalates: in a science lesson he inserts the class gerbil Lemmiwinks into Mr. Slave's rectum, and the episode follows Lemmiwinks' epic journey through the digestive tract, narrated like a fantasy quest. Chef, the only adult who believes the kids, reports Garrison — and is sent to tolerance training for his trouble. When the boys skip class, Mr. Mackey sentences them to an Auschwitz-styled 'Tolerance Camp' to cure their supposed intolerance. In the end Garrison's scheme collapses, the boys are vindicated, and Lemmiwinks emerges — changed — from the other end.

Featured characters: Mr. Garrison and Mr. Slave, debuting Mr. Slave; Lemmiwinks the gerbil, on his inner quest; Stan, Kyle, Cartman and Butters; Chef; Mr. Mackey; the Museum of Tolerance guide.

Locations: the fourth-grade classroom; the Museum of Tolerance; the Tolerance Camp; the interior of Mr. Slave.

Key events & continuity: Mr. Slave and Lemmiwinks debut; Garrison's sue-the-school scheme backfires; the boys are punished for 'intolerance' at the Museum of Tolerance and the Tolerance Camp; Lemmiwinks' quest becomes a recurring legend.

entries.n: S06E15 — The Biggest Douche in the Universe
entries.t:
Cartman is rushed to the hospital, and the doctors warn he needs a 'time transplant.' Stan and Kyle visit — and discover that Kenny's soul, drunk along with his ashes months ago, is now possessing Cartman's body, happily greeting them while Cartman himself fumes from inside. Chef suggests they consult the TV psychic John Edward. The whole crew flies to New York, enduring an in-flight Rob Schneider movie in which Schneider turns into a stapler, and lines up for Edward's show — where the psychic's cold-reading act ('I'm sensing an M...') is exposed as pure guesswork. Edward cannot exorcise Kenny, so Cartman and Chef travel to the moors of Scotland, where Chef's parents attempt a voodoo exorcism. The ritual works: Kenny's soul is drawn out of Cartman — and, with no body to return to, ascends to Heaven at last. Cartman is free of his passenger, the psychic is discredited, and Kenny's long absence finally ends in the afterlife. Liane insists on the New York trip over the doctor's objections about Cartman's 'time,' and the family endures the world's most disinterested in-flight movie on the way.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman, possessed by Kenny; Kenny McCormick's soul; Stan Marsh, Kyle Broflovski and Chef; John Edward, the TV psychic; Chef's parents.

Locations: the hospital; New York and the psychic's studio; the Scottish moors.

Key events & continuity: Kenny's soul has been trapped in Cartman since 'A Ladder to Heaven' — here it is finally released and ascends; John Edward's cold reading is brutally satirized; the Rob Schneider stapler gag becomes a running joke.
k: the biggest douche in the universe

entries.n: S06E16 — My Future Self n' Me
entries.t:
The boys find a marijuana joint left behind by older kids and Stan tosses it aside — it is just a plant, touching it cannot hurt you. That night, in a thunderstorm, a 32-year-old wreck shows up at the Marsh door claiming to be Stan from the future: juvie, drugs, alcohol, a ruined life, all beginning the day he touched marijuana. The only way to save him, he says, is for young Stan to stay clean, study hard and stay motivated. Terrified, Stan asks Butters to tutor him — and discovers Butters has his own slovenly 'future self' living at his house. Suspicious, Stan checks the man's wallet: a key card expiring in 2002, address 3451 Colfax Ave — the Motivation Corp. building. The boys stake it out and watch another couple hire an actor to play their son's future self. The whole thing is a scam: parents hire actors to scare kids straight about drugs. Stan confronts his parents, the actor drops the act, and the episode ends with the real moral — that lying to kids about drugs backfires — delivered with the show's usual subtlety.

Featured characters: Stan Marsh; Butters Stotch; the fake future Stans; Randy and Sharon Marsh; Chris and Linda Stotch; Craig's gang.

Locations: the secluded spot where the joint is found; the Marsh home; the Stotch home; the Motivation Corp. building.

Key events & continuity: the 'future self' scam is exposed as a parental scare tactic run by Motivation Corp.; Stan and Butters both get fake future selves; the episode's real target is dishonest anti-drug messaging.

Cartman's naughty-or-nice audit, conducted by Kyle's cousin Kyle Schwartz, comes back catastrophic: he has been so naughty that curing cancer and AIDS would still leave him owing Santa two presents. His only hope is the single nicest act ever — so he resolves to bring Christmas to the suffering people of Iraq. At the town tree-lighting, Jimmy starts singing 'The Twelve Days of Christmas,' which, thanks to his stutter, will take him the entire episode. Using Mr. Hankey's Poo-Choo train, the boys ride to the North Pole and convince Santa to make the trip, with the Underpants Gnomes prepping the sleigh. Over Iraq, Santa is shot down by a rocket-propelled grenade: reindeer dead, Santa captured and tortured. The boys mount a rescue, Christmas hangs in the balance, and in the chaos Santa is freed and manages to deliver his run — with a little help from a certain jolly intervention. Cartman gets his 'nice' on the ledger, Jimmy finally finishes his song, and Christmas is saved by the skin of its teeth. Kyle Schwartz's audit is merciless — Cartman has been so naughty that even curing cancer and AIDS within the week would still leave him in Santa's debt.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman; Santa Claus; Mr. Hankey; Jesus; Jimmy Valmer and his twelve days; Kyle Schwartz, the naughty-or-nice accountant; the Underpants Gnomes; the Iraqi captors.

Locations: South Park's tree-lighting ceremony; the North Pole; Iraq.

Key events & continuity: Cartman's nicest-act-ever scheme takes Santa to a war zone; Santa is shot down and tortured over Iraq; Jimmy's stuttered carol runs the full episode; Christmas is saved and Cartman's ledger is balanced.

The episode opens as a near-exact replay of the very first episode — Cartman rambling about an alien abduction dream — until the boys realize they are stuck in a repeat and decide to deal with Cartman's anal probe once and for all. After a proctologist and a scientist fail, Cartman will only activate the probe's satellite if Kyle sticks a finger up his rear; Kyle finally snaps and does it, enduring Cartman's torment the whole time. The scientist reverses the probe's polarity through an absurd word-association chain — candy bars to wrappers to Christmas to cold to Alaska to polar bears to polarity — and the alien Visitors arrive. The boys and Chef flee, are abducted anyway, and wake aboard the ship to meet Najix, an alien who took Randy Marsh's form to please them. The truth: Earth is an intergalactic reality show, and the network is cancelling it. The boys plead humanity's case before the alien producers, arguing the show still has value, and the cancellation is reversed — Earth gets renewed, the boys are returned home, and the probe stays exactly where it is.

Featured characters: Stan Marsh, Kyle Broflovski, Eric Cartman and Kenny McCormick; Chef; Najix the alien; the Visitors; the alien network executives.

Locations: South Park; the scientist's lab; the alien ship and the network's offices.

Key events & continuity: the 100th-episode-adjacent premiere replays the series' first episode; Earth is revealed as a cancelled-and-renewed reality show; Kenny is back with the group as if never gone; Cartman's anal probe saga continues.

After Jimmy's comedy act is snubbed in favor of an inspirational speech by Christopher Reeve — whom Jimmy dismisses as a wannabe poser, not a genuine cripple — Timmy and Jimmy form their own club for the truly disabled, and name it the Crips. Unaware of the notorious street gang sharing the name, they decide they want to join the real Crips, with Jimmy theorizing that Crips were crippled at birth and Bloods were crippled in accidents. The Denver Crips leader tells them to 'pop some punk ass Bloods'; thinking this means buying treats for them, they wander town looking for Bloods and find a crew at a convenience store. A trucker swerves to avoid hitting them and blows up the whole gas station, wiping out thirteen Bloods — and the Crips welcome Jimmy ('Four Legs') and Timmy ('Roller') as their baddest members. Meanwhile Christopher Reeve's stem-cell-powered 'miracles' are exposed as monstrous, and the episode closes with the boys as unwitting gang legends, having no idea what they have joined. Stan advises the others to stay out of it entirely, and the three walk away while Jimmy and Timmy march toward the gang life in total innocence.

Featured characters: Jimmy Valmer and Timmy Burch; Christopher Reeve; Stan Marsh, Kyle Broflovski, Eric Cartman and Kenny McCormick; the Denver Crips leader.

Locations: South Park; the Denver gang territory; the Ribs-N-Gas convenience store.

Key events & continuity: Jimmy and Timmy accidentally join the Crips and become gang legends; Jimmy's feud with Christopher Reeve over 'real' disability; the boys' misunderstanding of gang slang drives every disaster.

After detention for sculpting a clay penis and mouthing off in art class, the boys take revenge by toilet-papering their art teacher Mrs. Streibel's house at night. Kyle is horrified to learn she has kids, and the guilt eats him alive — nightmares, visions of the Streibel family, the works. When the boys are called to the counselor's office, Cartman fabricates an absurdly detailed alibi involving a bowling alley, Ally Sheedy, five Scientologists, a wrong bus to Rancho de Burritos Rojos and a ride home from a one-fingered man named Gary Bushwell. Kyle cannot keep the details straight and Cartman grows convinced he will confess. Meanwhile Officer Barbrady investigates, dusting for prints and pursuing the case with uncharacteristic competence. The tension builds as Kyle's conscience wars with Cartman's threats — until the truth comes out in a way that satisfies no one: the boys are caught, punished, and Kyle learns that guilt, unlike toilet paper, does not wash off in the rain. Kyle's nightmares star the Streibel children, and every summons to the counselor's office convinces the boys their toilet-paper crime is about to be exposed. Cartman coaches Kyle on the alibi's details, terrified the weak link will crack.

Featured characters: Kyle Broflovski, consumed by guilt; Eric Cartman, Stan Marsh and Kenny McCormick; Mrs. Streibel; Officer Barbrady; the counselor.

Locations: Mrs. Streibel's house, draped in toilet paper; the school counselor's office; the bowling alley of the alibi.

Key events & continuity: the TP-ing of the teacher's house and Kyle's guilt spiral; Cartman's legendary multi-layered alibi; Barbrady's rare competent investigation.

entries.n: S07E04 — I'm a Little Bit Country
entries.t:
When Mr. Garrison lets anyone protesting the Iraq war leave school early, every kid suddenly opposes the war — knowing nothing about it. Interviewed on camera about what the Founding Fathers would think, the boys embarrass themselves by not knowing who the Founders were, and Garrison assigns them to figure it out. Stan, Kyle and Kenny actually study; Cartman tries to trigger a colonial-era flashback by dropping a rock on his own head, then by electrocuting himself in a bathtub full of History Channel documentaries. He falls into a coma and dreams himself into 1776 Philadelphia, where he bumbles into delivering the message that leads to the Declaration of Independence. Meanwhile the town splits into pro-war and anti-war rallies — held at the same place on the same day — which devolve into a giant brawl. Cartman wakes from his coma with the Founders' answer: America must remain divided, because having both sides keeps the country free — 'dissent and disagreement are the American way,' or in his words, the country works because it argues with itself. Both rallies declare victory and go home.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman, the time-traveling messenger; Stan Marsh, Kyle Broflovski and Kenny McCormick; Mr. Garrison; the pro-war and anti-war townspeople; the Founding Fathers.

Locations: South Park Elementary; the dueling rally grounds; colonial Philadelphia, 1776.

Key events & continuity: the 100th episode; Cartman's coma-dream inserts him into the founding of America; the town's war debate ends in a brawl and a both-sides moral; the Founders' message endorses perpetual disagreement.

entries.n: S07E05 — Fat Butt and Pancake Head
entries.t:
For the school's cultural diversity day, Kyle delivers a painstaking report on Latinos in technology. Cartman follows with a report on Latino culture in the arts — starring his hand as a ventriloquist puppet of Jennifer Lopez, complete with a shrieking exaggerated accent, taco obsession and an inability to pronounce the J in Jennifer. The Latino judges inexplicably award Cartman first place and a $20 mall gift certificate, enraging Kyle. At the mall, Cartman records a music video of his hand-puppet 'Ms. Lopez' singing about tacos and burritos and taco-flavored kisses — and the video somehow reaches the real Jennifer Lopez's record label, which mistakes the hand for the actual star. The real Lopez is sidelined while Cartman's hand becomes a sensation, and when the real singer confronts him, Cartman insists the hand has a mind of its own. The hand-puppet even 'falls in love' with Cartman, leading to a jealous, deranged real Lopez trying to kill the hand. In the end the hand is exposed, the real Lopez reclaims her career, and Kyle is left sputtering at a universe that rewarded Cartman's racist puppet act.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman and his hand, 'Ms. Lopez'; the real Jennifer Lopez; Kyle Broflovski; the diversity-day judges.

Locations: South Park Elementary's diversity day stage; the mall recording booth; the record label offices.

Key events & continuity: Cartman's hand-puppet Jennifer Lopez becomes a pop star; the real Lopez is replaced by a hand and tries to murder it; Kyle's legitimate report loses to a racist ventriloquist act.

The boys start a detective agency, solving neighborhood 'crimes' for a dollar. Their first case: a pie missing from an elderly couple's windowsill. Examining the scene — and ignoring the dog with pie on its face — they conclude the husband planned to brutally murder his wife over the pie and dump her in the lake. The horrified couple pays the dollar just to make them leave. Next: recovering young Sarah Peterson's stolen doll. They interrogate Butters as a suspect for no reason, using good-cop-bad-cop, and Cartman decides Butters must produce a semen sample in Cartman's bathroom. A tip leads them to the real thieves' house, where they wrestle the doll back. Their success gets them deputized as junior officers by the South Park police — and immediately thrown into real danger: a hostage situation at the school, a drug bust, a standoff with actual armed criminals. Playing cop stops being fun when the guns are real. The boys beg to be un-deputized, the police agree they are in over their heads, and the detective agency closes up shop.

Featured characters: Stan Marsh, Kyle Broflovski, Eric Cartman and Kenny McCormick, the detectives; Butters Stotch, the interrogated innocent; Sarah Peterson; the South Park police; the elderly pie couple.

Locations: the detective headquarters; the pie crime scene; the doll thieves' house; the hostage standoff.

Key events & continuity: the boys are made junior deputies and face real armed criminals; Butters' forced 'semen sample' interrogation; the detective agency folds once detective work turns genuinely dangerous.

The families visit the Three Feathers Indian Casino on the reservation; the boys are too young to gamble, so they catch the Native American comedy show instead, baffled by the humor. Gerald Broflovski loses the family house at blackjack — and tries to pin it on Kyle for wanting to leave. It turns out Gerald is not alone: Chief Runs With Premise has been raking in the town's money and now uses it to buy South Park outright, planning to bulldoze it for a superhighway to Denver. The whole town is evicted with no way to buy itself back. The boys huddle with the other kids — including a new boy named Alex — to save the town: Butters suggests a dog parade, Cartman suggests giving Kyle a disease, and Stan lands on the real plan. They advise the parents to pool their remaining money and gamble it all at the casino in one desperate shot to win the town back. Against the odds the gamble works — the town wins back its deed — and the superhighway dies on the drawing board, with the casino's scheme collapsing.

Featured characters: Stan Marsh, Kyle Broflovski, Eric Cartman and Kenny McCormick; Gerald Broflovski; Chief Runs With Premise; Alex, the new boy; Butters Stotch.

Locations: the Three Feathers Indian Casino; the casino comedy club; the evicted town of South Park.

Key events & continuity: the casino buys South Park to build a superhighway; Gerald gambles away the Broflovski house; the town gambles everything to win itself back and succeeds.

Stan, Cartman and Kenny show up at the bus stop in flamboyant new outfits, speaking in exaggerated effeminate voices — Stan has ruined his pajama top and replaced it with a fishnet vest, Kenny sports a pink-purple parka. They mock Kyle's normal clothes as outdated and give him a makeover. At home Sheila is horrified, but the fad is everywhere: the town's men have all gone metrosexual under the influence of Queer Eye for the Straight Guy, suddenly bathing regularly and brushing three times a day, which the women love. At school even Pip and Timmy have caught it, and Craig's crew argues with Cartman's over who is gayer. Only Chef and Kyle resist. Chef advises Kyle to be himself and wait for the fad to pass. Mr. Garrison, meanwhile, is furious — not at the fad but at being upstaged. The truth comes out: the metrosexual craze was engineered by the Queer Eye hosts as a plot to make all men gay and take over the world, and Kyle, Chef and Garrison expose and stop it. South Park's men revert to their usual slovenly selves, and Kyle learns the value of outlasting a fad.

Featured characters: Kyle Broflovski, the holdout; Chef; Mr. Garrison; Stan Marsh, Eric Cartman and Kenny McCormick, the converted; the Queer Eye hosts; Craig, Tweek, Tolkien and Jason.

Locations: the bus stop; the Marsh and Broflovski homes; South Park Elementary.

Key events & continuity: the metrosexual fad sweeps South Park's men; the Queer Eye hosts are exposed as scheming to turn the world gay; Kyle and Chef wait out the fad and are vindicated.

Stan, Kyle, Cartman and Kenny form a rock band called Moop, but cannot agree on a direction. Cartman pitches Christian rock — the Christian market is a goldmine — and Kyle calls it the stupidest idea ever. They bet $10 on whose band goes platinum first. Kicked out of Moop, Cartman recruits Butters on drums and Tolkien on bass — Tolkien protests he does not even own a bass, then finds one in his basement and turns out to be a natural — for his Christian rock band Faith + 1. At Christfest, Cartman hijacks the stage and Faith + 1 explodes: he simply takes love ballads, swaps in Jesus's name, and sounds like he is serenading Christ himself. The band tops the Christian charts. Meanwhile Stan, Kyle and Kenny, seeking 'inspiration,' blow their money on CDs and get nowhere; their big break comes when they realize they can just download music illegally — landing them in trouble that torpedoes Moop entirely. Cartman wins the bet and the platinum, having proven that cynicism, not faith, sells Christian rock. Tolkien only agrees to play bass after finding the instrument in his own basement, to his visible annoyance, and Butters throws himself into drumming with total sincerity.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman; Butters Stotch and Tolkien Black of Faith + 1; Stan Marsh, Kyle Broflovski and Kenny McCormick of Moop.

Locations: the garage rehearsals; Christfest; the Christian rock charts.

Key events & continuity: Cartman's Faith + 1 goes platinum with Jesus-swapped love songs; Moop collapses after the boys turn to music piracy; Cartman wins the $10 bet and proves his cynical thesis.

At the farmers market, Father Maxi holds a memorial for nine people killed the day before by an elderly driver — and another senior crashes the service mid-eulogy. Stan asks Randy why old people still have licenses; Randy calls it a delicate issue, which Grandpa Marvin Marsh overhears. Then a senior couple drives their Buick off a bridge into Stark's Pond, running over a fisherman, convinced the pond is the Country Kitchen Buffet parking lot. Public outrage pressures the DMV to strip seniors of their licenses. Marvin and the town's elderly meet at the community center — struggling to remember why they gathered — and decide to fight back: they barricade themselves, arm themselves, and take hostages rather than surrender their keys, in a parody of Red Dawn. The standoff escalates until the seniors' own confusion undermines them, the kids are caught in the middle, and the town is forced to confront that the elderly will not go quietly. In the end a compromise of sorts is reached, but South Park's roads are no safer than before. The seniors' community-center meeting keeps derailing as everyone forgets why they gathered, until Marvin finally rallies them to armed resistance.

Featured characters: Grandpa Marvin Marsh; Stan Marsh and Randy Marsh; Father Maxi; the senior-citizen resistance; the DMV.

Locations: the farmers market; Stark's Pond; the community center, turned into a senior stronghold.

Key events & continuity: the seniors wage a Red Dawn-style armed resistance against losing their licenses; multiple senior-driving fatalities open the episode; the town's elderly refuse to surrender their keys.

Kyle invites Stan, Kenny and Butters to celebrate his birthday at Casa Bonita — Cartman's dream restaurant. Cartman is ecstatic until Kyle reveals he invited Butters instead of him, screening a montage of every anti-Semitic insult Cartman has ever thrown at him: Butters is simply a better friend. Cartman launches a campaign to prove he is nice, but kindness is so foreign to him that his attempts are transparently awful. Next he asks Jimmy to teach him niceness, understands none of it, and then beats Jimmy up in front of Kyle while pretending to defend Kyle's mother — prompting Kyle's deadpan: 'You really think beating up handicapped kids is nice?' Still uninvited, Cartman escalates: he lures Butters into hiding, convincing him the town is under apocalyptic threat, and stashes him in an abandoned bomb shelter with a week of supplies while he takes Butters' place at the birthday dinner. Cartman finally gets his Casa Bonita trip — cliff divers, sopapillas, the works — but the police find Butters, the scheme unravels, and Kyle's birthday ends with Cartman exposed and Butters rescued from the shelter.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman; Kyle Broflovski; Butters Stotch, hidden in the shelter; Stan Marsh and Kenny McCormick; Jimmy Valmer.

Locations: Casa Bonita, the legendary restaurant; the abandoned bomb shelter; South Park.

Key events & continuity: Cartman hides Butters in a bomb shelter to steal his birthday invitation; Kyle's montage of Cartman's abuse explains the snub; Cartman gets his Casa Bonita visit at the cost of total exposure.

A new family from Utah moves to South Park, and their son Gary is impossibly perfect — straight A's, stellar manners — which infuriates the boys. Stan is drafted to beat Gary up on the playground, but Gary's relentless politeness disarms him completely; Stan walks away with a dinner invitation. At the Harrison home Stan finds a genuinely warm family: five kids, two parents, and a Family Home Evening of games, performances and scripture reading. He hears the story of Joseph Smith — the angel, the golden plates, the claim that Native Americans were once white — and is baffled that everyone just believed it without proof. Randy decides the Mormons are brainwashing Stan and storms over to confront them, only to be charmed too. The episode retells Smith's story in full, complete with a cheerful musical number about dumb-dumb-dumb-dumb-dumb beliefs, and ends with Stan rejecting Mormonism — not because the Harrisons are not nice, but because he cannot accept a religion founded on a story no one verified. Gary, hurt, tells Stan that maybe he just needs the religion, and walks away. Randy marches over to accuse the Harrisons of brainwashing, only to be disarmed by the same relentless niceness that got Stan.

Featured characters: Stan Marsh; Gary Harrison; the Harrison family; Randy Marsh; Joseph Smith, in the animated retelling.

Locations: South Park Elementary's playground; the Harrison home; upstate New York, in the Joseph Smith story.

Key events & continuity: the Harrison family debuts as South Park's Mormon neighbors; Joseph Smith's story is retold in full; Stan befriends then rejects Gary over the faith's unverifiable origins.

Mr. Mackey assembles the school for an anti-smoking presentation by the motivational troupe 'Butt Out!,' whose rap about the dangers of cigarettes is so unbearable that the boys decide smoking must be cool and light up behind the school at the loading dock. Caught coughing by Mackey, they ditch the cigarettes just in time — but a discarded butt sets a garbage container ablaze and the fire spreads: South Park Elementary nearly burns to the ground. With the school in ruins, the parents arrive to learn the boys were caught smoking, and the town spirals into an anti-smoking panic. The boys, now branded as smokers, are sent to a draconian anti-smoking camp, while the 'Butt Out!' troupe's sanctimony only makes rebellion more appealing. The episode pits the kids' contrarian smoking against the adults' hysterical overcorrection, and neither side covers itself in glory. In the end the school is rebuilt, the panic subsides, and the boys have learned that the fastest way to make kids do something is to rap at them about not doing it. Mackey catches them mid-cough behind the school, and the boys' attempt to look innocent collapses the moment the garbage container ignites.

Featured characters: Stan Marsh, Kyle Broflovski, Eric Cartman and Kenny McCormick; Mr. Mackey; Principal Victoria; the 'Butt Out!' troupe; the boys' parents.

Locations: the South Park Elementary gymnasium; the loading dock; the burned-down school; the anti-smoking camp.

Key events & continuity: the boys take up smoking to spite the 'Butt Out!' performance and accidentally burn down the school; the town's anti-smoking panic mirrors the kids' rebellion; the school is destroyed and rebuilt.

Bebe informs Stan on the football field that Wendy has dumped him — she still wants to be friends, no further explanation. Stan collapses into a full depressive spiral: crying in the rain on a bridge, staring at photos of Wendy, mainlining 80s breakup ballads. He begs Kyle to intercede; Wendy's only answer is that Stan is nice but she does not want to be together. He sends Jimmy as an emissary, but Jimmy's stutter turns 'continuing source of inspiration' into a profane insult, and Wendy tells Stan to get lost. To cheer him up, the boys take Stan to Raisins — a restaurant famous for its wings and its flirtatious waitresses, who call every customer 'sweetie.' Stan latches onto one waitress, Lexus, and starts spending all his time and money there, convinced she truly cares for him. Meanwhile Butters, whose own heartbreak is fresher than anyone knew, delivers the episode's thesis: he is sad, but he is not going to let it turn him bitter — he chooses to stay sweet. Stan finally gets it, lets Wendy go, and walks out of Raisins a little wiser. Stan's bridge-crying, rain-soaked photo-staring grief becomes the episode's visual refrain before the boys drag him to Raisins.

Featured characters: Stan Marsh; Wendy Testaburger; Butters Stotch; Kyle Broflovski; Jimmy Valmer; Bebe Stevens; Lexus the Raisins waitress.

Locations: the football field; the rain-soaked bridge; Raisins restaurant.

Key events & continuity: Wendy breaks up with Stan, ending their long-running relationship; Butters' 'stay sweet' speech becomes one of the show's most quoted moments; Stan's Raisins obsession resolves when he accepts the breakup.

The Broflovskis are celebrating Hanukkah when Harry and Elise Gintz, a Canadian couple, arrive announcing they are Ike's biological parents, come to take him home. They gave Ike up during a turbulent time in Canada and have regretted it ever since. A new Canadian law from the Prime Minister requires all Canadian-born children living in America to be returned, and a South Park court cannot overrule a foreign law. Ike — birth name Peter — leaves for Canada the next day, devastating Gerald and Sheila. Two weeks later, Kyle finds his parents broken: Sheila wanders the house like a zombie and Gerald cannot stop crying. Moved by their grief, the whole town pools its Christmas gift money to send Kyle's family to Ottawa to plead with the Prime Minister. The kids are furious about losing their presents until Kyle proposes the boys go to Canada themselves and bring Ike back, saving everyone's gift money.

They fly north in a rickety Cessna run by City Wok owner Tuong Lu Kim, who dozes off and parachutes out, leaving the boys to crash-land in Canada unharmed. On the country's "only road" to Ottawa they meet Scott, a hostile Canadian who vows to stop them; Rick, a Mountie forced to ride a sheep after budget cuts; a French-Canadian mime; and Steve, a Newfoundlander whose boat gets them to Ottawa. The boys weep their way past Parliament guards and confront the Prime Minister, a giant floating head. Kyle's impassioned speech about family moves the Gintzes, but the Prime Minister vaporizes Kenny to prove his tyranny. While he rants, Stan pulls back a curtain to reveal Saddam Hussein operating the head from a spider-hole. Saddam is arrested, the laws are voided, and the Gintzes relent, letting Ike return to the Broflovskis. Cartman's watch beeps: it is Christmas Day. Kyle punches him once in the nose as promised; Cartman wails for his mother. Rick invites everyone to a Canadian Christmas parade, though Stan sighs his longed-for Christmas adventure passed him by.

Featured characters: Kyle Broflovski, who drives the rescue; Ike Broflovski (birth name Peter); Harry and Elise Gintz; Gerald and Sheila Broflovski; Stan, Cartman, and Kenny; Tuong Lu Kim; Scott the hostile Canadian; Rick the Mountie; Steve the Newfoundlander; Saddam Hussein.

Locations: the Broflovski home, South Park, the Cessna, the "only road" in Canada, Newfoundland, Ottawa's Parliament Buildings.

Key events & continuity: Saddam Hussein is exposed as Canada's secret Prime Minister and his laws are nullified; Kenny is vaporized and later returns; Ike's birth parents and birth name Peter enter continuity; the town sacrifices and then recovers its Christmas gift money; Cartman's promised fight with Kyle ends with one reluctant punch.

At the county fair, the boys talk a weapons-stall vendor into selling them real East Asian weapons by claiming they are orphan brothers whose parents died in a car accident. Stan takes two tonfas, Cartman two sais, Kyle two nunchaku, and Kenny a shuriken. They begin a pretend game as four anime ninjas, and whenever they play the world shifts into stylized anime — letterboxed, the boys drawn as adults, Japanese-style music behind them. After showing off to a jealous Craig, they reject Butters, who returns as Professor Chaos, bringer of destruction and doom. The ninjas clash with him: Stan's flame bounces off Chaos's titanium cape, Kyle freezes him with an icy blast, Cartman begs Kyle to restore his revoked powers — and is turned into a chicken — and Kenny hurls a shuriken into Professor Chaos's eye. The anime style snaps back to reality: a shuriken is lodged in Butters's eye and he is wailing in agony.

Fearing punishment, the boys disguise Butters badly as a dog using fur shaved off Sparky and rush him to an animal hospital. On the way, Craig and other kids who bought weapons of their own waylay them, and the two ninja factions fight an epic battle backed by the "Let's Fighting Love" song. When the dust settles, Butters is gone. His disguise fools the doctor, who ships him to the animal shelter, where the vet prepares to put him to sleep — only to find him escaped. The boys try to return the weapons to destroy the evidence, but the vendor refuses refunds. Learning Butters is near the fair auction, Cartman claims the power of invisibility, strips naked, and runs onstage to grab him. He has no such power, so he simply flashes the audience moments before Butters stumbles onstage. The crowd is outraged not by the violence but by Cartman's nudity. Butters finally gets treated: the shuriken removed, his wound bandaged under an eye patch. Kyle makes Cartman the scapegoat, and everyone agrees. The boys conclude parents care far more about nudity than violence, then slip back into their ninja forms and keep playing.

Featured characters: Stan, Kyle, Cartman, and Kenny as the four ninjas; Butters Stotch as Professor Chaos; Craig Tucker and his crew; the weapons vendor; Sparky, unwilling fur donor.

Locations: the county fair weapons stall, the anime fantasy battlescapes, the animal hospital, the animal shelter, the fair auction stage.

Key events & continuity: Butters's Professor Chaos persona appears in combat; the "Let's Fighting Love" anime song debuts; Kenny's shuriken genuinely maims Butters, leaving him with an eye patch; the boys' takeaway — adults panic about nudity while shrugging at violence — becomes a recurring theme.

Jimmy and Timmy prepare to compete in the Special Olympics in Denver and ask the boys to cheer them on. Cartman scoffs until he spots the $1,000 grand prize — then schemes to fake a disability, crush the competition, and pocket the money. He trains himself in a montage of handicapped mimicry: studying kids on the special-ed bus, cutting his hair badly, watching a Kid Rock performance, rigging his shoes to fake a club foot, and cinching a bicycle helmet tight enough to deform his face. He guilt-trips his mother into registering him by claiming he wants to understand how handicapped kids face the world. Meanwhile, while bench-pressing with Timmy, Jimmy is approached by Nathan lurking in a dark corner, who offers him undetectable steroids to guarantee victory. Jimmy takes them and the drugs warp him: he grows aggressive, his girlfriend Nancy dumps him, and he flies into a roid rage so violent he attacks Nancy and his own mother.

Timmy discovers the steroids in Jimmy's bag and is heartbroken, but can only say "Timmy!" and "Jimmy!" — he cannot explain what he saw to Mr. Mackey. Kyle spends the episode trying to talk Cartman out of his scheme, so disgusted that he worries Cartman will go to Hell and even calls himself Cartman's friend; Cartman ignores him, dismissing Kyle's moral authority because he is Jewish. At the games, Cartman's plan collapses: he never accounted for the handicapped athletes being in peak condition after weeks of training, so he finishes dead last while a steroid-fueled Jimmy takes first and is named the year's Special Olympian. Jimmy recognizes Cartman was faking and nearly attacks him, but Timmy restrains him. Then, at the microphone, Jimmy comes clean: steroids are cheating, no different from pretending to be handicapped to enter the Special Olympics. He returns his medal and gives a heartfelt speech the crowd applauds. Cartman collects a $50 Shakey's Pizza gift voucher as a spirit award and afterward claims he faked the disability to teach Jimmy a lesson about steroids — a lie the boys refuse to buy.

Featured characters: Jimmy Valmer, whose steroid arc drives the story; Timmy Burch, who discovers the cheating; Eric Cartman, scheming for the prize money; Kyle Broflovski, Cartman's would-be conscience; Nathan, the steroid supplier; Nancy, Jimmy's girlfriend; Liane Cartman; Mr. Mackey.

Locations: South Park, the Special Olympics venue in Denver, the school counselor's office.

Key events & continuity: Nathan debuts as Jimmy's rival and recurring antagonist; Jimmy's steroid use ends in a public confession and a returned medal; Cartman's fake-disability scheme fails and he finishes last; Timmy proves he can see through both cheaters; Kyle's Hell remark marks how far even he thinks Cartman has gone.

entries.n: S08E03 — The Passion of the Jew
entries.t:
In Liane's new minivan, Cartman taunts Kyle with claims from The Passion of the Christ — which he has watched 34 times — that the film proves the Jews are evil for freeing the killer Barabbas instead of Jesus. Kyle, rattled, sees the movie himself, endures Christ's final hours in horror, and leaves consumed with guilt over his Jewishness, dreaming of killing Jesus. Broken, he tells Cartman "you were right," which Cartman savors, praying to a Mel Gibson picture and vowing to organize the masses. Cartman holds a backyard rally in a Hitler-like brown uniform, gathering townspeople under the guise of rediscovering Christianity while secretly planning a second Holocaust, urging each attendee to bring one more person to see the film before "the cleansing."

Meanwhile Stan and Kenny see the movie, conclude it sucked, and demand their money back. Told to take it up with the producer, Stan calls a fan-club 1-800 number — run by Cartman, who hangs up on him — learns Gibson lives in Malibu, and drags Kenny there. They break into Gibson's mansion and find a raving masochist who refuses a refund; they steal cash from his wallet and flee. Father Maxi advises Kyle — who invents a fictitious friend to voice his guilt — that atonement is the answer. Kyle proposes at his synagogue that the Jewish community formally apologize to Christians for Jesus's death, as America apologized for slavery and Germany for the Holocaust; his parents and the congregation are outraged, while the rabbi insists people will realize it is just a movie. Outside, Cartman's followers goose-step down the street chanting German they mistake for Aramaic. The congregation marches on the theater to have the film pulled just as Cartman's mob approaches — and Gibson arrives chasing Stan and Kenny's bus in a tanker truck, screaming for his $18 back. The tanker explodes in front of the theater. Cartman offers Gibson his followers, but Gibson is fully unhinged and defecates into Cartman's face. Stan argues that Christians should follow Jesus's teachings, not fixate on how he died — that fixation belonged to the Dark Ages and got people killed. The townspeople abandon Cartman, and Kyle, his respect for Gibson destroyed, returns to normal.

Featured characters: Kyle Broflovski, consumed by film-induced guilt; Eric Cartman, building a neo-Nazi movement; Stan Marsh and Kenny McCormick, chasing a refund; Mel Gibson as a deranged masochist; Father Maxi; Gerald and Sheila Broflovski.

Locations: Liane's minivan, the theater, Cartman's backyard, Gibson's Malibu mansion, the synagogue.

Key events & continuity: Cartman's fan club becomes a Hitler-style movement with German chants the crowd mistakes for Aramaic; Stan's speech reframes the moral around Jesus's teachings; Gibson's insanity cures Kyle's guilt; Cartman ends humiliated.

entries.n: S08E04 — You Got F'd in the A
entries.t:
While the boys play with R/C cars, a troupe of kids from Orange County shows up, dances at them, and "serves" them before leaving with insults. The boys have no idea what being served means; Chef does, and calls their parents in alarm. Randy Marsh is furious his son was served and retaliates by teaching Stan a few basic line-dancing steps to Billy Ray Cyrus's "Achy Breaky Heart." When the Orange County kids return, Stan serves them back, and Cartman declares they just "got F'd in the A" — which the crew takes as a formal dance-contest challenge. Sharon pressures Randy over escalating things, so he goes to apologize to the Orange County coach — who instead serves Randy with devastating moves, hospitalizing him with the worst case of being served the doctors have ever seen. From his bed, Randy orders Stan to avenge him.

Stan assembles a team: Michael, one of the Goth Kids; Yao, a Dance Dance Revolution prodigy; and Mercedes, one of the Raisins girls. For a fifth member, Mercedes suggests Butters Stotch — once Colorado's tap-dancing champion. Butters runs away screaming, and a flashback explains why: two years earlier, at the national Tap-Dancing Finals, his shoe flew off mid-routine, struck a stage light, and set off a chain of calamities that killed eight audience members — eleven total, counting a pregnant woman and two suicides afterward. Butters flatly refuses to dance again. The team settles for Jeffy, a dancing duck from a local farm whose repertoire is limited to drug-and-sex parodies of "The Crawdad Song." On performance day, Jeffy sprains an ankle in rehearsal, seemingly forcing a forfeit — until Butters arrives in his tap outfit just in time. During the routine, Butters's shoe flies off again, hits a stage light, and drops a rafter of lights onto the Orange County team, killing them all. Horrified, blood-stained, and screaming, Butters is carried off and hailed as a hero as South Park wins by default.

Featured characters: Stan Marsh, team captain by paternal decree; Randy Marsh, hospitalized by dance; Butters Stotch, the traumatized tap champion; Michael the Goth Kid; Yao the DDR expert; Mercedes of the Raisins girls; Jeffy the dancing duck; Chef; Sharon Marsh; the Orange County dance crew and their coach.

Locations: the R/C car hangout spot, the Marsh home, the hospital, the farm, the dance contest stage, the flashback Tap-Dancing Finals arena.

Key events & continuity: Butters's tap-dancing past is established with its catastrophic body count; "serving" is treated as a genuine physical affliction doctors diagnose; the Orange County crew is wiped out in the finale, handing South Park a default victory; Randy's line-dancing to "Achy Breaky Heart" becomes his signature move.
k: you got f'd in the a

entries.t:
Cartman disguises himself as a robot called the A.W.E.S.O.M.-O 4000 and has himself delivered in a crate to Butters's doorstep with a Japanese address, planning to befriend the gullible Butters and extract his embarrassing secrets. The plan backfires immediately: Butters confides that he knows one of Cartman's secrets — a videotape of Cartman dressed as Britney Spears making out with a cardboard cutout of Justin Timberlake — which he will show the whole town the next time Cartman pranks him. Terrified, Cartman tears through Butters's room hunting for the tape while staying in costume, and starves because Butters believes robots don't eat. When Kyle, Stan, and Kenny check on him, Cartman begs them to play along. With Liane's agreement — she is letting him off punishment for trying to exterminate the Jews two weeks prior — and Butters's parents, who know it is Cartman but think Butters is in on the game, AWESOM-O is allowed to accompany Butters on a trip to Los Angeles to visit his aunt. Starving and miserable in the costume, Cartman sneaks off to a bathroom to eat toothpaste.

In Hollywood, movie producers hear about the robot and hire him from Butters to generate movie ideas; Cartman pitches over a thousand nonsensical concepts, 800 of them starring Adam Sandler, which the gullible producers buy. Then the U.S. military hears about AWESOM-O and captures him to convert him into a weapon. Cartman insists he is a kid, but the military concludes he is an AI robot programmed to seem human. A sympathetic scientist tries to save him, but Butters arrives to rescue AWESOM-O, forcing Cartman to keep up the disguise — and the military kills the scientist for interfering. Butters pleads for AWESOM-O's life and the general is moved. Then Cartman farts, and his identity is exposed. Butters makes good on his promise, showing the Britney Spears tape to the whole town, the producers, and the military. Butters celebrates his victorious revenge while everyone laughs at a humiliated Cartman, whom the general dismisses with a slur before Cartman mutters, "Lame!"

Featured characters: Eric Cartman as AWESOM-O; Butters Stotch, holding the tape; Stan, Kyle, and Kenny; Liane Cartman; Butters's parents; the Hollywood producers; the military general; the sympathetic scientist.

Locations: Butters's doorstep and bedroom, Los Angeles, the Hollywood studio, the secret military base, South Park.

Key events & continuity: direct callback to the previous episode — Cartman was being punished for trying to exterminate the Jews; Butters finally gets revenge on Cartman and the tape is shown publicly; AWESOM-O's thousand-plus movie pitches, mostly Adam Sandler vehicles, become a running joke about Hollywood.

The boys notice the Donovans' old house has been bought. A masked boy named Blanket greets them and invites them in. Inside are arcade games, toys, and a backyard circus, where "Mr. Jefferson" in a fake mustache invites them to climb his Wishing Tree and bursts into song. Jefferson ignores Kyle when he points out Blanket cannot climb. Jefferson neglects Blanket while doting on the others, leaving Kyle to clean his scraped knee himself. Blanket reveals he is a test-tube baby who never knew his mother. Kyle concludes Jefferson would rather be a kid than raise one; Cartman warns him not to ruin it. Told the Jeffersons are wealthy and black, police plant drugs and blood in his home overnight to frame him. When Jefferson returns, they see his skin isn't black and abort, horrified they nearly jailed a white man.

Jefferson, dressed as Peter Pan, wakes Stan at his window wanting to play; Cartman climbs through too, and Kyle arrives with Blanket, found alone outside. They all sleep over in Stan's bed, and Stan dreams of Cartman and Jefferson making out. In the morning, Stan's parents find Jefferson in bed and reprimand him; he pays them $100 each to stay quiet and leaves. Barred from going outside, Blanket greets the boys from his window; Jefferson dangles him out of it, and a nose-taking game goes wrong when Blanket pulls off his father's nose. As his face falls apart from years of plastic surgery, Jefferson calls his California surgeon. The boys sneak in to rescue Blanket, swapping in a disguised Kenny — Jefferson tosses him too high and Kenny's head smashes through the ceiling, killing him. Outside, police wait to arrest Jefferson on molestation charges from Santa Barbara, where Yates learns they framed a rich black man who fled before trial. Cartman defends Jefferson: he never had a childhood because he worked all the time when young. Kyle adds that while both are understandable, Jefferson must grow up because he has a child of his own now. Jefferson vows to be a father to Blanket and gives away his wealth to the needy — leaving no reason to arrest him, since he is no longer rich.

Featured characters: "Mr. Jefferson" and Blanket; Stan, Kyle, Cartman, Kenny; Harrison Yates and the Park County police; Randy and Sharon Marsh.

Locations: the Jeffersons' mansion, Stark's Pond, Stan's house, the police station.

Key events & continuity: Kenny dies when thrown through a ceiling; Yates learns Santa Barbara police framed Jefferson, who fled before trial; police abort their frame-up upon seeing Jefferson isn't black, though Yates's wife insists framing wealthy black people is "in his blood"; Jefferson gives away his fortune and commits to fatherhood.

A strange alien-looking man steps out of a glowing portal and is promptly hit by a car. When the boys offer to shovel a woman's driveway, Cartman demands $8,000 and settles for $15; Kyle hits him with a shovel for lounging. Inside, they catch a CNN report: the man came from a thousand years in the future seeking work because of overpopulation — his earnings will feed his family in 3045 — and his portal follows one-way "Terminator rules." Soon more future-people arrive: hairless, a uniform blend of all races, speaking a guttural mix of all world languages. The boys lose their shoveling jobs to immigrants working for 25 cents.

At a union meeting, construction worker Darryl Weathers rails that the newcomers work for almost nothing, and the room erupts in "DEY TOOK OUR JEBS!!" — a chant that degrades into "Dey tuk er jerbs!" and finally "Derka Dur!" Stan dubs the immigrants "goobacks," after the goo coating them from time travel. The Marshes hire one as a housekeeper for 10 cents an hour while Randy lectures Stan against judging them. Weathers debates an "aging hippie liberal douche" on cable news and can only answer with the chant. When the congressman rules shooting border-crossers inhumane, Weathers decides the group must "stop the future from happening." At a fast-food joint staffed by immigrants, Stan screams slurs at the cashier just as his parents walk in — earning a grounding for his "intolerant mouth." The protesters strip naked and pile together in front of the immigrant district, Little Future, convinced mass gay sex will stop the future. Even Randy rages when an immigrant geologist takes his job for less. At the rally, Stan takes the microphone and admits it is wrong to call them "goobacks" — they are no different from anyone else — and argues the present should make the future better so they won't need to come. South Park cleans itself up — planting trees, recycling, giving to the poor, cleaner energy — and the immigrants fade. Then Stan stops: "this is gay." Kyle agrees. Cartman calls it gayer than the pile. Stan apologizes: "Everyone back in the pile." The men rush back yelling "Derka der!"

Featured characters: Stan Marsh; Darryl Weathers, the union foreman; Randy and Sharon Marsh; Kyle and Cartman; Mr. Garrison; the future immigrants.

Locations: South Park, the time portal, the union hall, Little Future, the fast-food restaurant, the protest at the time border.

Key events & continuity: the "Dey took our jobs!" chant debuts and devolves into "Derka Dur!"; the portal's one-way "Terminator rules" are established; Stan coins and later renounces the slur "goobacks"; the pile gag is restored after the cleanup is judged too gay.

During a pep rally, a local PETA group protests South Park Elementary's cow mascot, and the school agrees to let students vote for a new one. Embarrassed by the bland official choices, the kids write in joke candidates — but split over whether it should be a "giant douche" or a "turd sandwich." Kyle rallies support for the giant douche while Cartman campaigns for the turd sandwich; Kenny sides with Kyle, partly because Cartman recently broke his cat's leg, and Cartman wins Butters by slanting the question about which is funnier. The vote ties, forcing a runoff marked by bribes and scare tactics. Stan alone refuses to vote for either, declaring the whole exercise pointless. His parents are unimpressed and insist he vote, the town turns on him, and P. Diddy terrorizes him with a literal Vote or Die campaign. Not wanting to die, Stan concedes — but when he tries to vote turd sandwich, Kyle refuses to allow it and demands he vote giant douche. Realizing his best friend was only using him to beat Cartman, Stan refuses to vote again. The school banishes him from town: placed on horseback, bound, a bucket over his head, sent into the woods.

He reaches the PETA encampment, where the humans have grown intimate with the animals to the point of bestiality. The head member finally gives Stan a real reason to vote: an election is always between a giant douche and a turd sandwich, because they are the only people who suck up enough to make it that far in politics. P. Diddy arrives to kill Stan but is distracted when a PETA member throws blood on his fur coat; enraged, he slaughters the entire camp. Stan takes a bullet in the shoulder but escapes. Back in South Park, convinced at last, he votes turd sandwich — and the giant douche still wins 1,410 to 36. Randy assures him all votes matter even for the losing side. Then Mr. Garrison bursts in: the PETA members have been found murdered, so the cow is reinstated as mascot. Randy cheerfully tells Stan his vote didn't matter after all.

Featured characters: Stan Marsh, the non-voter; Kyle Broflovski and Eric Cartman, rival campaign managers; Kenny McCormick; Butters Stotch; Randy and Sharon Marsh; P. Diddy; the PETA encampment; Mr. Garrison.

Locations: South Park Elementary, the Marsh home, the woods, the PETA encampment.

Key events & continuity: the giant douche vs. turd sandwich framing of elections becomes one of the show's most quoted bits; Stan is formally banished and un-banished; P. Diddy's Vote or Die campaign ends with him massacring the PETA camp; the cow mascot is restored, rendering the entire election moot.

entries.n: S08E09 — Something Wall-Mart This Way Comes
entries.t:
Cartman bets Kyle five dollars that people shit their pants when they die. A new Wall-Mart opens at Metzger's Field, and the town succumbs to its bargains — Randy sneaks in at odd hours and buys in bulk. Only Kyle is uneasy. The next morning, Main Street is a ghost town: Jim's Drugs, Tom's Rhinoplasty, everything shuttered, everyone shopping at Wall-Mart instead. The boys rally a boycott. The store president defends Wall-Mart aloud while scribbling that it isn't safe to speak inside, then hangs himself as they leave — and shits his pants, winning Cartman the bet. The town burns the Wall-Mart down singing "Kumbaya," but it is rebuilt overnight on orders from the "higher-ups" in Bentonville, Arkansas. Kyle, Stan, and Kenny travel to Bentonville to stop it at the source. The store "speaks" to Cartman, warning him; he catches up pretending to join them and slashes the bus tires, but they reach headquarters anyway. President Harvey Brown tells them to find and destroy Wall-Mart's "heart" — then shoots himself, shitting his pants. Cartman declares Kyle owes him ten bucks.

Back in a dilapidated South Park, the boys approach dressed like the Frog Brothers. Cartman confronts them with a knife, declaring he was working with the store all along to protect its terrific bargains. Kenny holds Cartman off while Stan and Kyle enter; Randy, clutching a sale axe, succumbs to a $9.98 screwdriver set but hands over his keys. In the television department, a man who says he is Wall-Mart points them beyond a plasma screen — to a mirror. "You. The consumer. I take many forms, but I am one single entity: desire." The boys smash the mirror; the building implodes, and dying Wall-Mart shits its pants. Cartman crows that Kyle owes him fifteen. Randy gives a speech: Wall-Mart was "us," and keeping the town's charm means spending a little more. Jimbo suggests Jim's Drugs — which grows in a time lapse until it resembles Wall-Mart. The town burns it down, and everyone heads for True Value instead. The cycle continues.

Featured characters: Stan, Kyle, Cartman, and Kenny; Randy Marsh, consumed by bargains; the Wall-Mart store president; Harvey Brown; the man who is Wall-Mart; Jimbo.

Locations: Metzger's Field, the Wall-Mart, Main Street's shuttered shops, Bentonville Arkansas and Wall-Mart HQ, Jim's Drugs.

Key events & continuity: Cartman's death-bet escalates from $5 to $10 to $15 as executives keep dying and shitting their pants; Wall-Mart is revealed as a single entity — consumer desire — with its heart a mirror; Randy's "Wall-Mart was us" speech; the final gag shows Jim's Drugs becoming the new Wall-Mart, proving the cycle repeats.

Stan panics: Trent Boyett, their preschool classmate, is being released from Juvenile Hall. In flashback, they recall playing "fireman," starting a real fire they planned to extinguish. They have Trent, the toughest preschooler, light it over Butters's warning. They urinated on the flames and declared they had "saved the school"; when Miss Claridge tried to extinguish it, she was engulfed, and they urinated on her too. When the cops arrived, the boys scapegoated Trent and called him a liar; Butters refused to defend him. Dragged away, Trent warned them to pray he never got out. Now Miss Claridge is confined to a motorized wheelchair, communicating only by beeps — once for yes, twice for no. A furious Trent tells a guard, "I've got some business to take care of."

Butters's parents lock him outside, where Trent waits. Butters wastes his five-second head start apologizing; Trent beats him into the hospital. Meanwhile Miss Claridge's wheelchair battery dies mid-street, and the townspeople assume she has grown despondent. The boys beg the 6th graders for protection; the price is a photo of Stan's mom's breasts, so Stan photographs Cartman's buttocks with nipples drawn. The 6th graders fall for it, but Trent beats them anyway. The boys ask Shelly, who agrees if they confess to Miss Claridge — she wants to be the only one who beats them up. They find Miss Claridge stalled in the street as Trent arrives. He says they had five years — missing a talking Christmas Poo and a mechanized Barbra Streisand — and once his revenge is done, the matter is settled. Cartman fires his mom's taser at Trent, misses, and shocks Miss Claridge instead; her wheelchair spins out of control, crashes into a propane shop, and explodes — setting her ablaze before a hydrant douses the flames. The cops, convinced Trent crippled her years ago, assume he tried to finish her; the boys call him a liar once more. Asked if Trent tried to kill her, Miss Claridge beeps twice — no — but the cop hears "yes, yes" and arrests Trent again. The boys are safe for another five years. Cartman moons the departing Trent, forgetting the nipples on his butt; the battered 6th graders return, are fooled again, and drag Cartman into "the bushes."

Featured characters: Trent Boyett; Stan, Kyle, Cartman, Kenny; young Butters; Miss Claridge; Shelly; the 6th graders.

Locations: the preschool (flashback), Juvenile Hall, the Stotch home, the street, the propane shop.

Key events & continuity: the boys' preschool arson and scapegoating of Trent is established; Miss Claridge's beep-code causes Trent's re-arrest through a misunderstanding; Trent name-checks the talking Christmas Poo and mechanized Barbra Streisand; Cartman's fake-breasts photo fools the 6th graders twice.

The boys tape "Super School News," a newscast for South Park Elementary's closed-circuit TV: Cartman and Jimmy anchor, Butters covers entertainment, Stan reports from the field, Tolkien does weather, and Kyle does sports. Their teacher Mr. Meryl delivers the ratings: horrible, trailing far behind Craig's home-video show "Animals Close-Up With a Wide-Angle Lens" — set to "Yakety Sax" — which they consider pointless and banal. Even Kenny is helping Craig, which Cartman calls betrayal, though he had mocked Kenny for being poor to keep him off the show. The team vows a ratings booster: they rebrand as "Sexy Action School News" and add flashy bits, including Panda Madness Minutes in which the anchors spontaneously dance with pandas. It beats Craig's original but falls behind his follow-up, "Animals Close-Up With a Wide-Angle Lens Wearing Hats." Desperate for ideas, the boys get high on cough syrup. They hallucinate, run wild, pass out, and wake disoriented — watching Craig's show, a naked Butters face-down in Kyle's lap, their notepads empty. Remembering they found Craig's show brilliant while high, they conclude the school must be perpetually high on cough syrup and produce a special report that gets cough syrup banned. Ratings collapse, Craig's show is cancelled, and the kids cough endlessly. To stress the importance of ratings, the AV teacher suspends Craig and recommends removing his testicles. Victorious, the news team discovers the curse of a hit show: every episode must be just as good. In the writers' room they come up with nothing and decide to just bail.

Featured characters: Cartman, Jimmy, Butters, Stan, Tolkien, and Kyle as the news team; Craig Tucker; Kenny McCormick; Mr. Meryl; the AV teacher.

Locations: South Park Elementary, the closed-circuit studio, the writers' room.

Key events & continuity: the show-within-a-show ratings war escalates through increasingly absurd Craig sequels; Panda Madness Minutes debuts; the boys' cough-syrup ban accidentally torpedoes Craig's ratings; Craig is suspended and threatened with testicle removal; the team abandons the show rather than face the sophomore curse.

entries.n: S08E12 — Stupid Spoiled Whore Video Playset
entries.t:
Paris Hilton appears at the South Park Mall; Wendy is mocked for not knowing her. Hilton opens Stupid Spoiled Whore — mispronouncing the town as "Gouth Dark" — stocked with lewd clothing and "Skanque" perfume. Wendy is appalled. As her limo pulls away, Hilton's dog steals the driver's gun and shoots itself; she shrieks that another dog killed itself. The girls get the Stupid Spoiled Whore Video Playset — night-vision filter, fake money, losable cell phone, 16 hits of ecstasy — and Wendy flees. Grieving Tinkerbell, Hilton takes Butters as her replacement pet, dressing him in a bear costume as "Mr. Biggles" — though he believes he is her boyfriend. Hilton offers his parents $200 million; they demand $250 million and tell Butters to earn it himself, suggesting coal mining. He fails. In her limo, Butters finds a photo album: all Hilton's pets killed themselves — Tinkerbell with the gun, Patches by hanging, Scrambles by slit wrists, Cuddles by seppuku. Butters flees, costing his father $250 million; his dad grounds him.

Wendy tricks her father into visiting the store to shut it down, but he is seduced and vows to make her the "stupidest, most spoiled whore of them all." Bebe throws a Stupid Spoiled Whore party, excluding Wendy as too smart to qualify. The girls, in skimpy outfits, proposition boys in the hallway; the boys are terrified — Stan is held down and forced to kiss Red, Clyde emerges from "2 Minutes in the Closet" in tears muttering "Owie!" — and Cartman, ignored, flips each girl off. Wendy seeks out Mr. Slave, the biggest whore she knows, who explains whorehood is inborn, then storms Bebe's party.
