Nelson summons the students to the gym: when Cartman enters, everyone yells "Hello Fatso!" Cartman is furious — until Nelson steps out and Cartman dissolves into laughter again. To clear his name, Randy founds the Randy Marsh African American Scholarship Foundation; leaving the opening, he's chased by shotgun rednecks — until fellow "Nigger-Guys" led by Seinfeld's Michael Richards rescue him. Fed up, Stan demands why Tolkien is still angry; Butters interrupts — Cartman's fighting Dr. Nelson. Nelson, a karate black belt, plans to beat Cartman to prove words shouldn't hurt; Cartman easily wins. The "Nigger-Guys" lobby the Senate to ban "Nigger-Guy"; it passes — saying both words within seven words is now prosecutable. Pinned, Nelson "gives up," then lands a cheap shot; Cartman keeps laughing. Nelson storms off claiming he "proved" his point, which nobody understood. Finally Stan gets it: he'll never understand how the N-word feels because he's not black — what Tolkien wanted to hear.

Featured characters: Randy Marsh, the "Nigger-Guy"; Stan; Tolkien; Eric Cartman; Dr. David Nelson; Jesse Jackson; Michael Richards.

Locations: the Wheel of Fortune studio, the school, the gym, the comedy club, the Senate.

Key events & continuity: Randy says the N-word on live TV solving "Naggers"; the "Nigger-Guy" label follows him until the Senate bans it; Jackson accepts a butt-kiss apology; Cartman's laughter defeats Nelson's campaign and karate; Stan finally tells Tolkien he'll never understand.

Stan, Kyle, and Kenny see Cartman's scrapbook of sleepover pranks on Butters — and learn Butters is coming tonight for the "best" prank ever. The next day Cartman brags he put Butters's penis in his mouth while he slept, calling Butters gay. Kyle points out the obvious: since Cartman did the putting, he's the one who'll look gay. As a joke, Kyle tells him to have Butters return the favor to "cancel out the gay polarity." Cartman believes him. That night he blindfolds Butters and tricks him toward oral sex — but Stephen catches them first. Cartman flees; Stephen, taking it out of context, tells Butters he's bi-curious. Butters plays along, clueless.

On Priest Maxi's advice, Butters is sent to Camp New Grace, where they "pray away the gay" — housing bi-curious boys together and teaching them Jesus. It's doing more harm than good: the counselors are unsympathetic and suicides seem regular. Meanwhile Cartman learns Kyle lied about gay polarity, but consoles himself that "no one will ever know" if he destroys the photo. Too late: the boys already saw it and threaten to tell unless he's "super-nice." Cartman vows to swap Kyle's face onto it — then finds the picture gone. He accuses Kyle, who denies it; Liane phones Sheila, who confirms Kyle doesn't have it. With no other move, Cartman decides to show the picture himself at show and tell, robbing Kyle of the satisfaction. At camp, Butters is roomed with Bradley; both are punished over a men's underwear catalog. Bradley realizes he "likes" Butters; Butters takes it as friendship. Convinced he's unfixable, Bradley runs off threatening suicide. At school, Cartman starts his "artsy photographs" show and tell. At the bridge, counselors warn Butters he'll make it worse. Butters snaps: he's sick of being told he's confused — he wasn't until people said so — and if he's made in God's image, God must be a little bi-curious. Bradley climbs down. Stephen takes Butters home, musing he might be bi-curious too, leaving Butters genuinely confused. Back at school, Cartman finally shows the photo to gasps — just as Mr. Mackey arrives with his mom's message: the picture was lost in his room all along. Cartman: "Lame..."

Featured characters: Eric Cartman; Butters; Stan, Kyle, Kenny; Stephen; Bradley; Priest Maxi; Liane; Sheila; Mr. Mackey.

Locations: Cartman's house, Camp New Grace, South Park Elementary, the bridge.

Key events & continuity: Cartman's "best prank" backfires via Kyle's fake "gay polarity" science; Butters is sent to a pray-the-gay-away camp where his speech talks Bradley off the bridge; the compromising photo was lost in Cartman's room the whole time; Cartman's show-and-tell reveal lands with a "Lame..."

Garrison warns of a Denver lice breakout; Cartman insists only poor people — Kenny — get lice. The gym inspection finds Clyde has lice; he gets special shampoo. Inside Clyde's head lives a lice civilization. Travis Mayfield spots a human doctor and warns Vice President Greg the outside world is reacting — calling for a lice-wide evacuation. Nobody takes him seriously except his wife Kelly. Then it rains — Clyde showering — and Travis reads it as an omen, urging Kelly and daughter Hope to flee to another "world." The shampoo kills; most of the population melts in the acid. Travis, Kelly, and Hope flee to the "trees" (hair follicles) — until a great wind (Clyde drying his hair) knocks masses off. Kelly's arm breaks; she falls to her death, leaving Travis screaming, alone with Hope.

Cartman asks Garrison who had lice; she won't name names. He researches detection. Travis wakes among the VP and disfigured survivors. Most stay; Travis, Hope, an unnamed female louse, and the VP head for the "Forbidden Zone" (Clyde's face). The VP loads a pistol. Cartman invites the boys for a blood test, claiming the guilty party's blood will leap from the dish. The rigged test implicates Kenny, who flees. At Clyde's, the boys plan Kenny's sock bath — wet soap, dirty socks — and Clyde phones Garrison to warn her. In the Forbidden Zone, the VP shoots the female louse dead, planning to repopulate their world and purge Travis's kind. Travis is shot in the knees at the Zone's edge (the back of Clyde's neck). Arguing whether their world is conscious, the VP fires into the ground; Clyde feels it, grabs him, and hurls him onto the sidewalk, killing him. At the park, the boys prep Kenny's sock bath until Kyle stops them: the lice were HIS. Stan is stunned — he thought they were his. Then Cartman admits he had lice too and was framing Kenny. Garrison arrives with the truth: everyone in class had lice, and it spreads fast. The students (except Clyde) give Kenny the sock bath anyway, for lying. Dying, Travis is carried by a fly to a land where bigger red lice have lived in peace for "generations" — revealed as Angelina Jolie's pubic hair. The lice were crabs.

Featured characters: Travis, Kelly, and Hope; Vice President Greg; Clyde; Eric Cartman; Stan, Kyle, Kenny; Ms. Garrison.

Locations: the school, the gym, Clyde's head, the Forbidden Zone, the park, Angelina Jolie's pubic hair.

Key events & continuity: the lice apocalypse parallels the kids' witch hunt; Cartman's rigged test frames Kenny; Kyle and Cartman confess; the whole class had lice; Kenny gets the sock bath for lying; Travis's "paradise" is crabs.

New student Baahir Hassan Abdul Hakeem arrives; Cartman freaks out: he's a terrorist. Cartman has sick-at-home Kyle check Baahir's MySpace. The only anomaly: favorite band White Stripes online, Blink-182 in class. Cartman calls Officer Barbrady; the school is evacuated. Butters invites Baahir for checkers. Cartman has Kyle Google upcoming events: Hillary Clinton is holding a rally in South Park today. Cartman calls the CIA to cancel the rally. Hillary refuses to be bullied by terrorist threats. Her aide Chris warns the Russian cell: they know about the bomb. It was meant for Boston; heightened security moved it to South Park. Cartman searches the rally crowd for Baahir, doesn't find him, and heads for his house. Onstage, Hillary speaks while the CIA releases a bomb-sniffing pig — which locates the bomb in Hillary's vagina.

CIA head Alan Thompson teams with Cartman to raid Baahir's house. Kyle traced a rally YouTube account to Russian leader Vladimir Stolfsky — an old-school communist per his MySpace and blog. The raid finds no detonator — Baahir is at Butters's house. Cartman interrogates Baahir's parents, torturing them by farting in their faces. Kyle and Stan track Vladimir's purchases via his podcasts and eBay links; Homeland Security bursts in and takes over, then the FBI, then the ATF, then the President's staff. Kyle seizes control using each agency's own takeover line: "Not anymore you're not." Baahir's mother gets a call: he's at Butters's. Cartman goes in alone — and he and Baahir are captured by Vladimir, acting for America's "first enemy." Cartman guesses Russians, then Germans, then Germans again, before the disbelieving answer: the British. Baahir warns the British are using them; Vladimir shrugs, "Maybe, but we'll be rich." The British plan: the bomb distracts America while they sail over in wooden boats to "end the American Revolution." Troops stop the Russians, jets sink the British. Learning her ships are sunk, Queen Elizabeth II puts a handgun in her mouth and fires. Cartman takes credit: Muslims weren't responsible, but his intolerance uncovered the plot. Baahir's family leaves the country over the town's racism — to Butters's dismay, which Cartman also claims credit for.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman, counter-terrorist; Baahir; Kyle (sick at home); Stan; Butters; Hillary Clinton; Vladimir Stolfsky; Alan Thompson; Queen Elizabeth II.

Locations: the school, the rally, Baahir's house, Butters's house, the warehouse.

Key events & continuity: the "snuke" is in Hillary Clinton's vagina, found by a bomb-sniffing pig; the true villains are the British; the Queen kills herself when her fleet sinks; Cartman credits his intolerance; Baahir's family leaves over the town's racism.

Coloring eggs, Stan asks what it has to do with Jesus' resurrection. Randy's answer is vague, so Stan asks a mall Easter Bunny — "just Easter," "just go with it" — who makes a mysterious call. Soon Stan is chased by men in bunny suits. At home, Randy reveals the "Hare Club for Men," guardians of Easter's secret, and takes Stan to their headquarters; the club reveres a rabbit named Snowball. Ninjas ambush; members shield Snowball; Randy hands the rabbit to Stan: run. Stan escapes as the ninjas execute a resisting hare and interrogate Randy. He drags a reluctant, clueless Kyle into it.

They track down Professor Teabag, who explains: da Vinci was a Hare Club member, and Saint Peter was a rabbit painted as one in the Last Supper. No human could lead Christianity incorruptibly; rabbits were pure — hence the Pope's mitre shaped for rabbit ears. The Church buried the secret and installed a man; the Hare Club decorated eggs for generations to preserve it, and Snowball descends from St. Peter. The Vatican kidnapped Randy and the members, calling the secret blasphemy. Ninjas kill Teabag's butler; Teabag microwaves Peeps into an explosion that destroys the mansion, killing him and the ninjas. At the Vatican, Stan surrenders Snowball for the members' freedom and Snowball's safety. Donohue swore on two separate crucifixes — a "double cross" — and plans to make an example of them. Pope Benedict XVI objects — not "very Christian." Donohue: it's what Jesus would want. Then Jesus arrives — resurrected after being killed in Iraq — answering a member's prayer, confirming he intended rabbit popes. Benedict and the clergy agree; Donohue orders Benedict to execute Jesus. Benedict won't — killing Jesus isn't "very Christian." Enraged, Donohue seizes the mitre, captures everyone, and declares himself Pope. Kyle and Jesus are locked up while Donohue marches the rest to the block, where a gigantic pot awaits Snowball. In the cell, Jesus tells Kyle his powers only work when he's dead — Kyle must kill him so he resurrects outside, on condition Cartman never finds out. As Donohue raises the blade, the resurrected Jesus appears and kills him with a five-bladed sword. The crowd cheers; Snowball is elected Pope. A rabbit can't dictate how people live — "just as Jesus intended." Stan's lesson: don't ask questions; just dye the eggs. Randy is proud.

Featured characters: Stan; Kyle; Randy; Snowball; Teabag; Donohue; Pope Benedict XVI; Jesus.

Locations: the Marsh house, the South Park Mall, the Hare Club headquarters, Teabag's mansion, the Vatican.

Key events & continuity: the Hare Club guards Easter's secret; Saint Peter was a rabbit; Jesus confirms rabbit popes were the plan; Donohue dies; Snowball becomes Pope.

Furious after a bad blind date, Garrison assigns The Old Man and the Sea with an essay due Monday. Cartman has a plan: he orders Mexicans at a truck rental to read the book and write four essays. The boys enjoy their weekend. At the all-female gym Curves, Garrison curses men on the treadmill; Allison bonds with her over disliking men and invites her to the all-female bar Les Bos. Garrison realizes it's a lesbian bar and flees horrified; Allison talks her around, and they spend the night together.

Monday, the boys return for their essays — but the Mexicans read the book without writing essays; they wrote to their "esses" (friends) instead. The boys blame Cartman; everyone else did the reports. Garrison gives them more time — then announces she's gay. Stan: "Again?" The class cheers her on. That night Garrison returns to Les Bos confidently, until news breaks: the Persians are buying it out and closing it for good. Garrison refuses to leave, drags the lesbians to Mayor McDaniels — who sends them away — and rallies them not to give up. Persian rep Emir Hadi comes to reason and meets a wall. Garrison: "No. This isn't crazy. THIS IS LES BOS!" — then kicks him in the balls. The standoff hits the news; lesbians everywhere rally to their cause. Emir reports 30 lesbians won't budge and calls reinforcements. The "battle" is just pushing and shoving until the Persians tire and retreat. Their boss Rauf Xerxes is furious and comes to confront the lesbians personally. Garrison sends Mexicans to infiltrate Club Persh, the Persian base, for dirt. A day passes; the lesbians flag, Garrison brews coffee, and the Mexicans return with Xerxes intel. Garrison reveals she knows Xerxes is secretly a woman — exposure would end her, since women can't be boss in Persian culture. But lesbians accept women as they are; Xerxes is delighted, sleeps with Garrison, and lets Les Bos stay. Allison asks why Garrison isn't teaching: the school hired the Mexicans as substitutes. They're teaching Math — and Kyle says he's actually learning for once.

Featured characters: Janet Garrison; Allison; Emir Hadi; Rauf Xerxes; the Mexicans; Stan, Kyle, Kenny, Cartman; Mayor McDaniels.

Locations: South Park Elementary, Curves gym, Les Bos, the mayor's office, Club Persh, the truck rental.

Key events & continuity: Garrison comes out as a lesbian (again); the "esses" mix-up torpedoes the homework scheme; the 300-style standoff saves Les Bos; Xerxes is secretly a woman and defects; the Mexicans become substitutes.

entries.n: S11E07 — Night of the Living Homeless
entries.t:
Homeless people take over the boys' court. Kyle feels sorry for them; Cartman stages a skateboard jump over one as a showcase. The City Council debates dehumanizing solutions; only Alexis Testaburger defends the homeless. The advisor warns: give no money, or more will come. That night Kyle gives a beggar twenty dollars; the man demands more. By morning a crowd gathers outside Kyle's house. Kyle confesses; Cartman thinks he gathered jump fodder. Randy is swarmed; he gives change and more keep coming. He joins Gerald, Jimbo, and the Stotches on the Community Center roof.

The homeless overrun the town; Stan and Kyle spot their fathers on the roof before the news is cut off. The mayor's aide Ted picks them up — then his car is hit by a truck, killing him instantly. The boys escape through the sewers to the scientist's house. Gerald gives away his change trying to reach a bus station, then begs for it back — making the adults think he's one of them. Cartman plans to jump ALL the homeless; Kyle snaps he barely cleared one. The scientist explains the homeless live off change like food — no amount is ever enough — and says Evergreen faced the same crisis and stopped it. The homeless break in; the boys flee while the scientist shoots himself repeatedly to no effect. On the roof, new refugees arrive and food runs low. Councilman Glen's house is foreclosed — he's homeless now. He begs change for storage; Randy shoots him dead. In destroyed Evergreen, three camouflaged men explain: the homeless gathered enough change to buy houses, and the paranoia ("you wouldn't know if the person next door was homeless") destroyed the town — nobody realizing homeownership ended homelessness. One man killed his wife for being "homeless." Kyle finds a pamphlet advertising South Park to the homeless: Evergreen just exported its problem. The "dead" wife, horribly burned, attacks; everyone dies except the boys. The boys rig a bus and lure the homeless to California by singing, with Gerald trailing behind begging for change. In California, Cartman jumps three homeless people while Stan can't see how it helps.

Featured characters: Stan, Kyle, Cartman, Kenny; Randy; Gerald; Glen; the scientist; Alexis Testaburger; Ted.

Locations: the court, the Community Center roof, the sewers, the scientist's house, Evergreen, California.

Key events & continuity: Kyle's $20 triggers the swarm; Randy shoots Glen; the homeless live off change; Evergreen destroyed itself over homeowner paranoia and exported its homeless; the boys bus them to California.

At a toy store, Cartman meets Thomas, a boy with Tourette's, and sees scheme potential. Diagnosed; the school will be informed. The next day he swears at everyone, even Principal Victoria and Mr. Mackey — no consequences, thanks to the diagnosis. Kyle calls him a faker. Cartman explains the scheme's brilliance and invites Kyle to be a "Buzzkill" and try stopping him.  Garrison complains to Victoria, who introduces Mr. Donaldson of a Tourette's tolerance foundation. Kyle declares Cartman is faking — but Donaldson, also a sufferer, dubs Kyle a bully. Kyle is dragged to a Children's Therapy Center support group, where the kids describe how hard Tourette's is to live with. Kyle apologizes to the group — and is forced to apologize to Cartman too. Cartman skips off, leaving Thomas evidence he's faking.

Chris Hansen announces a letter from a "brave little boy with Tourette's" (Cartman) who wants filming. Kyle confronts him over the planned on-air hate speech; Cartman says he's already won. Cartman rhapsodizes about saying whatever comes to mind — then blurts that he wet his bed last night. At Whistlin' Willy's, Cartman is announced as the national TV spokesperson for Tourette's. A worried Thomas teams with Kyle — and blurts that Cartman is faking, plus his own secrets: crying at night over having no dad, a crush on Patty Nelson. Cartman realizes he's lost the ability to filter anything. He asks Butters for "cousin" advice, then blurts they "touched wieners" and flees. He cancels on Hansen — his grandmother died — then blurts she's fine. Hansen once tracked a pedophile for To Catch a Predator; the man was found and committed suicide. Hansen hopes Cartman won't be found the same way — and Cartman admits he urinated himself. Five minutes before air, Cartman prays for a miracle while blaming God. Outside, Kyle and Thomas hatch a plan: Thomas lures pedophiles inside pretending it's his home. They recognize Hansen and shoot themselves in the head. The audience flees; Thomas curses out Hansen. Craig calls Thomas the luckiest boy alive. In the empty studio, Kyle tells Cartman he's beaten. Cartman hugs and thanks him: Kyle saved him from live humiliation. He skips off to find a psychiatrist as Kyle and Thomas exclaim, "Aw, shit!"

Featured characters: Eric Cartman; Kyle; Thomas; Chris Hansen; Mr. Donaldson; Liane; Principal Victoria; Mr. Mackey; Ms. Garrison; Butters; Craig.

Locations: the toy store, South Park Elementary, the Children's Therapy Center, Whistlin' Willy's, the Dateline studio.

Key events & continuity: Cartman fakes Tourette's to swear consequence-free; Kyle is forced to apologize to a faker; Cartman loses his mental filter; Thomas outs him; the pedophile ambush saves Cartman from live TV; he hugs Kyle in gratitude.

A doctor visit reveals Randy is badly constipated. After weeks without going, his trip to the toilet is agonizing — but before flushing, he notices the size of the dump and is amazed. Sharon and Shelly are disgusted; Stan is awestruck. At the bar, Randy and Jimbo show Gerald, Stephen, Stuart, and Skeeter, who tell him to apply for the world record. The European Fecal Standards and Measurements Board confirms it: the world's biggest crap. The previous holder is Bono — and he's not happy. At Randy's award ceremony, a message arrives from Bono claiming HE made the world's biggest crap; the Board strips Randy and restores Bono. After days of misery, the bar guys convince Randy to go for the record again. Three weeks later, Bono learns of the attempt and demands Randy crap in front of the Board — but Randy's doctor says he can't travel. Stan goes to Bono's mansion to beg the star to let his dad win, since Randy has never won anything; Bono refuses. Stan pleads: let his dad be number one, and Bono can be happy as number two. Bono viciously attacks Stan, threatening him to say he's not number two. The butler warns Stan his dad will die attempting a bigger crap. Stan asks how Bono crapped so much and lived — and the butler reveals the secret. In Zurich, Stan tells the Board that Bono wasn't the record holder — he WAS the record. A Board member admits he crapped Bono out and raised him into what he is, explaining how Bono can do so much good yet still be such a piece of crap. Randy then produces a crap so enormous he's blasted skyward, sitting atop it. The "Emmy Award winning series" sign — displayed at the bottom of the screen all episode — appears, and a Board member grabs it and sticks it in Randy's crap.

Featured characters: Randy Marsh; Stan Marsh; Bono; the butler; Jimbo Kern; Gerald Broflovski; Stephen Stotch; Stuart McCormick; Skeeter; Sharon and Shelly Marsh.

Locations: the Marsh bathroom, the local bar, the award ceremony, Bono's mansion, Zurich, the European Fecal Standards and Measurements Board.

Key events & continuity: Randy holds — then loses, then reclaims — the world's biggest crap record; Bono is revealed to be a literal piece of crap, crapped out by a Board member; Randy's record-breaking crap launches him into the sky; the episode's running "Emmy Award winning series" gag ends stuck in the crap.

Cartman has the boys hunting a Leprechaun he's supposedly seen three days running. Kyle doesn't buy it. Over walkie-talkies, Cartman coordinates Clyde with the net, Tolkien with diversion traps, and Butters as lookout. Kyle protests: Cartman's dodging a deal — no Leprechaun, Cartman pays Kyle ten dollars; proven Leprechaun, Kyle sucks his balls. Butters spots something; Tolkien springs the trap. It's a real Leprechaun. Chased into a hidden cage, it teleports out, saying he came to warn of a terrorist attack but they're making him late. Cartman produces the signed contract; Kyle is speechless. That night Cartman crashes the Broflovski dinner demanding fulfillment; Kyle refuses.

The next day, Kyle insists to Stan, Kenny, Butters, and Jimmy that he won't do it and Leprechauns aren't real despite what he saw. A strange man takes them aboard his "imagination flying machine" to Imaginationland, home of every imagined being ever. A terrorist detonates in the crowd, killing many imaginary beings. The boys escape on a dragon's back, except Butters, left behind and beaten. Kyle wakes convinced it was a dream, relieved about the balls. He phones Stan, who had the same dream — until Sharon enters with the Stotches asking if Stan has seen Butters. At the Pentagon, General Deckter plays a terrorist video: Butters reading a statement. In court, the judge rules Kyle must suck Cartman's balls within 24 hours or face arrest. Deckter brings in Hollywood filmmakers. Shyamalan offers only irrelevant twists; Bay offers only explosions. Mel Gibson has the useful idea: review the video for anyone not fictional. Butters is real. Deckter orders them to identify him. In Imaginationland, the terrorists will use Rockety Rocket to smash the barrier sealing the evil side; the strange man tells Butters to think of a way to save them. Cartman throws a party celebrating Kyle's humiliation; as Kyle prepares, he and Stan are snatched by a military helicopter. Cartman runs after it screaming.  Butters's speech fails; the terrorists fire Rockety Rocket, shattering the barrier as evil prepares to emerge. Cartman hitchhikes home, telling the driver a robbed man no longer cares about danger — then lustfully wipes a photo of Kyle's mouth.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman; Kyle; Stan; Butters; Kenny; Jimmy; the Leprechaun; General Deckter; Mel Gibson.

Locations: the woods, the snow fort, Imaginationland, the Pentagon, the courtroom.

Key events & continuity: part one of the trilogy; the Leprechaun contract binds Kyle to 24 hours; terrorists attack Imaginationland and take Butters; the barrier falls; the Pentagon learns Butters is real.

Butters wakes to his parents with breakfast, explaining his Imaginationland dream — he'd hallucinated it with his eyes closed. He wakes in Imaginationland passed out, wetting himself. The evil side breaches the barrier; the terrorists proclaim "Allah!" but die in seconds. The injured Mayor sends Butters fleeing from Predator and Stormtroopers. At the Pentagon, the boys blame "some guy in a big balloon." An advisor suggests the Chinese portal, accidentally revealing America has one too. Cartman dreams of Kyle's sewn-shut lips, then wakes on a coach. Shown "Project Imagination Doorway," the boys explain the Mayor's balloon song; a few bars trip a monitor, so the scientists make them sing it exactly. The dying Mayor sarcastically tells Butters to tap his shoes three times, then sends Snarf and the Lollipop King to Castle Sunshine through the Gumdrop Forest. On Yum Yum Mountain, the evil argue over who's most evil until the Woodland Critters arrive: same side, stop arguing — "Kill them, then rape their bodies so we can use their blood as lubricant." Cartman phones the Pentagon for Kyle's location; an adviser denies the Doorway exists while explaining it. The boys nail the song; the portal opens. Crossing the forest, the trio finds the evil torturing Strawberry Shortcake; the critters leave to hunt someone with AIDS to finish her. At the Pentagon, soldiers prepare to enter; Cartman bursts in and Kyle is dragged off to fulfill the contract. Kyle warns of the bigger crisis; Cartman yawns and dresses as royalty. The soldiers meet the Woodland Critters; Stan remembers them from Cartman's story — too late, they're being raped. A soldier summons everyone to the main room; Cartman follows, outraged. At the castle gates, Snarf and the Lollipop King enter; Butters is seized as a suspected terrorist. ManBearPig comes through the Pentagon portal and strangles Kyle; the scientists suck it back and send Stan through too. Butters faces the Council of Nine — Jesus says fight; he's sent to Aslan. Kyle appears dead; Cartman, furious a dead Kyle can't suck his balls, revives him with CPR. The Council names Butters the key. The military prepares to nuke the imagination. Cartman waits at Kyle's bedside, ready.

Featured characters: Butters; Stan; Kyle; Cartman; Deckter; ManBearPig; the Council of Nine; the Woodland Critters; Snarf; the Lollipop King.

Locations: Imaginationland, the Pentagon, Project Imagination Doorway, Castle Sunshine, the Gumdrop Forest, Yum Yum Mountain, Washington D.C.

Key events & continuity: part two of the trilogy; the barrier is breached; the portal opens by song; the critters rape the soldiers; ManBearPig strangles Kyle, Stan is pulled through; Cartman revives Kyle with CPR to save the bet; the Council names Butters the key; the military prepares to nuke imagination.

Aslan recalls happy Imaginationland before the terrorists and the fallen barrier; the final battle looms with too few defenders — but Butters has an unknown power. At the hospital, Kyle wakes to Stan's voice in his head; Cartman arrives with a ball-less sundae: Stan's through the portal and they're nuking it. At the castle, Gandalf explains Butters is real — he can imagine things into existence. First: bring back Santa. Butters focuses and conjures a demonic "Grounded!" father instead; shaken, he tries again. Kyle watches the news: Gore leaked the ManBearPig tape; Deckter will nuke their imaginations — imaginary things aren't real, though it overrides Cartman vs. Broflovski. Kyle reaches Stan through imagination; Stan: stall the missile. Jesus leads the charge; Butters imagines a golden-axe Santa that slaughters evil. Barred from the Pentagon, Kyle joins the hippies. A captured "spy" is dragged in: Stan. Butters: "I imagined Stan." Stan: real — a nuke is coming. Cartman bursts into the Pentagon: imaginary characters are real — dragged out yelling "Leprechauns are real Goddammit!" Kyle: he can't stop the launch. Stan: convince them imaginary characters ARE real. Kyle: that proves Cartman right. Stan: no choice. Kyle crashes through the Pentagon glass; his speech — imaginary characters outlive and outweigh real people, making them very real — aborts the launch. Cartman claims the bet; Kyle explodes: forget it. Gore smacks the console — "ManBearPig has to die!" — and the portal sucks everything through, missile included. The missile detonates over the battlefield; Butters climbs from the void and imagines everything back, evil behind the barrier again. Cartman: anyone can make anything real — imagining himself as King with an imaginary Kyle sucking his imaginary balls. Kyle: imaginary. Cartman: Kyle said imaginary things were real; Deckter backs him. The Mayor: whatever you imagine to be real, is real. Butters wakes to his parents: all a dream. Stephen: wasn't — read it in the paper; grounded. His powers don't work in the real world. "Aw, shit."

Featured characters: Butters, the Chosen One; Stan; Kyle; Cartman; Aslan; the Council of Nine; Santa; Al Gore; ManBearPig; General Deckter; the Woodland Critters.

Locations: Imaginationland, Castle Sunshine, the Gumdrop Forest, the Pentagon, the hospital, Washington D.C.

Key events & continuity: the trilogy concludes; Butters's imagination turns the battle and rebuilds Imaginationland after the missile; Kyle's speech makes imaginary things legally real, aborting the nuke; Gore's console-smashing sucks the missile through; Cartman gets an imaginary win — and wins the argument; Butters wakes grounded, his powers useless in the real world.

Stan and Kyle are the undisputed kings of Guitar Hero, racking up a 100,000-point co-op run in front of an adoring crowd of classmates while Randy sulks that nobody respects his actual electric guitar. Their score catches the eye of Charles Kincade, a smooth talent agent who signs the pair to a one-year contract and dangles a tantalizing goal in front of them: one million points. At a glitzy agency party, the boys are treated like rock royalty. But behind the scenes, Charles quietly poisons the partnership, telling Stan that Kyle is dead weight holding him back. Stan reluctantly trades his best friend for Thad Jarvis, a humorless prodigy who shreds expert-level charts on an unplugged controller at Café Monet. Kyle, heartbroken, retreats to the local bowling alley, where a sympathetic bartender named Mick hires him to play weekend sets just to cheer him up. Stan's new career curdles fast. Stressed and lonely, he gets hooked on Heroin Hero, a bleak parody game with no score and no win condition — you just chase a pink dragon you'll never catch. By the day of the big million-point showcase at the arcade, Stan is a strung-out wreck who bombs the performance in front of everyone. Rock bottom reached, he ditches the drugs, the manager, and the ego, and shows up at the bowling alley to admit the obvious: he needs Kyle. Back at Stan's house, with their friends watching, the reunited duo finally nail the million points together. Their reward is the game flashing a vicious insult at them on screen, and they walk away from the whole rock-star fantasy for good, leaving Cartman and Butters to pick up the controllers.

Featured characters: Stan Marsh and Kyle Broflovski, whose friendship fractures and heals around the game; Charles Kincade, the manipulative talent manager; Thad Jarvis, the soulless expert player; Randy Marsh, whose real-guitar skills impress no one; Mick, the kind bartender who gives Kyle a gig.

Locations: Stan's living room, the Kincade Talent Agency mansion party, Café Monet, the video arcade, the bowling alley, and the game store that sells Stan Heroin Hero.

Key events & continuity: Randy's genuine musicianship is dismissed as old-fashioned next to plastic controllers, a running sore point for him; Stan's Heroin Hero spiral parodies rock-star drug clichés, complete with a Rehab Hero he turns down; the final on-screen insult deflates the entire quest for points, and the episode closes with Cartman and Butters taking over the game — Butters already scheming to betray Cartman after their "sex and drugs party."

The fourth-grade girls have compiled a secret ranking of every boy from cutest to ugliest, and Butters' panicked announcement of its existence throws the boys into chaos. Cartman launches two increasingly desperate heists — "Operation Cannot Possibly Fail" and its sequel — and the second one works: Kenny snatches the list from its keeper, Nelly, and the boys barricade themselves in the bathroom to read it. The ranking puts Clyde on top and Kyle dead last. Kyle, who never cared about his looks before, unravels completely — he mopes through dinner, gets taunted at his bedroom window by Cartman, and ends up sitting with the genuinely grotesque "Ugly Kids" before deciding the only answer is to burn the school down. He buys arson supplies at True Value and is visited in the night by the ghost of Abraham Lincoln, who shows him that beautiful people coast and end up hollow while the unattractive develop character through struggle. Meanwhile Stan, worried sick about his friend, gets Wendy to investigate, and she uncovers the truth: the list was rigged. Nobody voted Clyde cutest — Bebe doctored the tally because Clyde's father owns a shoe store, and dating the popular kid means free shoes for the committee girls. When Wendy confronts Bebe, things escalate to a gun standoff in the school. A stray shot flies out the window and kills Kenny at his own dinner table, Pop-Tarts popping from the toaster as his family stares. Bebe is hauled off by police. Back with Kyle, Wendy reveals the forgery, and Kyle — persuaded by Lincoln's lesson — asks her to burn the list without him ever learning his real rank. The two old almost-sweethearts share a warm moment, and Stan promptly ruins it by vomiting all over Wendy.

Featured characters: Kyle Broflovski, whose confidence collapses; Wendy Testaburger, who plays detective; Bebe Stevens, the corrupt list-master; Stan Marsh, caught between his friend and his ex; Cartman, gleeful tormentor; Clyde Donovan, the fraudulent heartthrob; and the ghost of Abraham Lincoln.

Locations: South Park Elementary's hallways and boys' bathroom, the girls' secret meeting hall, Wendy's house, True Value hardware, and Kyle's bedroom.

Key events & continuity: the rigged-list conspiracy exposes how the girls' social order really works, with Lola and Jenny threatening Wendy into silence; Lincoln's ghost delivers the episode's moral about beauty versus character; Kenny dies by freak stray bullet, one of his most random deaths; Bebe's arrest leaves her fate unknown; and the Stan/Wendy almost-reunion ends in vomit, keeping their relationship in limbo.

A routine tonsillectomy at Hell's Pass Hospital goes horribly wrong when Cartman receives HIV-infected blood from a botched transfusion. The doctors try to smooth it over with the promised post-surgery ice cream, which Cartman hurls to the floor. Back at school, the class is told to treat him normally, but Kyle can't stop laughing at the cosmic justice of it all after years of Cartman's cruelty — and Cartman notices every smirk. His benefit concert is a humiliation: with the public having moved on to caring about cancer instead, only Butters and Jimmy show up, and Jimmy Buffett plays instead of the expected Elton John. Pushed past his limit by Kyle's open schadenfreude, Cartman breaks into the Broflovski house at night with Butters as lookout and injects Kyle's mouth with a syringe of his own infected blood. Kyle's fury is volcanic — he brawls with Cartman at school, trashes Cartman's bedroom (decapitating Clyde Frog), and is only stopped from smashing the Xbox 360 when Cartman dangles a possible cure: Magic Johnson, who has supposedly lived with AIDS for decades without issue. The two fly to Los Angeles on tickets scammed by pretending to have "all-over" cancer, since AIDS is considered too retro to earn sympathy. At Johnson's mansion they discover his bedroom piled high with cash — he sleeps on his money because he doesn't trust banks — and leap to the obvious conclusion: money is the cure. An experimental injection of cold hard cash into Kyle's bloodstream works perfectly, curing all three of them. They're celebrated as heroes with a triumphant concert, and Kyle's protests that Cartman infected him deliberately fall on deaf ears. The episode ends with Cartman declaring them even and Kyle vowing to smash the Xbox anyway.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman and Kyle Broflovski, locked in their most vicious feud yet; Butters Stotch, the reluctant accomplice; Magic Johnson, whose mattress fortune becomes a miracle cure; Dr. Doctor; Principal Victoria and Mr. Mackey, who force absurd mutual apologies.

Locations: Hell's Pass Hospital, South Park Elementary, Cartman's and Kyle's bedrooms, and Magic Johnson's cash-stuffed Los Angeles home.

Key events & continuity: Cartman's deliberate infection of Kyle is one of his cruelest acts, and Kyle's retaliatory rampage — including the death of Clyde Frog — shows how far their hatred has escalated; the "cure by cash injection" becomes town legend; and Kyle's unresolved vow to destroy the Xbox keeps the score unsettled.

When the boys hear that a photographer earned $100,000 for a candid shot of Britney Spears, they hatch a plan to snap their own lucrative picture — Butters even dresses as a squirrel to lure her into an compromising pose. Sneaking past her security by claiming to be her children, they corner a broken, exhausted Britney, who mistakes them for her actual kids and, in despair, shoots herself in the head. She survives with half her skull gone. Horrified and guilt-ridden, Stan and Kyle try to make amends by spiriting her away from the relentless press, attempting to board a train to the North Pole, with Kyle disguising himself as Britney to buy time. But the paparazzi and townspeople track them to a small village, where the awful truth comes out: the entire spectacle is a ritual human sacrifice. The crowd — including Randy, Sharon, Sheila, Gerald, and half of South Park — needs Britney dead to ensure a good harvest, and they photograph her to death on the village floor while Stan and Kyle watch in horror. Later, at the supermarket, Sheila admires the season's excellent corn crop, and when the news teases the next rising star — Miley Cyrus — Randy cheerfully notes the next harvest will be even better. Everyone, including a defeated Stan and Kyle, joins in the eerie sacrificial chant.

Featured characters: Stan and Kyle, the only ones who see the horror for what it is; Britney Spears, hounded past the breaking point; Cartman and Butters, who flee the suicide scene; and the paparazzi mob, revealed as ritual participants.

Locations: Britney's hideout, the hospital, the North Pole-bound train, the sacrificial village, and the South Park supermarket.

Key events & continuity: the episode establishes South Park's cyclical celebrity-sacrifice tradition — fame literally feeds the harvest — with the adults fully complicit; Britney's half-head survival and public death are played as inevitable rather than tragic to anyone but the boys; and the final shot of Stan and Kyle joining the chant signals their grim resignation that the machine can't be fought.

Mr. Mackey's well-meaning lesson on the dangers of choking yourself to get high backfires spectacularly when Kenny decides to try it, and Butters innocently asks whether cat urine can get you high. The answer — technically it's the concentrated spray cats use to mark territory — sends the boys to Cartman's house, where they get Kenny buzzed off Mr. Kitty's spray. Kenny plunges into a lavish animated fantasy world filled with beautiful, scantily-clad women, a full homage to the film Heavy Metal. The new craze, dubbed "cheesing," sweeps the headlines, and Gerald gets a law passed banishing all cats from South Park. Cartman, ever the opportunist with a soft spot for felines, starts hiding rescued cats in his attic. When Stan, Kyle, and Butters catch Kenny cheesing again, they confiscate his cat — and Kyle gets grounded when Sheila finds it in his drawer. Gerald takes the cat to the basement intending to surrender it, but the temptation proves too much: he was a cheeser back in the day, and he falls right back into the fantasy, where he literally fights Kenny over the dream woman. In reality, the two are just wrestling in a park sandbox while a crowd gathers and Gerald is exposed. Shamed, Gerald declares that cats aren't the problem — people are — and the ban is lifted. The boys congratulate themselves on a lesson learned, though Kyle can't help noting that Cartman's attic full of hidden cats reminds him of something from history, which Cartman angrily denies. Kenny, meanwhile, has already moved on to getting high on flowers.

Featured characters: Kenny McCormick, the enthusiastic cheeser; Eric Cartman, unlikely cat rescuer; Gerald Broflovski, hiding a secret past; Kyle, Stan, and Butters, the would-be interventionists; Mr. Kitty.

Locations: South Park Elementary, Cartman's cat-packed attic, the Broflovski basement, and the park sandbox that hosts the "epic" showdown.

Key events & continuity: Gerald's history as a cheeser is a new revelation about Kyle's straight-laced dad; the episode's final beat pointedly invokes Cartman's attic as a parallel he refuses to acknowledge; and Kenny's instant pivot to a new high undercuts the boys' belief that anything was actually resolved.

When America's "Canada Appreciation Day" turns out to be a mocking farce, Stephen Abootman, head of the World Canadian Bureau, leads the entire nation of Canada into a strike, demanding "some of that Internet money" without specifying how much or why. Kyle worries about his little brother Ike, shivering on a picket line, and the boys decide to broker peace. Their plan: film Butters singing a ridiculous song, upload it to YouTube, and hand Canada the ad revenue. The video is an instant viral hit, and the boys queue up at the Colorado Department of Internet Money alongside real viral stars — Tay Zonday, Chris Crocker, and the Star Wars Kid — who promptly start murdering each other over who's most famous. The boys collect ten million "theoretical dollars," one per view, only to have the World Canadian Bureau reject it because it isn't real money. Abootman, terrified of admitting he led his country into a pointless strike, doubles down even as Denmark moves in to take striking Canadians' jobs and Terrance and Phillip agitate to end it. Finally Kyle grabs the phone with the UN and begs them to give Canada something small while pretending it's big. The UN's grand settlement: Bennigan's coupons and bubblegum for every Canadian. Canada declares victory. Back home, Kyle tells Ike the strike is over and recites his lesson about the internet not yet being a mature way to make money. At the victory party, Terrance and Phillip do the math: the strike cost Canada $10.4 million, and the coupons and gum are worth about $3,008. The enraged nation sets Abootman and his aides adrift on an ice floe.

Featured characters: Kyle and Ike Broflovski; Stephen Abootman, the blustering strike leader; Terrance and Phillip, the voices of Canadian reason; Butters, the accidental viral star; and a parade of feuding internet celebrities.

Locations: the frozen Canadian picket lines, the Department of Internet Money queue, the World Canadian Bureau, and UN negotiation lines.

Key events & continuity: Ike's presence on the strike line raises the personal stakes for Kyle; the "theoretical dollars" gag skewers early internet monetization hype; Abootman's ice-floe banishment continues the show's tradition of punishing failed Canadian leaders; and Kyle's closing monologue about digital distribution is delivered with total sincerity by a fourth-grader.

Mrs. Garrison suffers a breakdown in class — smashing windows and furniture — after realizing that, despite everything, she is still a man at heart. Ordered by Principal Victoria and Mr. Mackey to get her personal life sorted before returning to teaching, she storms off on a quest to become whole again. Her journey leads her to the laboratory behind the famous Vacanti mouse, where she pays the scientists her entire fortune to grow her a new penis on the back of a mouse. The experiment works, but the mouse — and its precious cargo — escapes into the wild, sending Garrison on a frantic, undignified chase through South Park, including a disastrous case of mistaken identity in a Komfort Inn sauna. Meanwhile, with the classroom teacherless, Principal Victoria reluctantly lets Cartman take charge of test review. Cartman rules with a pointer and intimidation, and when the class inexplicably aces the quiz (thanks to Kenny stealing the answer key), the Denver County school board recruits him to teach struggling students at Jim Davis High School — for $300. Rebranding himself as "Eric Cartminez" with a hasty comb-over, Cartman discovers his true pedagogical gift: teaching kids how to cheat. Citing Bill Belichick as his role model, he drills his students in the art of the excuse ("I misinterpreted the rules"), coaches a pregnant student toward an abortion as "the ultimate form of cheating," and preps them with cheat sheets for a heavily monitored exam. Against all odds, every single student scores 100%. Garrison finally recaptures her runaway anatomy, and Cartman's teaching career ends in inexplicable triumph.

Featured characters: Mrs./Mr. Garrison, on a deeply personal quest; Eric Cartman, the world's worst inspirational teacher; the escaped mouse and its cargo; Mrs. Miller, the overwhelmed Jim Davis teacher; and Juanita, the student Cartman "helps."

Locations: the fourth-grade classroom, the Research Group Laboratories, Jim Davis High School, the Stotch household, and the Komfort Inn sauna.

Key events & continuity: Garrison's arc continues her long, tortured relationship with her own identity, having swung from man to woman and back toward manhood; Cartman's cheating curriculum is a dark mirror of his own moral code, and his perfect test scores stand as a bleak joke about the education system rewarding the wrong lessons.

The Marsh family wakes up to a catastrophe: the internet is gone. Not slow — gone. Stan, Shelly, and Randy rush to the Broflovskis', but Kyle's computer is dead too, and soon the whole town, then the whole nation, is offline. News broadcasters can't even report the news without it. Then word spreads that somewhere out in California there's still internet, and Randy packs the family into the car and heads west. At the refugee camp, desperate users are issued tickets and granted forty seconds each online. Shelly is frantic to email her boyfriend Amir, whom she's never actually met in person, and punches Stan every time he tries to comfort her. Randy, realizing forty seconds isn't enough for his private browsing, sneaks into the room housing the internet itself for an extended session, and is discovered by camp wardens mid-act, covered head to toe in what he insists is "ectoplasm" from a ghost. His session also burns through the last of the region's bandwidth. Meanwhile, scientists have located the physical internet — depicted as a giant wireless router in an underground cavern — and Kyle, brought in as humanity's last hope, diagnoses the problem instantly. He pulls the giant plug out of the wall, waits a few seconds, and plugs it back in. The internet returns. At the celebration, Shelly finally meets Amir face to face — he's been in line behind her the whole time — and the two exchange a few agonizingly awkward words before he promises to email her. Randy closes with a solemn speech warning everyone not to "over log," and to limit porn to twice a day.

Featured characters: Randy Marsh, whose addiction drives the B-plot; Kyle Broflovski, the only one who thinks to reboot; Stan, Shelly, and Sharon Marsh; and Amir, Shelly's online-only boyfriend.

Locations: the Marsh and Broflovski homes, the California internet refugee camp, and the cavern housing the physical internet.

Key events & continuity: the episode literalizes the internet as a single giant router, making Kyle's unplug-and-replug fix the most technically accurate joke in the series; Randy's "ectoplasm" excuse becomes an instant classic; and Shelly's awkward first meeting with Amir punctures her entire online romance in seconds.

Mr. Garrison takes the fourth grade on a field trip to Pioneer Village, a living-history museum where the staff stay in character as 1864 settlers no matter what — and he orders the kids to pair up and hold hands. Cartman gets stuck with Butters, who takes the hand-holding order with total literal seriousness and refuses to let go until they're back on the bus. When Cartman discovers the "Super Phun Thyme" amusement center two blocks away, he drags a protesting, hand-locked Butters along for bumper cars, arcade games, and air hockey against himself. Back at the village, things go sideways: a gang of trigger-happy thieves led by Franz, fresh from robbing a Burger King, takes the whole class hostage and demands the code to a locked mine-shaft door. The pioneers won't break character even at gunpoint — one is executed by Pioneer Paul just for trying. Stan, Wendy, Jimmy, and Kyle escape to an office and call the police, but the standoff stalls until Stan makes the ultimate sacrifice — looking like a total dork in front of Wendy — by posing as a clueless out-of-towner, giving the villagers an in-character way to reveal the code: 1864. Meanwhile Cartman and Butters, assuming the arriving police are after them for ditching, try to sneak back in and get spotted by a thief. When ordered to put their hands on their heads, Butters simply will not let go of Cartman's hand — and when threatened with having their hands shot off, Butters picks Cartman up and hurls him bodily at the gunman. A grenade knocks both boys out, the police storm in, and the crisis ends. The workday bell rings, every pioneer instantly drops character, and they all head to T.G.I. Friday's for jalapeño poppers. The episode closes with an injured Butters dragging an unconscious Cartman onto the bus, announcing "my partner is back on the bus," and finally letting go before collapsing.

Featured characters: Butters Stotch, whose unbreakable grip saves the day; Eric Cartman, dragged literally through his own scheme; Stan Marsh, who sacrifices his dignity; Franz and his thieves; and the Pioneer Village staff, committed to 1864 to the death.

Locations: Pioneer Village, the Super Phun Thyme amusement center, the mine-shaft door, and the school bus.

Key events & continuity: Butters' literal obedience to "don't let go until you're back on the bus" becomes both the episode's running gag and its heroic climax; the pioneers' refusal to break character — even under lethal threat — is played completely straight; and Franz's parting lesson about appreciating modern conveniences lands as the obligatory moral.

After watching the Beijing Olympics opening ceremony, Cartman becomes convinced that China, with its two billion people and terrifying pageantry, is about to conquer America. Nobody will listen — Kyle is too consumed by a different trauma to even call Cartman racist. Kyle, Stan, Kenny, Clyde, and Jimmy are all haunted by the same psychic wound: they believe Steven Spielberg and George Lucas literally raped Indiana Jones with their latest sequel. Kyle's nightmares show the two directors physically assaulting the hero on screen, and the boys march on a lawyer's office demanding prosecution, eventually winning over the attorney, the police, and finally securing an arrest warrant. Officers find Spielberg and Lucas at Skywalker Ranch mid-assault on a Stormtrooper, with the bodies of their previous victims in the closet. Meanwhile, Cartman recruits the only ally he can find — Butters, lured with warnings that the Chinese will murder his parents — and together they form the "American Liberation Front." In stereotypical disguises, they infiltrate a P.F. Chang's to uncover China's plans, end up taking the restaurant hostage when asked to leave, and Butters keeps accidentally shooting people in the crotch. The standoff dissolves when news of the directors' arrest breaks and everyone bursts into tears of vindication, leaving Cartman and Butters confused. Butters, for the record, thought the movie was good.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman, gripped by xenophobic panic; Butters, his trigger-happy deputy; Kyle, Stan, Kenny, Clyde, and Jimmy, united in cinematic grief; Steven Spielberg and George Lucas, literalized as villains; and Sergeant Yates, who weeps along with everyone else once he understands.

Locations: Cartman's bedroom, the bus stop, P.F. Chang's restaurant, the police station, and Skywalker Ranch.

Key events & continuity: the episode runs two parallel delusions — Cartman's Red Scare and the boys' auteur-rape metaphor — that never intersect until the final scene; Butters' accidental crotch-shooting becomes a running gag; and the arrest of two of Hollywood's biggest directors is treated as genuine legal justice by the entire town.

Wendy delivers a breast cancer awareness presentation in class, and Cartman mocks it relentlessly while a defeated Mr. Garrison does nothing. When the jeering continues after class, Wendy finally snaps and challenges Cartman to a fight after school. Word spreads like wildfire — Butters rallies the fourth grade, Bebe alerts the girls, Ike informs the kindergarteners, and even the Goth Kids hear about it. Terrified of a beating and of being labeled a coward, Cartman tries every weaselly tactic to get out of it: fake apologies, bribery, a janitor's-closet plea deal, and even swallowing his own underwear to prove his sincerity, which only disgusts Wendy further. He begs Stan to intervene, then deliberately gets himself detention by defecating on Mr. Garrison's desk — only to learn through the window that Wendy has rescheduled for the next morning. In his most shameless move yet, Cartman shows up at Wendy's house sobbing into his mother's blouse, playing the bullied victim until Wendy's furious parents force her to promise there will be no fight. Safe behind parental protection, Cartman spends the next day gloating, reading a mocking "report" full of breast-cancer jokes in class. Wendy is summoned to Principal Victoria's office, expecting punishment — instead, Victoria reveals she is a breast cancer survivor, and in a thinly veiled metaphor about cancer being "pure evil" that "can't be reasoned with," makes it clear Wendy must fight the "fat little lump" no matter the cost. Wendy walks onto the playground, the whole school watching, and beats Cartman senseless while the crowd cheers. Afterward, a battered Cartman worries he's no longer the cool kid; the boys inform him he was never cool and they've always hated him — which he cheerfully interprets as them trying to make him feel better.

Featured characters: Wendy Testaburger, pushed past her limit; Eric Cartman, at his most cowardly and manipulative; Principal Victoria, whose survivor story becomes a call to arms; and the entire student body as audience.

Locations: the classroom, the janitor's closet, detention with Mr. Mackey, Wendy's living room, and the school playground.

Key events & continuity: Victoria's secret history as a cancer survivor is revealed for the first time; Cartman's victim performance at Wendy's house is one of his most shameless cons; and the boys' parting confession — that they've always hated him — is immediately, hilariously misread by Cartman as kindness.

Annoyed by the plague of Peruvian pan-flute bands cluttering every street corner, Stan discovers the bands pull in $200 a day and talks Kyle, Cartman, and Kenny into starting their own — funded by Craig's $100 birthday money, surrendered reluctantly. Their timing is terrible: Michael Chertoff, head of Homeland Security, has seized military control to round up every flute band in America purely because he finds them annoying. The boys are swept up in the raid, fail to convince the guards they're not Peruvian, and learn they're being shipped to Guantanamo Bay. Craig spends the entire ordeal furiously cataloguing everything the scheme has cost him. Meanwhile Randy, who has taken to filming his family's every moment with a new camcorder, captures the crackdown on tape. Interrogated by the government, the boys are deemed just useful enough to be shipped to Peru on a mission to "take down the country," though Kyle suspects there's more to it. Back in South Park, guinea-pig-like creatures begin tearing through the town while Randy films the destruction. At the Pentagon, Chertoff finally drops the act — confessing his own role in the crisis, murdering his aide General Davis, and revealing himself as a monstrous creature. His victory monologue lays out the scheme: the guinea pigs are rising, the flute bands are being eliminated, and the one person who could stop him is being flown to the middle of nowhere. He smiles at a photograph of his nemesis: Craig Tucker.

Featured characters: Stan, Kyle, Cartman, and Kenny, accidental musicians; Craig Tucker, the world's most aggrieved investor; Michael Chertoff, secretly a monster; Randy Marsh, compulsive documentarian; and General Davis.

Locations: the South Park mall, the Homeland Security detention center, the Miami holding zone, the C-130 to Peru, and the Marsh household under guinea-pig siege.

Key events & continuity: the Department of Homeland Security's war on flute bands is personal, not political — Chertoff just hates the music; Craig's $100 becomes the episode's running ledger of grievances; and the cliffhanger reveal of Chertoff's true form sets up the two-parter's conclusion.

Giant guinea pigs — some in bee costumes, some in rabbit costumes, one a full "guinea-saurus rex" — are rampaging across the globe while the Marsh family hides out, Randy still filming everything. The boys, stranded in the Andes after their plane runs out of fuel, trek through a jungle of giant fruit and lose both pilots to bee larvae before discovering an ancient temple. Its wall drawings lay out a prophecy: the Peruvian flute bands were the world's guardians, holding the giant guinea pigs in the jungle, and their capture would unleash the beasts. The final panel shows Craig repelling a guinea pig — he is the chosen one. Meanwhile the Marshes flee from a Best Buy rooftop into a storeroom as "guinea bees" and "guinea rabbits" close in, and Sharon finally snaps and punches Randy's camera. At Machu Picchu, the boys confront the Homeland Security director, who orders them shot as flute bands. Stan talks him down, the director launches into a full villain monologue, a guard shoots him in the back — and he transforms into a giant "guinea pirate." Craig, wanting no part of any of this, tries to walk away, steps on the wrong stone tile, and suddenly fires energy beams from his eyes, paralyzing the guinea pirate. In the aftermath, the flute bands are freed and pipe the guinea pigs back into the jungle, and Craig narrates the closing monologue over a pan-flute cover of "Cars": he will never trust the gang again. The boys show up at his door dressed as a mariachi band, presumably to pitch him another investment, and he slams the door. The final sting: the guinea pirate has broken out of jail and is stomping through the city in a black-and-white prison uniform.

Featured characters: Craig Tucker, the reluctant messiah; Stan, Kyle, Cartman, and Kenny; Randy, Sharon, and Shelly Marsh; the Stotch family; and the guinea pirate, formerly the head of Homeland Security.

Locations: the Andes jungle and its prophetic temple, Machu Picchu, the Best Buy rooftop and storeroom, and Craig's front door.

Key events & continuity: the prophecy reframes the much-mocked flute bands as sacred guardians; Craig's eye-beams activate by pure accident, underlining his unwilling-chosen-one status; Randy's big reveal — he never put a tape in the camcorder — voids his entire documentary; and the escaped guinea pirate dangles a sequel that never comes.

On election night, South Park splits in two: Obama supporters, led by a drunken Randy, riot joyfully through the streets, while McCain supporters — including Ike, the Stotches, and most of the school staff — mourn indoors. Ike attempts suicide by leaping from a first-story window and has to be rushed to the hospital by Stan and Kyle. But the real story is happening in Washington: Obama and McCain are secretly partners, members of an elite crew of professional thieves who staged the entire presidential race as cover for stealing the Hope Diamond from the Smithsonian. Using a forgotten escape tunnel that runs from the Oval Office to the museum, Obama slips in to grab the gem while McCain's crew poses as construction workers outside — with Sarah Palin and a Michelle Obama who is only pretending to be his wife in on the job. The plan depends on the whole country being too distracted by election results to notice. Back in South Park, the chaos escalates: Randy gets fired for fighting his boss, revelers tip Officer Barbrady's cruiser, Cartman loots unattended houses for televisions to resell, and the Stotches build an "ark" for McCain supporters convinced civilization is ending. At the hospital, Ike wakes from his faked injury to detonate a plane full of candidate lookalike dummies and falsify the medical records, completing the crew's escape plan. At the last moment, Obama bails on the getaway — he wants to try actually being president, and Michelle and the kids agree to keep pretending to be the First Family. The next morning, the Stotches open their ark to find society intact, Randy wakes up pantsless, TV-less, and jobless, and bitterly decides he should have voted for McCain after all.

Featured characters: Barack Obama and John McCain, secret heist partners; Ike Broflovski, the crew's inside man; Randy Marsh, the ultimate sore winner; Cartman, election-night looter; and the Stotch family, doomsday preppers.

Locations: the White House and its secret tunnel, the Smithsonian, South Park's rioting streets, the Stotches' ark, and the packed emergency room.

Key events & continuity: Ike's "suicide attempt" is revealed as a calculated part of the heist; Randy's election-night bender costs him his pants, his television, and his job in one evening; and Obama's decision to stay behind reframes the entire caper as his origin story as president.

A new fad sweeps South Park Elementary: everyone is suddenly singing and dancing in the hallways, High School Musical-style, and the boys are the only ones not participating. After watching the movie, they despise it and swear they'll never join in — Cartman even tries to asphyxiate himself under his mom's hybrid car, which fails because hybrids "don't do the trick anymore." But the pressure mounts when Stan notices Wendy getting chummy with Bridon Gueermo, a third-grader and the fad's golden boy, during the musical numbers. Confronting Bridon, Stan learns the kid would rather play basketball — but his flamboyant, theater-obsessed father forbids it as a "sissy" sport and enforces the rule with comically weak slaps that somehow terrify everyone, including Child Services. Stan coaches Bridon to stand up for himself; Bridon finally punches his dad in the nose, his mother joins in beating the man senseless, and Bridon makes the basketball team. Meanwhile Kyle, Cartman, and Kenny fall in with Scott Malkinson, an unpopular kid mocked for his lisp and diabetes, purely because he's outside the fad. Desperate not to lose Wendy and their status, the boys cave: they study the High School Musical films intensely and stage an elaborate song-and-dance number about following your dreams. Nobody cares — the whole school has already abandoned singing to watch Bridon play basketball. Scott delivers the epitaph: everyone only liked the singing because Bridon was doing it. Stan is left fuming that they mastered choreography for absolutely nothing.

Featured characters: Stan Marsh, jealous and desperate; Bridon Gueermo, the reluctant star; Mr. Gueermo, the slap-happy stage father; Wendy Testaburger; and Scott Malkinson, the fad-proof outsider.

Locations: the school cafeteria and hallways, the Gueermo household, the basketball court, and the movie theater.

Key events & continuity: Bridon's arc — from musical-theater prisoner to basketball player — kills the fad overnight, proving it was never about the music; Stan's jealousy over Wendy drives the entire plot; and the boys' vow against the fad collapses the moment social standing is at stake, ending in a fully choreographed humiliation.

Butters bursts into computer class insisting he's seen vampires all over the school, and Cartman "helpfully" suggests he document their movements — just to get rid of him. What Butters finds is the South Park Vampire Society: kids in Hot Topic finery who drink Clammato juice and call it "feeding." When his tape recorder betrays him, Butters brandishes a crucifix at them before fleeing. The Goth Kids are even more horrified than Butters — not by vampires, but by posers they consider diet-goth: no smoking, plastic fangs, and juice. After another grounding-level scolding from his parents over pantry organization, Butters decides vampires don't get yelled at by their moms and dads, and asks to join the vamps. They take him to the mall, dress him in black, dye his hair, fit him with plastic teeth, and initiate him with Clammato. Empowered, Butters declares himself "ungroundable" — beyond the rules of human parents — and even sneaks into Cartman's room at night to feed on him, failing, vomiting, and leaving Liane with the impression Butters made a confused romantic advance. The Goth Kids, tired of being confused with the vamps, kidnap the head vampire, force him to admit he's a fake, and mail him to Scottsdale — the most miserable place they can think of. Butters, talked down by the goths, burns down the Hot Topic and returns home human again. His parents' joy at having a groundable son lasts about ten seconds: he's grounded immediately for the pantry. The Goth Kids close the episode with a school assembly clarifying the difference between goth and vampire, flipping off the audience to thunderous applause.

Featured characters: Butters Stotch, the gullible convert; the Vampire Society; the Goth Kids, defending their brand; Stephen and Linda Stotch; and Cartman, the almost-victim.

Locations: South Park Elementary's gym, the South Park Mall's Hot Topic, the Stotch home, and Cartman's bedroom.

Key events & continuity: "Ungroundable" enters the Stotch family lexicon as Butters' ultimate loophole, and its loss is genuinely mourned by his parents; the Goth Kids' hatred of the vamps establishes the show's lasting goth-vs-vampire rivalry; and Butters' Hot Topic arson is treated as a healthy resolution.

To everyone's astonishment, Kenny has landed a girlfriend: Tammy, a fifth-grader with a wild reputation — Butters has heard she performed a sex act on another boy in a T.G.I. Friday's parking lot. When Stan, Kyle, and Cartman try to warn Kenny, he's thrilled rather than dismayed, and Tammy cheerfully confirms the rumor, explaining she only did it because watching the Jonas Brothers made her aroused. Kenny drags Tammy to a Jonas Brothers concert, where the evening takes an unexpected turn: instead of the backstage hookup the girls expect, the brothers pressure Tammy and the other girls into wearing purity rings and spreading the abstinence gospel. Kenny reluctantly dons a ring to keep his girlfriend happy, and promptly becomes dull, distant, and boring to be around. Meanwhile the truth emerges backstage: the Jonas Brothers are being forced to push the rings by their boss — Mickey Mouse himself, a foul-mouthed, violent corporate tyrant who beats the brothers when they complain that the purity branding is overshadowing their music. Mickey's real scheme: the rings let him market sex to young girls while maintaining a veneer of innocence. When Stan, Kyle, and Cartman confront the band on television in Denver, Mickey tranquilizes them, drags them backstage, and rants about his contempt for youth and Christians — unaware the boys have switched on the microphone and raised the curtain, broadcasting his tirade to the concert crowd and national TV. The audience turns on him, the brothers storm off, and Mickey, enraged, swells to gigantic size and starts breathing fire and stomping through Denver. Tammy and Kenny ditch their rings — Tammy suggesting a celebratory return to T.G.I. Friday's — and Kenny promptly contracts syphilis and dies, proving Cartman's warning about the dangers of the situation entirely correct.

Featured characters: Kenny McCormick and Tammy; the Jonas Brothers, unwilling purity mascots; Mickey Mouse, the monstrous boss; and Stan, Kyle, and Cartman, amateur exposers.

Locations: T.G.I. Friday's parking lot, the Jonas Brothers concert, the Denver television studio, and backstage.

Key events & continuity: Mickey Mouse is established as a genuine in-universe villain, a corporate overlord rather than a mascot; Kenny dies of syphilis — his first death since Season 11 — played as the punchline to Cartman's paranoia; and the purity-ring craze collapses the moment its true purpose is exposed.

Eric Cartman has reinvented himself as the Coon, a claw-fingered vigilante who stalks South Park's parks at night, scratching the faces of men he catches kissing women on the grounds that they must be rapists. He reports his "findings" to a deeply unimpressed Sergeant Yates, distributes "Who is the Coon?" T-shirts at the police station, and is baffled when nobody at the bus stop or school has heard of him. His big coming-out — a rooftop appearance at Walgreens, followed by the first annual "Coonicon" at the Airport Hilton — is a total bust: no one shows, and a waiter mistakes him for someone else entirely. Worse, a rival has appeared: Mysterion, a genuinely competent kid vigilante who earns public adoration and the police's respect for handling real (if minor) crimes. Consumed with jealousy, Cartman tries to unmask Mysterion, interrogates classmates, and even seeks intelligence from Professor Chaos — Butters' own supervillain alter ego — who instead sics General Disarray on him. Chaos soon escalates on his own, threatening to blow up a hospital unless Mysterion reveals himself. At the construction-site showdown, Mysterion battles Chaos and Disarray while a sniper's bullet is waved off by Yates ("bullets won't harm the Professor"), and the Coon swoops in at the last second to slash the defeated Chaos and claim shared credit. Cornered by his own threat that more attacks will come unless Mysterion unmasks, Cartman watches as Mysterion agrees — but the reveal is deliberately unreadable, and the crowd never speaks the name aloud. Cartman insists he knew the identity all along. The Coon walks away convinced his scheme worked: Mysterion ends up jailed for vigilantism, and Cartman is South Park's official hero.

Featured characters: Cartman as the Coon; Mysterion, the superior rival; Professor Chaos and General Disarray; Sergeant Yates; and Wendy, whose innocent question about Mysterion's gender sends Cartman into a panic.

Locations: the park, the Park County Police Station, the Walgreens roof, the Airport Hilton, and the construction site.

Key events & continuity: this is the debut of the Coon and Mysterion, the superhero identities that will define the show's next major saga; Mysterion's unmasking is deliberately withheld, preserving the mystery; and Cartman's "victory" — achieved by doing nothing and causing the problem — sets the template for his entire superhero career.

The economy is in freefall, and Randy Marsh has a philosophy to explain it — delivered while blending margaritas in his absurdly expensive new automatic margarita machine, the "Margaritaville," purchased on credit he doesn't have. His gospel: the townspeople have angered the Economy with reckless spending, and must now appease it like a vengeful god — wearing bedsheet togas, washing less, spending nothing. The town embraces the cult of austerity. Kyle, disgusted by the idiocy, starts preaching the opposite: the economy isn't a living being, it's a shared fiction, and the way to fix it is to spend responsibly and have faith. His following grows, and Randy's camp decides the solution is to kill "the Jew." Cartman, bribed with a copy of Grand Theft Auto: Chinatown Wars, agrees to betray Kyle's location. At a Last Supper-style pizza gathering, Kyle tells his friends one of them will betray him — and Cartman cheerfully announces that whoever does it "is a dick." The next day, Kyle sets up a table with a credit-card machine and begins paying off the entire town's debts on a no-limit American Express Platinum Card he applied for days earlier, collapsing after clearing Randy's $17,000 tab. The news credits the recovery to one brave man: President Obama — leaving Kyle furious. In a parallel odyssey, Stan spends the episode trying to return Randy's Margaritaville mixer, only to be told the debt has been sold and resold up the chain until he reaches the U.S. Treasury itself — where policy is set by letting a decapitated chicken run around a board until it drops on a square, landing this time on "bailout." Stan hurls the mixer at the platform in disgust and walks out. The next morning, Randy owns the newer model — identical, but with a pointless salsa dispenser.

Featured characters: Randy Marsh, prophet of austerity; Kyle Broflovski, the economy's reluctant messiah; Stan Marsh, on a quixotic return quest; Cartman, the betrayer-for-hire; and the Treasury's chicken.

Locations: the Marsh kitchen, the town square, Kyle's debt-forgiveness table, the retail chain of debt, and the U.S. Treasury's chicken board.

Key events & continuity: Kyle literally takes on the town's debts in a direct messiah parallel, complete with betrayal and a Last Supper; the Treasury chicken becomes the show's definitive image of economic policy; and Randy's instant upgrade to Margaritaville 2.0 proves he learned nothing.

The boys gather at Cartman's for the new Terrance and Phillip — but it's an April Fool's prank: instead of their beloved Canadians, the network airs The Queef Sisters, a show built entirely around vaginal flatulence, which the boys despise. When Samantha Dunskin demonstrates the real thing on Butters' face at school, the boys are horrified, their fathers demand a town-wide ban on queefing, and Terrance and Phillip's show gets cancelled in favor of the Sisters' rising popularity. The deposed duo plots to murder their rivals, but the plan collapses when they meet the Sisters and instantly fall in love — the Sisters grew up idolizing them. After a brief falling-out and reconciliation, romance blooms. Meanwhile the town holds hearings on the Butters incident, where a female senator defends queefing by performing exact lines of dialogue from The Road Warrior, and the ban passes anyway — to the outrage of Sharon and Shelly, who call it pure sexism. Stan and Randy finally grasp the point: this was never about bodily functions, it was about women's rights. The men of South Park record an inspirational charity single, "Queef Free," and the episode ends with a double wedding: Terrance and Phillip marry the Queef Sisters, despite their obvious lingering disgust at the act itself.

Featured characters: Terrance and Phillip, dethroned and lovestruck; the Queef Sisters; Butters, the victim of the demonstration; Samantha Dunskin; Sharon and Shelly Marsh, the feminist conscience; and the boys' fathers, the would-be banners.

Locations: Cartman's living room, South Park Elementary, the town hearing, and the recording studio.

Key events & continuity: the episode is a point-for-point gender-flip of the show's own fart humor, forcing the male characters to confront their double standard; Terrance and Phillip's marriage to their replacements resolves their career crisis through romance rather than revenge; and "Queef Free" stands as the town's most pompous musical moment.

Jimmy Valmer invents a joke on the spot — "Do you like fishsticks? ... What are you, a gay fish?" — and it becomes a sensation, spreading from South Park to national television. But when Cartman shows up to mooch food, he promptly claims he co-created the joke, and his ego does the rest: through a series of increasingly grandiose false memories, Cartman convinces himself he saved Jimmy from a black widow, slew a dragon, and single-handedly wrote the punchline. Kyle tries an intervention, explaining that Cartman's ego performs mental gymnastics to protect itself — and Cartman weaponizes the exact speech against Jimmy, gaslighting the stuttering comedian into surrendering full credit on the Ellen DeGeneres show. Meanwhile, the one person on Earth who doesn't get the joke is Kanye West, who is convinced the whole world is spreading rumors that he is literally a gay fish. No explanation, however slow or visual — including a doctor confirming he has no gills — can penetrate. His crusade leads him to murder Carlos Mencia with a baseball bat for joke theft, and finally to kidnap Cartman and Jimmy for a dockside execution. At the last moment, Kanye has an epiphany, decides everyone was trying to help him all along, and leaps into the ocean to live as a gay fish, happily humping a grouper as the credits roll.

Featured characters: Jimmy Valmer, the true author; Eric Cartman, the credit thief; Kanye West, the joke's only victim; Kyle, the frustrated truth-teller; and Carlos Mencia, collateral damage.

Locations: Jimmy's house, the Ellen DeGeneres show, Kanye's house, and the dock.

Key events & continuity: Cartman's false-memory spiral is a landmark depiction of his pathological ego — Kyle's diagnosis becomes the episode's thesis; Kanye's transformation into a literal gay fish is played as a happy ending; and Jimmy, bullied out of his own creation, walks away with nothing but the truth.

Randy Marsh is determined that Stan will win the state Pinewood Derby, so he secretly installs a "device" in the car — which Stan learns from a news report is a superconducting magnet stolen from the Large Hadron Collider by Randy in a Princess Leia disguise. Coached by Randy, Stan lies to the scout leaders, wins first place with a record time, and watches his car shoot off the track, achieve warp speed, and vanish into space. Days later, two agents arrive: an alien species found the car and is coming to Earth.
