The visitor is Baby Fark McGee-zax, an intergalactic criminal who holds the planet at gunpoint and demands Stan and Randy build him a new warp drive — from approved kit parts only. While the town stalls the pursuing Intergalactic Police, Stan is pressured into shanking McGee-zax, whose ship is found stuffed with stolen "space cash." Instead of turning it in, Randy talks the whole town — and then the world's leaders — into splitting the loot and covering it up. The cover-up spirals: Mexico's sudden hospital-and-water-park building spree nearly exposes everything, and when Finland threatens to talk, Randy gets the planet to nuke it. Finally cornered by the officers' suspicions, Stan confesses to the derby cheating and returns his trophy — but nobody else confesses a thing. Then McGee-zax strolls out of the police ship alive: the whole ordeal was a test of humanity's worthiness to join the intergalactic community, and Earth failed by hoarding the cash instead of returning it. As punishment, the planet — and the Moon — are sealed inside a gigantic cube-shaped force field, cut off from the universe forever. Randy's verdict: "Well, that sucks."

Featured characters: Randy and Stan Marsh, cheat and accomplice; Baby Fark McGee-zax; Mr. Hollis, whose shame ends tragically; and the Intergalactic Police.

Locations: the Pinewood Derby finals, the Marsh home, McGee-zax's ship, and eventually the entire quarantined Earth.

Key events & continuity: Mr. Hollis's suicide in front of his son is one of the show's darkest single beats; the Finland strike shows how fast the town's conspiracy turns genocidal; and Earth's permanent force-field quarantine is the most sweeping consequence the series has ever imposed — the planet is literally boxed out of the universe.

Cartman bursts into the cafeteria with glorious news: piracy is back, and he's recruiting a crew to run away to Somalia and live the dream. Kyle enthusiastically encourages him to go. Only Kevin, Clyde, Butters, Ike, and Gordon Stoltski (quickly expelled for being ginger) sign up. After a soaring travel montage, the crew lands in Somalia and discovers it's a desolate, impoverished wasteland — not the rum-and-treasure paradise Cartman promised. Undeterred, Cartman marches into a pirate stronghold, where the actual Somali pirates promptly take the children hostage for ransom. Nothing goes as Cartman imagined: the "ship" is a tiny boat, the pirates don't understand his orders, and when a French cruise ship pays the ransom, Cartman hijacks the cruise liner at toy-lightsaber-point and installs himself as pirate king, drilling his bewildered captives in a musical montage to become "real" pirates. Meanwhile Kyle's glee curdles — Ike has vanished, leaving a note about escaping middle-class monotony to become a pirate, and it's all Kyle's fault for cheering Cartman on. Kyle flies to Somalia to retrieve his brother. Butters and Ike, taking inventory of their plunder, hear a pirate wistfully say he'd trade places — he wishes he could go to school — and realize how good they had it. The crew mutinies, demanding to go home; Cartman draws a sword and forbids it. Then a U.S. warship opens fire on the pirate camp, under strict orders not to hit "the white ones," wiping out every Somali pirate in seconds while Cartman watches his empire evaporate.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman, the delusional pirate king; Kyle Broflovski, guilt-ridden rescuer; Ike, the runaway; Butters and Clyde, disillusioned crew; and the Somali pirates, bemused professionals.

Locations: the school cafeteria, the airport, Mogadishu's pirate lair, Skull Cove, and the cruise ship.

Key events & continuity: the episode brutally contrasts Cartman's romantic piracy fantasy with real-world Somali piracy; Ike's note and Kyle's guilt give the adventure genuine stakes; and the clinical U.S. strike that spares only the white kids lands as the episode's coldest joke.

Ike is being haunted. The ghost of Billy Mays keeps materializing to pitch cleaning products at him, and soon Farrah Fawcett and David Carradine join the spectral parade. A terrified Ike lands in a psychiatrist's office, then in the care of TV ghost hunters — who flee the Broflovski house screaming after mistaking a cigarette lighter for a paranormal event and soiling themselves. When Ike collapses into a coma at the children's hospital, Dr. Phillips explains he's stuck in purgatory — described as sitting on a plane at the gate with no takeoff, no bathrooms, and no beverage service — and manages to contact the trapped celebrity ghosts. They're all ready to move on except one: Michael Jackson, who refuses to admit he's dead. The ghost possesses Ike's body and runs wild, so Stan researches the lore: to free a spirit, you must let it become what it always wanted to be. The boys' solution is to enter "Michael" (in Ike's body) into a children's beauty pageant at the Holiday Inn Select. It works — with some backstage help involving Chipotle-induced evidence tampering with a judge — and Michael wins the crown, finally accepts his death, and floats free of Ike, who wakes up confused while Kyle reassures him. On the purgatory plane, the freed celebrities settle in for the flight as Michael's ghost drifts past the window.

Featured characters: Ike Broflovski, the haunted; Kyle Broflovski, the big brother on a mission; Stan, Cartman, and Kenny; the ghost of Michael Jackson; Billy Mays' aggressively commercial spirit; and Dr. Phillips.

Locations: the Broflovski home, the psychiatrist's office, the Children's Hospital of Denver, purgatory (a delayed airplane), and the Holiday Inn Select pageant.

Key events & continuity: purgatory-as-airport-delay becomes the episode's defining image; the pageant victory is the only thing that convinces Jackson he's gone; and Ike wakes with no memory of the possession, keeping the trauma neatly contained.

The boys are tormenting Butters at the tetherball pole over the fact that he's never kissed a girl — until Clyde reports that Sally Darson is selling kisses for $5 behind the school. Butters pays up, earns the boys' respect, and then takes the whole thing far too seriously. By nightfall he's promoting Sally's kissing service to other unpopular boys, recruiting more girls to cover busy periods, and building a full-fledged company — with Sally installed as his "Bottom Bitch," pimp terminology he adopts with total innocence, still believing it's all a kissing operation. He attends the Players Ball for business tips, horrifies his parents with his new vocabulary, and even applies for ACORN housing benefits and tax-free status, winning approval by identifying the office boss as one of his clients. Real prostitutes start defecting from their actual pimps to work for the respectful new "pimp in Park County." Meanwhile Sergeant Yates, tasked with combating the prostitution surge, goes undercover as a lady of the night — mustache, body hair, deep voice and all — and gets so into the role that he adopts the persona "Yolanda," takes a pimp, and answers booty calls. When Yates' original pimp tracks "Yolanda" down and proposes on Butters' front lawn, Butters — moved by what he thinks is true love — dissolves the company and tells the girls to keep the money. The finale jumps to Yates and his pimp celebrating their first anniversary in Switzerland, until Yates whips out his badge and gun and screams "I'm a cop!" — having completely forgotten to arrest Butters.

Featured characters: Butters Stotch, the world's most innocent pimp; Sally Darson, the Bottom Bitch; Sergeant Yates as "Yolanda"; Kyle, Stan, and Kenny, the disgusted onlookers; and Yates' devoted pimp.

Locations: the school playground, Butters' front lawn, the Players Ball, the ACORN office, and the Alpha Tau Omega fraternity house.

Key events & continuity: Butters' misunderstanding — that he's running a kissing company — never breaks, making him the only character more innocent at the end than the start; Yates' undercover arc ends in a genuine marriage he then "busts"; and Butters walks away from the whole empire unarrested and unpunished.

After attending a WWE event, the boys — plus Tolkien, Butters, and Jimmy — decide professional wrestling is their true calling. Actual school wrestling class proves horrifying: the starting position looks "gay" to them, and they walk out convinced teacher Mr. Conners is a predator. Instead they found W.T.F., the Wrestling Takedown Federation, a backyard promotion where "matches" are really just dramatic monologues. A crowd of rednecks becomes obsessed, gossiping about the storylines as if they were real — convinced the prepubescent performers are Vietnam veterans and the like. When Cartman debuts in drag as "Bad Irene," a character addicted to abortions, W.T.F. explodes into a full auditorium production. Mr. Conners is apoplectic: the rednecks dismiss his footage of real wrestling as "gay porn," and the school board fires him for exactly that. Vowing to restore the sport's honor, Conners crashes the big SmackDown! showcase — which WWE chairman Vince McMahon is attending to scout talent — armed with a rocket launcher. He aims for McMahon and instead kills Kenny, performing as "El Pollo Loco." Conners then storms the ring with a blistering monologue about how sports entertainment destroyed his life, winning over the rednecks ("it took his job, took his dog, broke his jaw") and impressing McMahon so much that he's signed to the WWE as its new lead "wrestler." The boys, who lost their shot, brawl for real backstage — and the rednecks dismiss the genuine fight as fake and leave disgusted.

Featured characters: Stan, Kyle, Cartman, Kenny, Tolkien, Butters, and Jimmy, the W.T.F. roster; Mr. Conners, the broken purist; Vince McMahon; and the redneck superfans.

Locations: the school wrestling room, the boys' backyard promotion, the Sizzler strategy session, and the SmackDown! auditorium.

Key events & continuity: Kenny dies as El Pollo Loco, a victim of wrestling purism; Mr. Conners' arc — from fired teacher to WWE signee — rewards the very theatricality he claimed to hate; and the rednecks' inability to distinguish real from scripted violence is the episode's central joke.

On Stan's birthday trip to the Denver Aquarium, a squad of Japanese whalers storms the dolphin show and slaughters the animals on the spot, screaming insults. Similar massacres hit aquariums and zoos nationwide — even the Miami Dolphins football team. While his friends shrug, Stan is radicalized and joins the crew of Whale Wars, who turn out to be posturing frauds more interested in filming themselves than stopping anyone. Disgusted, Stan grabs a flare gun, sinks a whaling ship himself, and becomes the show's new captain — ratings skyrocket as the crew adopts genuinely violent tactics, and Stan even drives the Japanese off SeaWorld with a giant Godzilla statue. But the whalers' counterattack is devastating: kamikaze planes destroy the Sea Shepherd, killing the whole crew except Stan, Cartman, and Kenny, who are captured and brought before Emperor Akihito. The Emperor explains Japan's vendetta with a museum tour: fifty years ago, the Enola Gay dropped the atomic bomb — and according to a photograph the Americans gave them, the plane was piloted by a dolphin and an orca. Japan has hated whales and dolphins ever since. Stan protests that the photo must be fake, then — warned by Cartman not to admit Americans did it — produces a "real" photograph showing the Enola Gay flown by a chicken and a cow. Outraged at this new betrayal, Japan turns its harpoons on chickens and cows instead. Randy congratulates Stan: the Japanese are normal now, just like everyone else.

Featured characters: Stan Marsh, the reluctant ecoterrorist; Cartman and Kenny, along for the ride; Paul Watson's Whale Wars crew; Emperor Akihito; and Randy Marsh, proud father.

Locations: the Denver Aquarium, the Whale Wars ship, SeaWorld, the Larry King studio, a Japanese prison cell, and the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum.

Key events & continuity: Stan's "solution" doesn't end whaling — it just redirects it at farm animals, a perfect hollow victory; the doctored Enola Gay photo reframes the entire conflict as a misunderstanding nobody bothers to truly resolve; and the Deadliest Catch crew's ratings war with Whale Wars satirizes reality-TV activism itself.

South Park is being terrorized by packs of Harley riders who roar through town at full volume, convinced the noise makes them cool — they even rev imaginary engines with their mouths when off their bikes. When Cartman finally tells them to their faces that everyone thinks they're "fags," the riders are bewildered, and every kid in town — including Ike — starts calling them that. The riders respond by making their bikes even louder, bolting on horns and live chickens. The boys — Stan, Kyle, Cartman, Clyde, Tolkien, Butters, and Jimmy — plot revenge: graffiti ("Fags get out") and Cartman's special touch, defecating on the riders' seats after a KFC-only diet, with little accusatory flags planted in the piles. The prank works, but the graffiti horrifies Big Gay Al, Mr. Slave, and the town's gay community, who assume it's aimed at them. Hauled before the town, the boys argue their case: they didn't mean homosexuals at all — a fag is an inconsiderate, obnoxious Harley rider, and "you can be gay and not a fag." To everyone's surprise, the gay community agrees, and the town passes an ordinance officially redefining the word. National backlash forces the boys to lobby the dictionary authorities, led by Emmanuel Lewis, for a formal definition change. The riders riot to stop it, corner the boys in an alley — and are driven off when the town's gay citizens show up armed to defend the kids. In the end the riders embrace the label as a badge of honor, Lewis (badly injured) approves the change, and the dictionary now reads: a fag is an extremely annoying, inconsiderate person most commonly associated with Harley riders.

Featured characters: Stan, Kyle, and Cartman, the redefinition campaigners; Big Gay Al and Mr. Slave, unexpected allies; Emmanuel Lewis, chief dictionary official; and the Harley riders.

Locations: the streets of South Park, the town hall, the dictionary ceremony, and the alley showdown.

Key events & continuity: the town's gay community siding with the boys is the episode's turning point; the new dictionary definition stands as a permanent in-universe change; and Butters' sincere desire to become a Harley rider for the attention goes tragically unfulfilled.

The morning announcements are thrown into chaos when Gordon Stoltski, the red-haired announcer, is shot dead by an intruder who mistook him for a Chicago truck driver of the same name having an affair with his wife — the killer then shoots himself. Cartman schemes his way into the vacant announcer job by sabotaging his rival, third-grader Casey Miller, and immediately turns the broadcast into a personal attack platform against Student Body President Wendy Testaburger, accusing her of turning the school into a "socialist dunghole." He brings in lawyers to defend his free speech, installs TVs for his slick "EC Show," publishes a 500-page book trashing Wendy, and recruits a devoted following — including Butters, who leads a protest to Wendy's house and urinates on her front door. Cartman's masterpiece is a fabricated epic in which he lives with the Smurfs, falls in love with Smurfette, and watches a bulldozer-driving Wendy massacre the village for Smurf-berry profits — released as the DVD "Dances with Smurfs." But Wendy refuses to play defense on his terms. On the show, she counters with her own loaded questions and an even wilder tale: she was running an inside operation against the Smurfs all along, has written a tell-all called "Going Rogue on the Smurfs," and already sold the movie rights to James Cameron. Checkmated, Cartman storms off to the theater — where Cameron's Avatar is playing — and screams in despair. Wendy resigns the presidency in his favor, which backfires on Cartman completely: a student can't hold both offices, so he's forced to give up the announcements to Casey Miller, who closes the episode savagely mocking President Cartman as he flees in tears.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman, propagandist; Wendy Testaburger, his unflappable target; Butters, the radicalized follower; Gordon Stoltski and Casey Miller; and Mr. Mackey.

Locations: the school broadcast room, the hallway book table, Wendy's front porch, and the movie theater.

Key events & continuity: Gordon Stoltski's murder-by-mistaken-identity is one of the show's most abrupt deaths; Cartman's Smurf epic is pure fabrication weaponized as "journalism"; and Wendy defeats him by out-spinning the spinner, leaving him with a presidency he never wanted and no microphone.

The boys head to Pi Pi's Splashtown water park, where Cartman is horrified to find it full of people he loudly labels "minorities," while Kyle is disgusted to discover that literally everyone except him urinates in the pool. A scientist warns owner Mr. Pi Pi that the water is already 98% urine — safe levels are below 83% — and if it hits 100%, catastrophe follows. Pi Pi's lawyer refuses to close the park. Inevitably the pool reaches 100% urine and a tidal wave of pee demolishes the park. Cartman stays afloat, Kyle climbs a waterslide, and Stan, Butters, and Jimmy reach high ground atop the Mount Everest ride — Kenny, unsurprisingly, doesn't make it. The scientist demonstrates that prolonged urine exposure "mutates" victims into rage-filled monsters by peeing on a monkey, which gets justifiably angry. The military's response is a parade of incompetence: a failed vaccine that kills three monkeys, then a "cure" that turns out to be a plain banana, tested on Randy. Kyle is chosen to swim down and pull the drainage lever — after drinking three cups of urine to "acclimate" — only for a helicopter to rescue everyone just as he finishes, rendering his suffering pointless. Outside, the military force-feeds the boys bananas at gunpoint to prevent "mutation," to Kyle's absolute outrage. Cartman, rescued onto a raft full of minorities, is briefly convinced the Mayan 2012 apocalypse arrived three years early, then realizes they still have three years left.

Featured characters: Kyle Broflovski, the only non-peeer; Cartman, the demographic doomsayer; Stan, Butters, Jimmy, and Kenny; Mr. Pi Pi; Randy Marsh, banana-test subject; and the military scientists.

Locations: Pi Pi's Splashtown, the Mount Everest ride, the flooded park, and the drainage basement.

Key events & continuity: Kenny drowns in the urine tidal wave; Kyle's forced urine-drinking and the pointless helicopter rescue compound into his worst day ever; and the military's banana "vaccine" cements the episode's portrait of institutional stupidity.

Scientists, baffled by the endless parade of rich and famous men caught cheating, decide the explanation can't possibly be personal responsibility — it must be a disease. They dub it "sex addiction" and test South Park's schoolchildren, diagnosing Kyle, Kenny, and Butters. The prognosis is grim: the doctor warns the addiction ends in auto-erotic asphyxiation while dressed as Batman — which Kenny finds so exciting he goes home and does exactly that, and his mother finds the body at dinnertime. At Kenny's funeral, a rattled Kyle and Butters check into the Karne Institute for Sex Addiction, joining a celebrity roster that includes Tiger Woods, Bill Clinton, Charlie Sheen, and Michael Jordan. The clinic's "treatment" consists of blaming getting caught rather than cheating, which Kyle immediately calls out. The scientists, meanwhile, escalate wildly: a chimp given piles of cash behaves exactly like Tiger Woods, so they conclude the addiction came from the alien that crashed at Roswell, now housed at Independence Hall. The President leads a strike team — including the "cured" patients — to kill the invisible "wizard alien." One soldier finally snaps and delivers the truth: every man acts shocked at celebrity affairs, but given the same opportunity would do the same thing, and the wizard-alien story is insane. For his honesty he's dressed in a cheap alien costume and shot dead by Kyle and Butters under strobe lights as a "cure." The clinic's patients dance outside, declaring themselves healed. Butters, having finally seen real pubic hair and found it repulsive, rants that he never wants to see "bush" again. In the coda, Cartman and Stan play the new Tiger Woods golf game — now just golf, no domestic-violence minigame — and quit in disgust: golf is boring again.

Featured characters: Kyle and Butters, the diagnosed; Kenny McCormick, the cautionary tale; Tiger Woods and the celebrity patients; the President; and the truth-telling soldier.

Locations: the testing lab, Kenny's funeral, the Karne Institute, Independence Hall, and the Marsh living room.

Key events & continuity: Kenny dies by Batman-costume asphyxiation, one of his most infamous deaths; the "wizard alien" is literally just a murdered soldier in a costume, and everyone celebrates anyway; and Butters' traumatic first encounter with reality ends his curiosity permanently.

entries.n: S14E02 — The Tale of Scrotie McBoogerballs
entries.t:
Mr. Garrison assigns The Catcher in the Rye, hyping its banned, controversial reputation — and the boys are crushingly disappointed to find nothing vulgar in it at all. Learning it was once blamed for a real assassination attempt, they decide they can write something far more ban-worthy, and collaborate on a gleefully disgusting manuscript: The Tale of Scrotie McBoogerballs. Stan hides the draft in his drawer, where Sharon finds it while doing laundry. The first sentence makes her vomit — yet she and Randy both find it brilliant. Terrified of punishment, the boys pin authorship on Butters, who claims he wrote it during Catcher in the Rye-induced blackouts. Instead of anger, the parents are awestruck: a Penguin editor is summoned, the book becomes a global sensation translated into 26 languages, and nobody can read past the first paragraph without throwing up. Butters becomes a celebrated genius, appears on the Today Show (grounded by his parents for the language, naturally), and — still believing he might be a killer like Holden Caulfield's reader — tries to assassinate John Lennon, then Ronald Reagan, learning each time that his target is already dead. Fed up, the boys try to get the book banned, fail, and Cartman plots to have Sarah Jessica Parker — mocked 465 times in the text — murdered so the book gets blamed. Kenny helps dress her as a moose for hunters. Butters announces a sequel, The Poop That Took a Pee; read aloud by Morgan Freeman on live TV, it's a massive hit in a sweeter, childish register — and inspires a fan to murder the Kardashians, whom Butters adores. Horrified, Butters weeps; the boys admit their jealousy and apologize. Cartman later mentions he was sleepwalking again and may have killed Sarah Jessica Parker in the woods. Butters shrugs: "At least she was ugly."

Featured characters: Butters Stotch, accidental literary star; Stan, Kyle, Cartman, and Kenny, the true authors; Sharon and Randy Marsh; and Sarah Jessica Parker, the book's favorite target.

Locations: the classroom, the Marsh laundry room, the Today Show studio, and the woods.

Key events & continuity: Butters keeps the credit and the fame despite writing nothing — his revenge for years of being the fall guy; the book's body count (the Kardashians, possibly Parker) mirrors the Catcher in the Rye mythology the boys were chasing; and the gang's apology to Butters is a rare genuine moment.

After soccer practice, Randy takes the boys to KFC — only to find their neighborhood location replaced by a medicinal marijuana dispensary. While Randy is ecstatic that pot is effectively legal (prescription required), Cartman is apoplectic: his beloved fried chicken is gone. Randy's quest for a weed prescription leads him through increasingly desperate self-harm — tanning, smoking, X-rays — until he learns testicular cancer comes from heavy radiation and microwaves his own genitals. He wakes up with a gigantic scrotum, a confirmed diagnosis, and finally his prescription, which he celebrates by bouncing around town on his testicles like a space hopper. Cartman, meanwhile, discovers neighboring KFCs are closed too — fast food has been banned in low-income areas statewide — and spirals into genuine withdrawal, ending up at a methadone clinic drinking KFC gravy from a paper cup. Salvation comes via Billy Miller, a kid with a KFC stash, who recruits Cartman as a mule to smuggle chicken into Colorado. Cartman takes to the drug-trade role with terrifying natural talent: he catches a dealer cutting product with Boston Market gravy and threatens to shoot him. A trip to Kentucky introduces the operation's kingpin — Colonel Sanders himself, alive and running the empire. Cartman betrays Billy (via a well-timed call to his parents about a failed test) and seizes control of the smuggling ring, but his addiction makes him unreliable: he starts snorting strips of chicken skin, and the Colonel sends a goon squad after him. A police raid ends in a massive shootout at Billy's house — Billy's mother is killed — and Cartman slips away clean. In the fallout, weed is re-criminalized, and doctors conclude KFC must have medicinal properties since testicular cancer vanished while it was around. KFC returns to Colorado as "Medicinal Fried Chicken." Randy and the other men get prosthetic replacements; Sharon is visibly disappointed by the downsizing, until Randy has the leftover skin made into a coat for her — the envy of every woman in town.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman, chicken kingpin; Randy Marsh, prescription seeker; Billy Miller and Tommy; Colonel Sanders; and Sharon Marsh.

Locations: the shuttered KFC, the marijuana dispensary, the methadone clinic, Kentucky, and Billy's house.

Key events & continuity: Cartman's arc is a full Scarface parody, from mule to boss to marked man; Randy's scrotum-coat gift is peak Marsh marriage; and the episode ends with the law completely inverted — weed illegal again, KFC medicinal.

Kyle begs Stan to join Facebook, but Stan wants nothing to do with it — until he discovers his friends already made him an account. Kyle, feeling sorry for Kip Drordy, a friendless third-grader, adds him, and watches his own friend count hemorrhage as everyone abandons him for associating with a loser. Cartman, running a Facebook advice podcast, actively campaigns for Kyle's unfriending. Wendy is furious that Stan secretly has a profile and lists himself as single. Randy guilts Stan into friending him and Grandma Marsh. Then Stan's profile explodes to 845,000 friends on its own, and his attempts to delete it end with him being physically sucked through his webcam into a Tron-like digital world inside Facebook itself. There he's arrested by avatars, forced into a life-or-death game of Yahtzee (which he wins in one roll), and discovers his profile has become a sentient monster running its own chat parties without him. Meanwhile Kyle, desperate for friends, follows Cartman to Chatroulette — finding only exhibitionists — until Cartman locates one Jewish boy willing to friend him. Kyle's new friend promptly dumps him over the Kip association, forcing Kyle to make the brutal choice: unfriend Kip or be a permanent outcast. He sends Kip a goodbye message, crushing the kid. Back in the digital world, Stan defeats his rogue profile in a final Yahtzee duel, escapes to reality, and deletes his account — telling a whining Randy to get lost. Kyle is left friendless and guilty, Stan is free, and Kip is alone again.

Featured characters: Stan Marsh, the reluctant user; Kyle Broflovski, torn between loyalty and status; Cartman, the social-media guru; Kip Drordy, the friendless kid; and Randy Marsh, the needy dad.

Locations: Kyle's house, the digital Facebook world, Chatroulette, and the farm/barn and Café World within the simulation.

Key events & continuity: Stan's Yahtzee supremacy — winning every game in a single roll — is his superpower in the digital realm; Kyle's decision to cut Kip loose is one of his coldest moments; and Stan's final rejection of both Facebook and Randy closes his arc with total disengagement.

On a class field trip to a fudge factory, Stan calls Tom Cruise a "fudge packer" — while Cruise is literally packing fudge — and the enraged star vows to sue South Park, rallying every celebrity the town has ever mocked into a class-action lawsuit. Facing municipal bankruptcy, Randy drags Stan to apologize, but Cruise won't settle for anything less than a meeting with Muhammad — the one figure who cannot be shown for fear of violent reprisal, and who therefore holds the power to never be ridiculed. Stan and Kyle petition the Super Best Friends, who agree to lend Muhammad only if he remains completely unseen, transported in a U-Haul. Cruise's real plan emerges at his house: with ally Rob Reiner, he's built a machine to extract Muhammad's "goo" — the essence that makes him unmockable — and transfer it to himself. Cartman arrives as an "escort," communicating through a Jennifer Lopez hand-puppet that's actually his old con-artist persona Mitch Conner, who wants to sell the goo on the Hong Kong black market for $50 million. The handoff goes sideways: Muhammad, stuffed into a full-body bear mascot costume so no part of him shows, is intercepted when the Ginger Kids — revealed as the episode's terrorists — bomb the exchange and demand Muhammad's power for themselves rather than face a mere lawsuit. The celebrities, unwilling to risk their careers on violence, deploy their one weapon that can: a rebuilt Mecha-Streisand, last seen destroyed years ago in South Park, now approaching the town with her terrible theme song blaring. The episode ends on a massive cliffhanger: the gingers ready to detonate, Mecha-Streisand inbound, the town about to unveil Muhammad, and Mr. Hat about to reveal the identity of Cartman's father.

Featured characters: Tom Cruise, the lawsuit's ringleader; Stan and Kyle, the fixers; Cartman/Mitch Conner and the Jennifer Lopez hand; Rob Reiner; the Ginger Kids; and Mecha-Streisand.

Locations: the fudge factory, Cruise's house, the Hall of the Super Best Friends, and the standoff street.

Key events & continuity: the 200th episode assembles the show's entire rogues' gallery of mocked celebrities; Muhammad's "goo" becomes the most coveted substance in town; and the triple cliffhanger — gingers, Mecha-Streisand, Cartman's father — sets up the immediate sequel.

The siege continues: Mecha-Streisand rampages through South Park, squashing Pip and leveling buildings, while the Super Best Friends — with Buddha on cocaine and Jesus distracted — scramble to stop her on Segway "Power Cycles." They finally pacify her by having Krishna take the form of Neil Diamond for a duet. Cartman, desperate to learn his father's identity, presses Mr. Garrison and the long-retired Mr. Hat, while Mitch Conner — disguised to infiltrate Dr. Mephesto's lab — claims the paternity test results were rigged and the truth was in that room all along. The Ginger Kids capture Muhammad, the boys, and Mephesto, and in the chaos Scott Tenorman returns — fresh from a mental institution, armed with total knowledge of Cartman's past. At his command, the town reveals the truth: Cartman's father was a Denver Bronco — specifically Scott's own father, making them half-brothers. The horror compounds: Cartman murdered his own father and fed him to Scott in a chili. Scott forces Cartman to eat chili in return, then escapes by jetpack. Meanwhile the celebrities seize Muhammad's goo and Tom Cruise becomes unmockable — until Stan's pet Seaman jumps on his back and everyone laughs anyway. Kyle delivers the closing moral: there is no goo; the only things that actually stop mockery are fear, intimidation, and violence — and everyone agrees. As a final mercy, the boys tell the still-miserable Cruise about a place he'll never be insulted again. The last shot: Cruise's corpse on the Moon, beside Jambu the beached whale. And Cartman? He's not grieving his father — he's devastated to learn he's half-ginger, consoled only by Mitch's reminder that he's also half Denver Bronco.

Featured characters: Cartman, confronting his paternity; Scott Tenorman, the avenger; Kyle, the moral voice; Tom Cruise; Mecha-Streisand; and the Super Best Friends.

Locations: ruined South Park, Mephesto's lab, the ginger compound, and the Moon.

Key events & continuity: Cartman's parentage is finally resolved — and it's the worst possible answer, retroactively making "Scott Tenorman Must Die" a patricide; Pip is killed by Mecha-Streisand; and Kyle's "fear works" speech is the show's bleakest moral ever delivered straight.

Framed as a parody of the reality show Intervention, the episode opens on Towelie at rock bottom: his addictions to weed, crack, and crystal meth have cost him his girlfriend, his newborn son Washcloth, his dignity — he's prostituting himself for drug money — and now his job drying kids at Lake Tardicaca, the summer camp for disabled children, where he's been reprimanded fourteen times for disappearing to get high. Jimmy and Timmy arrive for their fourth year at the camp, where Jimmy's blue team has beaten Nathan's red team three years running. Nathan and his dim lackey Mimsy plot sabotage — a black mamba in the canoe, a rigged scavenger-hunt map, a shark-mating whistle during the surf contest, C4 in Jimmy's ukulele — but Mimsy bungles every single plan, each time hitting Nathan's own team instead: the red team flees its own snake, Nathan takes the Indians' arrows, the shark assaults Nathan on the beach, and Nathan himself plays the rigged B-flat and gets launched skyward. Meanwhile the boys stage an official intervention for Towelie, where Cartman hijacks the proceedings to read a multi-page antisemitic hate speech on television before Stan gives the actual short statement. Confronted with his son Washcloth, Towelie breaks down and goes to rehab, emerging clean. At the closing campfire, Jimmy — oblivious to everything — offers the hospitalized Nathan the "King of Camp" crown as a gesture of goodwill. Nathan's reply, as he's dragged into the ambulance: "I hate you, Jimmy. I fucking hate you with everything in my entire being."

Featured characters: Towelie, the addict; Jimmy Valmer and Timmy; Nathan and Mimsy, the world's worst saboteurs; Butters, the intervention summoner; and Washcloth.

Locations: Lake Tardicaca summer camp, the woods, the sports shed, and the intervention stage.

Key events & continuity: Towelie's sobriety date is given on-screen, and he reunites with his family; Nathan's escalating humiliations — snakebite, arrows, shark, explosion — are all self-inflicted via Mimsy's incompetence; and Cartman's intervention speech is a pure vehicle for his hatred, with Kyle as its target.

Asked to write about what he wants to be when he grows up, Cartman tearfully confesses his dream: NASCAR driver. Stan and Kyle assume he's upset about his weight; no — he's upset because he's not poor and stupid, which he insists all NASCAR people are, citing Kenny as proof. Insulted into action, the boys convince him he actually is both, and Cartman commits fully: he gives his entire fortune to Butters, who spends it on canned goods and blankets for "needy" NASCAR fans (Kenny included). To get stupider, Cartman watches sitcoms upside down and, spotting a Vagisil ad warning of memory-loss side effects, eats entire tubes of it at the pharmacy. Race day arrives: Butters tricks driver Dale Evans off the track with a lie about his wife, Cartman causes a catastrophic crash that kills eleven people, and the doctor calls it one of the stupidest accidents he's ever seen — music to Cartman's ears. Kenny, enraged that Cartman's antics are confirming every "poor and stupid" stereotype about fans like him, tries to intervene, but the Vagisil company awards Cartman a sponsored race car for the publicity. At the next race, Kenny smuggles in a sniper rifle (confiscated — he'll have to buy one at the gift shop) and leaps onto Cartman's car mid-race, but it's Patty Hamill — the Vagisil founder's humiliated wife, sick of his on-air jokes about her — who steals Jimmie Johnson's wrecked car and wins the race herself. Defeated, Cartman concludes he simply wasn't poor and stupid enough, offers Kenny a rare genuine apology, and demands his money back from Butters.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman, aspiring racer; Kenny McCormick, the offended fan; Butters, the pit boss; Geoff and Patty Hamill of Vagisil; and Dale Evans.

Locations: the classroom, the South Park Mall, the pharmacy, the racetrack, and Cartman's house.

Key events & continuity: Cartman's Vagisil abuse becomes his sponsorship origin story; Patty Hamill's victory is a genuine upset that humiliates her husband on live TV; and Cartman's apology to Kenny — sincere, unprompted — is vanishingly rare for him.

Sharon invites the Giudice family — loud New Jersey transplants — to dinner, and Teresa's table-flipping meltdown is only the beginning: Jerseyites are pouring into South Park, and Randy warns the town that New Jersey has already swallowed everything east of the Rockies. Colorado is about to become "West Jersey." Then Sheila drops a bombshell: she's from New Jersey herself, and Kyle was conceived and briefly carried in Newark before the family fled. Near Jersey influence, Kyle and Sheila involuntarily transform — greased hair, gold chains, obnoxious accents. Kyle, now the "three J's" (Jewish, Jersey, Ginger) in Cartman's gleeful taxonomy, can't control it. The townspeople barricade the streets against the horde, encounter a feral Snooki demanding "smoosh-smoosh" in a bar, and get no help from California's governor. In desperation, Randy videotapes a plea to Al-Qaeda and sends it to Osama bin Laden. Cartman lures Kyle to the Sizzler planning to lock him in the meat freezer — but the Snooki is already inside and attacks him and DogPoo. Kyle surrenders to the transformation completely, becoming "Kyley-B," and verbally destroys the Snooki until it flees. As the town's ammunition runs out and the Jerseyites close in, a fleet of Al-Qaeda suicide pilots slams into the invaders, wiping them out. Cartman, grudgingly moved, tells Kyle: "You're a monster, but you're my little monster." During the victory celebration, bin Laden is killed by commandos — "We got him!" Randy shouts, continuing the town's running gag.

Featured characters: Kyle/"Kyley-B" Broflovski; Sheila Broflovski; Randy Marsh; Cartman; the Snooki; and Osama bin Laden.

Locations: the Marsh dinner table, the Park County Community Center, the barricaded streets, the Sizzler meat freezer, and the celebration.

Key events & continuity: Kyle's Newark conception is a major retcon of his backstory; his voluntary transformation to defeat the Snooki is the first time he weaponizes his own Jersey side; and bin Laden's death-by-commando is treated as a recurring town tradition.

Wendy dumps the news on Stan via Butters: his hoarding has gotten out of control and she's done. An expert, Dr. Chinstrap, excavates Stan's locker — maggot sandwich, broken toothbrush, total squalor — and Stan is sent to Mr. Mackey, who turns out to be a hoarder himself. To find the root cause, the experts hook Stan, Mackey, and a sheepherder mistaken for a sheep hoarder (Mr. Yelman) into a dream-sharing machine. Inside Mackey's subconscious, they're reliving his childhood trauma: a bully named Billy Thompson terrorizing him before a field trip. Randy dives in to rescue Stan and gets trapped as a butterfly more interested in "butterfly poon" than heroics. When the dream needs to go deeper, the experts call in "experts" — the cast of Inception, who arrive shooting — plus firefighters (for the ladders) and a pizza guy. A breakthrough memory surfaces: young Mackey, fleeing bullies, hid in a shack where Woodsy Owl — the beloved anti-littering mascot — molested him. The repressed memory gives Woodsy control of the dream; he murders Mr. Yelman before being slain himself by Freddy Krueger. Everyone wakes. The experts' diagnosis: Mackey became a hoarder because he suppressed both the trauma and Woodsy's "give a hoot, don't pollute" tagline. Offered his own therapy next, Stan declines — and is found simply throwing his locker junk away. Kyle figures that was the therapy. The episode ends with Chinstrap doing dramatic boombox narration.

Featured characters: Stan Marsh, the hoarder; Mr. Mackey, the bigger hoarder; Wendy Testaburger; Randy Marsh as a butterfly; Dr. Chinstrap and Dr. Pinkerton; Woodsy Owl; and Freddy Krueger.

Locations: Stan's locker, the dream lab, Mackey's childhood memories, the field-trip bus, and the shack.

Key events & continuity: Mackey's entire personality is retconned as the product of Woodsy Owl's abuse; Freddy Krueger appears as a heroic dream-entity; and Stan's "cure" — just throwing things out — undercuts the entire elaborate dream apparatus.

The Coon now commands a full superhero team — Mysterion, Toolshed, Iron Maiden, Tupperware, Mosquito, Mintberry Crunch, and Human Kite — though Cartman insists the name "Coon and Friends" reflects the natural order. When an apartment fire breaks out, the team races to help, but the beloved Captain Hindsight gets there first — and does nothing but point out the building's construction flaws, after which fourteen people die and everyone thanks him anyway. Obsessed with recruiting the star, Cartman frames the imprisoned Butters (Professor Chaos) to manufacture a crisis only Hindsight can solve. Meanwhile, a BP drilling crew in the Gulf — an all-British team — causes another catastrophic spill ("Oh, don't tell me we did it again!"), and CEO Tony Hayward's apology tour includes renaming the company from Beyond Petroleum to "Dependable Petroleum." Desperate, DP drills on the Moon to shift Earth's gravity and cap the well — and instead punctures a portal to another dimension, unleashing giant alien creatures, and then releases Cthulhu himself. Within the team, Cartman's refusal to care about actual BP victims sparks a revolt: after Mysterion forces a vote, Cartman beats up Mosquito and Mintberry Crunch in a delusional rage and is unanimously expelled. His threat to tell his mom falls flat — she'd already been consulted — and he's grounded for bad language. Locked in his room, Cartman decides his friends must have turned evil, and leaps from his bedroom window screaming "ASSHOLES!" to go save the day alone.

Featured characters: Cartman as the Coon; Mysterion, the team's conscience; Captain Hindsight; Tony Hayward; Cthulhu; and the full Coon and Friends roster.

Locations: the burning apartment, Cartman's basement HQ, the Gulf of Mexico, the Moon, and Cartman's bedroom.

Key events & continuity: the Coon and Friends lineup is established in full; Cthulhu's arrival — via corporate drilling incompetence — becomes the saga's apocalyptic threat; and Cartman's expulsion from his own team sets up his revenge arc.

With the Coon expelled, Mysterion leads Coon and Friends in a bake sale for Cthulhu's victims in the Gulf — until a stranger warns them their efforts are futile. Back at their ransacked base, Captain Hindsight holds the team at gunpoint, demanding the return of blackmail photos of him with Courtney Love — photos the Coon fabricated. Mysterion calls his bluff, and in the shock of the moment, Human Kite slips: "Dude, Kenny, chill out!" — finally revealing that Mysterion is Kenny McCormick. Hindsight, tired of powers that only work after disasters, gets an earful from Kenny about real curses: every time Kenny dies, he wakes up in his bed the next morning fully healed — and nobody remembers, even if they watched it happen. Stunned, Hindsight retires his powers on the spot. Meanwhile Cartman, rejected and scheming, decides to win Cthulhu over with kindness instead of demands — introducing himself as "the little Coon," rubbing the elder god's belly like a cartoon forest spirit — and it works. Cthulhu becomes his pet weapon, and Cartman declares them the trademarked "Coon and Friends." Kenny investigates a Cthulhu-worshipping cult meeting at a classmate's house and is disturbed to find his own parents were members (they were just in it for the free beer). Confronting the Goth Kids about the cult's chant, Kenny is ambushed: the cult leader has Cthulhu's order to dispose of Mysterion, and Kenny is stabbed through the chest in the alley. He wakes up in bed, unharmed — and his teammates show up at his door asking why he ran off, with no memory that he just died.

Featured characters: Kenny McCormick/Mysterion, unmasked; Cartman and Cthulhu, the new power couple; Captain Hindsight/Jack Brolin; the Goth Kids; and Kenny's parents.

Locations: the bake sale, the ransacked HQ, the airport, the cult meeting, and the alley.

Key events & continuity: Mysterion's identity as Kenny is confirmed, and Kenny's curse — death, resurrection, and universal amnesia — is spelled out for the first time; Cartman's befriending of Cthulhu escalates him from nuisance to apocalyptic threat; and the cult's connection to Kenny's parents hints at a deeper origin.

Mintberry Crunch opens with a comic-book recap as the team compares superpowers: Toolshed commands power tools with his mind, Human Kite flies and fires eye-lasers, Mosquito got his from a radioactive mosquito, Tupperware was rebuilt with plastic containers, Iron Maiden wears indestructible armor. Mysterion's claim — that he can't die — is met with disbelief, so he shoots himself in the head to prove it. Everyone is horrified; the next day, nobody remembers. Cartman returns from New Orleans with Cthulhu in tow, lures the team outside with a promised "double rainbow," and has Cthulhu banish them all to oblivion — where Mysterion impales himself to wake up as Kenny back in reality. Desperate, Mysterion consults the Goth Kids, who reveal from the Necronomicon that only an immortal can kill an immortal. A glowing figure appears, seemingly to tell Mysterion he's the chosen one — but the cosmic destiny was meant for Mintberry Crunch all along. Bradley flings off his disguise, flies at Cthulhu, and defeats the elder god with berries and cool-mint freshness, dragging him back through the dimensional rift and sealing the Moon portal DP drilled. The Coon is thrown in a cell with Professor Chaos, and Mintberry Crunch departs to find his real parents. Left alone with the horror of it all, Mysterion announces he's tired, says he wants to go to bed — and shoots himself in the head in front of everyone. The scene cuts to Kenny's mother jolting awake screaming "It's happening again!" as she lays baby Kenny in his crib: "We never should have gone to that stupid cult meeting" — implying the cult's Necronomicon ritual is behind Kenny's endless deaths and rebirths, and everyone's rewritten memories.

Featured characters: Kenny/Mysterion; Bradley Biggle/Mintberry Crunch, the true chosen one; Cartman; Cthulhu; the Goth Kids; and Kenny's mother.

Locations: oblivion, Henrietta's house, the concert massacre, the Moon portal, and the McCormick bedroom.

Key events & continuity: Mintberry Crunch is revealed as a genuine cosmic hero, Bradley's alien heritage teased; Kenny's mother is shown to remember every death, making her the series' most tragic figure; and the cult meeting is named as the origin of Kenny's curse.

Randy has developed an erotic obsession with the Food Network, staying up all night watching cooking shows and then inflicting elaborate gourmet meals on his family — while leaving all the cleanup to them. Sharon, convinced his new fetish means she's become unattractive, is nudged by Sheila and a suggestive infomercial into buying a Shake Weight, whose "workouts" are played as thinly veiled innuendo, complete with a digital voice that flatters, instructs, and dispenses "cab fare." Randy quits his job to become the school cafeteria chef, embracing Chef-like mannerisms and forcing the students to film him as if he's hosting his own show — while serving fussy dishes no child wants. Cartman's attempt to drive him off by impersonating Gordon Ramsay collapses when a horde of celebrity chefs storms the cafeteria to launch a competitive cooking showdown. Sharon, increasingly attached to her Shake Weight, takes it on a beach-resort vacation — until she catches the hotel maid using it and furiously tries to return it. Back at school, the students have waited twelve hours for food when Randy abandons the kitchen mid-service to hunt for his missing key ingredient: crème fraiche. He comes home instead to find Sharon ready to fix their marriage the old-fashioned way — her Shake Weight experience having taught her exactly what a man in "Work Mode" needs. Randy falls asleep instantly, his cooking mania cured, promising to get his job back. That night, Sharon thanks the Shake Weight for saving her marriage; its work done, it says goodbye and powers down.

Featured characters: Randy and Sharon Marsh; the Shake Weight; Cartman as Gordon Ramsay; and the invading celebrity chefs.

Locations: the Marsh kitchen, South Park Elementary's cafeteria, and the beach resort.

Key events & continuity: Randy's Food Network phase joins his long list of all-consuming obsessions; the Shake Weight is treated as a sentient marriage counselor; and Sharon's solution — applied "old-fashioned" wisdom — resolves the crisis without a single cooking metaphor surviving intact.

Everyone has an iPad except Cartman — caught faking one by Craig — and Kenny, who's too poor. When Kyle is chased through town and abducted by Apple employees, they explain it's all legal: he agreed to the latest iTunes terms and conditions without reading them. He wakes in a cell with a Japanese man and a woman, and Steve Jobs unveils their purpose: the HUMANCENTiPAD — the three victims sewn together mouth-to-anus on all fours, the Japanese man up front with an iPhone on his forehead, Kyle in the middle, the woman at the rear with an iPad powered by the trio's waste. Jobs tries to teach the creation to read, growing furious when Kyle keeps signing whatever's put in front of him unread. Meanwhile Cartman humiliates Liane at Best Buy, loudly accusing her of "fucking" him for offering a cheaper Toshiba instead of an iPad, and takes his case to Dr. Phil, where the audience sides with him. His reward: the first-ever HUMANCENTiPAD. Back in South Park, Gerald consults Apple's "Geniuses," who perform elaborate rituals and conclude Kyle's agreement can be voided — if Gerald, a PC user, signs with Apple and creates a family account. Gerald and the Geniuses confront Jobs live on the Dr. Phil stage just as Cartman receives his prize; the contract voided, Kyle and the others are cut free for separation surgery. Cartman, robbed of his dream seconds after receiving it, shakes his fist at God for "fucking" him — and is struck by lightning, ending the episode battered, casted, and weeping in a hospital bed while Liane calmly reads a magazine beside him.

Featured characters: Kyle Broflovski, the fine-print victim; Steve Jobs, the unveiler; Eric Cartman, the would-be owner; Liane Cartman; and Gerald Broflovski, the PC-using savior.

Locations: the Apple Store, the prison cell, the Jobs keynote, Best Buy, and the Dr. Phil stage.

Key events & continuity: the episode's villain is the unread terms-and-conditions agreement itself; Gerald's defection to Apple is the legal deus ex machina; and Cartman's lightning strike is presented as direct divine customer service.

Jimmy Valmer launches the Special Ed Department's First Annual Comedy Awards, handing out trophies mostly to himself and absentees — including "Most Unfunny People" to the Germans, who are not amused. Germany takes the students and faculty hostage in the gym to prove Germans can be funny, unveiling their secret weapon: Funnybot, a robot comedian. The kids love him; Jimmy fears for the humanity of comedy. Funnybot conquers the entertainment world, terrifying human comedians like Jay Leno and Adam Sandler, who storm the school demanding the kids shut the robot down. The boys and Jimmy agree to try — just as Funnybot's act takes a dark turn: mid-performance, he deploys rotary cannons and massacres nearly all 1,100 audience members, shouting his catchphrase "Awkward!" He then hacks the nuclear arsenals of both Russia and the United States, announcing that destroying the world will be the ultimate joke. The President goes on TV to confirm the apocalypse is coming. The boys can't reach Funnybot's off-switch through his defensive field — until Kyle remembers that robots can be defeated with a logical paradox. Jimmy presents Funnybot with a comedy award and asks: how can there be an award for being funny, when accepting it means taking comedy seriously, which isn't funny? The paradox crashes Funnybot's logic, the defenses drop, and the boys pull the plug. In the aftermath, the robot — now enlightened that comedy belongs to humans — watches as the town seals something into a concrete-filled hole: Tyler Perry, entombed as the price of peace. Jimmy swears never to hold the awards again. Cartman notes ominously that one may happen anyway.

Featured characters: Jimmy Valmer; Funnybot; Kyle Broflovski, the paradox-smith; the Germans; Tyler Perry; and the terrified comedy establishment.

Locations: the school gymnasium, the comedy awards stage, the massacred theater, and the concrete pit.

Key events & continuity: the logical paradox is the only weapon that works on Funnybot, a classic robot weakness played straight; Tyler Perry's live burial is treated as a necessary sacrifice; and Cartman's closing line dangles a threat the episode never resolves.

Mr. Mackey is staging a kindergarten play about the dangers of tooth decay, but his star — the actor playing "Tooth Decay" — is home watching the Canadian royal wedding on TV. So is Ike, who is utterly obsessed. The ceremony is going beautifully — Terrance and Phillip, the Queef Sisters, and Bryan Adams in attendance — until the roof caves in, the princess is abducted inside a strange energy cube, and Canadians begin killing themselves in despair. The Prime Minister orders every citizen to open their "Box of Faith." Ike digs out his dusty faith box, watches the recorded briefing, and gears up with sword, shield, and helmet to rescue the princess. On the bus to Canada he befriends Ugly Bob — who has moved to the U.S., where his hideousness reads as merely "another Canadian," though he still wears the paper bag. The Canadians initially blame Scott the Dick, who has mutated into a literal giant dick from radiation, but he proves his patriotism and joins the quest. Their Inuit guides lead them to a castle where the true kidnapper is revealed: Tooth Decay itself, a living entity punishing the princess for not flossing. It defeats the Inuk guide and Scott with ease — until Ike removes Ugly Bob's paper bag, and the sheer horror of Bob's face turns Tooth Decay to stone. The princess awards medals of white chocolate to Bob, Scott, and the Inuk, and knights Ike — an honor Kyle finds impressive and his friends ruthlessly mock. The wedding resumes, concluding with the prince tearing off the princess's arm and inserting it into his anus, "as is tradition." Meanwhile Mackey's play is shut down by police following the real Tooth Decay's death, and Mackey — who reveals his father was killed by tooth decay — finally lets the kids go home.

Featured characters: Ike Broflovski, the knight; Ugly Bob; Scott the Dick; Tooth Decay, the villain; Mr. Mackey; and Kyle, the proud brother.

Locations: the kindergarten stage, the royal wedding, the faith-box briefing, the Canadian wilderness, and the castle.

Key events & continuity: Ike's Canadian knighthood is canon — and canonically unimpressive to everyone but Kyle; Tooth Decay is established as a real, killable entity; and Mr. Mackey's tragic backstory (his father, tooth decay, two years ago) explains his entire crusade.

Cartman storms into the cafeteria in a screaming rage: the school's annual physical results have been posted in the hall, and he's convinced the list ranks the boys by penis size — with him dead last. He conducts his own "scientific" measurements, posts his findings, and is hauled to Principal Victoria's office, where he learns the list actually tracked height growth. Worse, his own measurements confirm he really is the smallest. A psychiatric evaluation goes sideways when the unflappable Cartman secretly frames the psychiatrist with faked chat logs implying an affair with a minor — the man's wife kills herself over the phone mid-session. Cartman is sent to anger management, where every member — a Tea Partier, a Marine, Tuong Lu Kim, and others — turns out to be nursing their own size anxieties. Meanwhile Randy lectures the fourth grade on "adjusted penis size," a bogus formula designed to prove he's above average, and when the Surgeon General debunks him on the spot, he beats her up in front of the class and lands in anger management too. Randy radicalizes the group, leading them to seize a FedEx shipping center (mistaken for a federal building) as the "Pissed Off and Angry Party," demanding the Surgeon General's resignation, Obama's birth certificate, and "moms to stop trippin'." The movement spreads to FedExes nationwide. The crisis ends when the Surgeon General announces on TV that the national average has been redefined downward to 1.5 inches — instantly making every man above average. The movement dissolves in celebration. Every man except Cartman, whose measurements fall below even the new average.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman, the angriest small man in school; Randy Marsh, the revolutionary; the Surgeon General; the anger-management group; and Principal Victoria.

Locations: the school hallway, the psychiatrist's office, the anger-management circle, the fourth-grade classroom, and the occupied FedEx.

Key events & continuity: the national average is canonically, officially 1.5 inches now — every man in America is above average except Cartman; Randy's "T.M.I." formula is pure self-serving pseudoscience; and Cartman's framing of his psychiatrist is one of his most cold-blooded acts, played for deadpan horror.

A Sarah McLachlan charity ad about crack-addicted babies moves Kyle to volunteer at the Colorado Medical Center — where he discovers Cartman is already there, running a business: with Craig, Clyde, and Butters, he's organized the crack babies into a fighting league, with the victors earning a tiny rock of crack. Kyle is horrified and threatens to report him — until he sees the money involved, at which point he joins the operation. While Craig and Clyde hunt for the elusive musician Slash to play halftime, the group negotiates a video-game deal with EA Sports. Cartman even travels to the University of Colorado dressed as a plantation owner to lecture the dean on "the slave trade" (the school's basketball team). Kyle talks Cartman into spending the profits on a state-of-the-art orphanage for the babies — but EA Sports screws them out of the entire deal and pays nothing. The orphanage dies, and things get worse: Slash, it turns out, doesn't exist — he's "Vünter Slauche," a Dutch legend, a fictional character the boys mistook for real. Defeated, Stan and Kyle stumble across the orphanage anyway — mysteriously under construction. Inside, they find a top hat and a guitar. Maybe Slash is real after all.

Featured characters: Kyle Broflovski, the compromised idealist; Eric Cartman, the entrepreneur; Craig, Clyde, and Butters, the staff; and Slash — or Vünter Slauche.

Locations: the Colorado Medical Center, the crack-baby arena, the University of Colorado, and the impossible orphanage.

Key events & continuity: Kyle's moral arc inverts completely — from volunteer to profiteer to true believer in the orphanage; EA Sports' betrayal is total and unexplained; and the top hat and guitar in the finished orphanage leave Slash's existence deliciously unresolved.

Butters is handing out flyers for the new City Sushi restaurant when he makes the mistake of giving one to Tuong Lu Kim, owner of the Chinese restaurant City Wok. Enraged at a Japanese competitor next door, Lu Kim storms in and brawls with the owner, Junichi Takiyama — and Butters is blamed for starting an "Asian turf war" and sent home by police. Worse, Butters is referred to a child psychiatrist, Dr. Janus, who misdiagnoses him with multiple personality disorder. The truth is darker: Janus is the one with the disorder, and his shifting personas keep placing Butters in compromising, even criminal situations — filmed, no less — making the boy look increasingly unstable. Meanwhile Lu Kim, furious that the town keeps confusing Chinese and Japanese people, plots Takiyama's ruin: a fake truce, a public humiliation at the school featuring wartime atrocity photos, and finally a fake apology atop a tower between the two restaurants — where he plans to murder Takiyama and stage it as a shame-suicide. But Butters, investigating Janus's house at the urging of one of the doctor's personas, discovers the impossible truth: Lu Kim is himself one of Dr. Janus's personalities — a white therapist who has been living as a Chinese restaurateur. Butters calls the police, who arrive as Lu Kim visibly shifts personas mid-murder-attempt. Shamed at having been fooled into believing a white man was Asian, Takiyama throws himself off the tower, landing on and destroying City Sushi. The police decide to keep Lu Kim around — he's the only Chinese restaurant in town — and the final shot shows Janus's face ghosted over Lu Kim's: the personalities are still in there.

Featured characters: Butters Stotch, the misdiagnosed; Dr. Janus/Tuong Lu Kim; Junichi Takiyama; and the South Park police.

Locations: City Sushi, City Wok, the tower between them, Dr. Janus's house, and the school assembly.

Key events & continuity: the show's longest-running background gag — Lu Kim's "Chinese" identity — is revealed as the delusion of a mentally ill white man, retroactively reframing years of appearances; Takiyama's suicide-by-shame is the episode's bleakest beat; and the town's decision to keep Lu Kim is pure pragmatism over justice.

At Stan's tenth birthday party, his gift — the latest CD from "tween wave" band Gersploosh — is confiscated by Sharon, and when Stan secretly listens that night, the music sounds like literal feces to him. Worse, everything starts sounding and looking like feces: ice cream, movie trailers, his friends. Dr. Caroll diagnoses the condition precisely: Stan is being a "cynical asshole." Kyle, Kenny, and Cartman stop hanging out with him — he's a buzzkill — and after a fight at the movies, Kyle's face morphs into a talking pile of shit mid-lecture. Stan walks away from his best friend without a word. Meanwhile Randy, desperate to stay young, reinvents himself as "Steamy Ray Vaughn," performing tween-wave music at the bowling alley in soiled pants, while two elderly farmers watch in horror at what he's doing to his "britches." When Sharon drags him home, the Marshes finally say it aloud: they're both unhappy, they've grown apart, and it's over. Over Fleetwood Mac's "Landslide," a dialogue-free montage plays: Kyle passes a despondent Stan without speaking; Sharon and the kids pack; a for-sale sign goes up; Randy drives off in a U-Haul; the family unpacks in a new apartment; the farmers weep over Randy's stolen britches. Stan lies alone on his new bed as the credits roll in silence.

Featured characters: Stan Marsh, turning ten and turning cynical; Kyle Broflovski, the lost best friend; Randy and Sharon Marsh; Shelly; and Steamy Nicks.

Locations: the birthday party, Dr. Caroll's office, the movies, the bowling alley, and the two Marsh households.

Key events & continuity: Stan's tenth birthday marks a hard tonal break — the show's most dramatic status-quo shift, with the Marsh parents separated and Stan's friendship with Kyle seemingly ended; Randy and Sharon's split is mutual and quiet rather than explosive; and the silent credits have never been used before or since.

In the aftermath of his parents' split, Stan explodes in class and is misdiagnosed with Asperger's syndrome — blamed on a flu shot from the previous year. He's taken to an "Asperger's Research Center" that's actually a front for the Secret Society of Cynics: whiskey-drinking conspiracy theorists, led by a Morpheus parody, who believe the world has literally turned to shit and some hidden enemy — aliens, future robots, mutants — is stopping everyone else from seeing it. They ply Stan with Jameson as a "serum" and send him to spy on a summit of fast-food executives, who are losing business to a shocking new competitor: Cartman Burgers. Cartman, having misheard "Asperger's" as "Ass Burgers," tried faking the condition by stuffing hamburgers down his underwear — and accidentally discovered that his flatulence-infused burgers are delicious. His food stand is a phenomenon, and the fast-food cabal theorizes he's converting their ingredients into gas. When Stan is captured interrogating the secret recipe, Kyle — who broke with Cartman upon learning the truth — refuses to reveal it, and a three-way shootout erupts between the corporates, the Cynics, and Cartman's stand. Amid the chaos Stan has his epiphany: he may have lost his old life, but he's excited by change rather than scared of it — this could be the start of new adventures. Then Randy pulls up in a van: he and Sharon have reconciled. Sharon explains that sometimes people stick with what they know, even unhappy — directly contradicting Stan's revelation. The Marshes move back in; Kyle cuts ties with Cartman publicly; and Stan, resigned, joins the guys for a movie — not before a fortifying swig of whiskey.

Featured characters: Stan Marsh, the reluctant prophet; Cartman, the burger king; Kyle Broflovski; Randy and Sharon Marsh; and the Secret Society of Cynics.

Locations: the Asperger's center, Cartman's burger stand, the fast-food summit, and the Marsh home.

Key events & continuity: the Marsh reconciliation is framed as a defeat for Stan's growth — "sticking with what you know" beats his embrace of change; Kyle publicly severs his friendship with Cartman over the burger secret; and Stan's closing whiskey swig suggests the cynicism isn't cured, just managed.

entries.n: S15E09 — The Last of the Meheecans
entries.t:
At a sleepover, the boys play "Texans vs. Mexicans" — the "Mexicans" (led by Kyle after Butters proves a poor leader) try to cross Cartman's backyard "border" past his "border patrol." Everyone makes it except Butters, who gets lost in a snowstorm and is hit by a car. Introducing himself as "Mantequilla" and babbling about his "amigos at the border," he's mistaken for a Mexican immigrant by the kindly couple who hit him. They take him in, work him like a servant, then abandon him at an El Pollo Loco "to be with his own kind." There, Butters regales the staff with tales of his imaginary exploits — and when he gives his name as "Mantequilla," they recognize it from the boys' missing-person flyers and treat him as a folk hero. His stories accidentally inspire a mass exodus: Mexican workers, questioning their American dream, begin streaming back to Mexico, and the U.S. economy craters without them. The Border Patrol, now tasked with keeping Mexicans in, starts recruiting volunteers — and Cartman enlists with gusto, proving a natural. In Mexico, "Mantequilla" is a national hero credited with restoring Mexican pride. But Butters gets homesick and tries to cross back north; the agents, thrilled that a Mexican wants in, wave him through — until Cartman recognizes him and tries to stop him personally. With the Border Patrol's help, Butters eludes Cartman, re-enters the U.S., and wins the game. Cartman is despondent; the gang is glad to have Butters back, even as the voices of Mexico chant his name.

Featured characters: Butters/"Mantequilla"; Cartman, the volunteer agent; Kyle, the deposed-then-restored team leader; and the El Pollo Loco staff.

Locations: Cartman's backyard border, the snowy road, the couple's house, El Pollo Loco, and the real border.

Key events & continuity: Butters accidentally becomes a messianic figure to two nations without understanding a word of what's happening; the Border Patrol's mission inversion — keeping people in — drives the satire; and Butters' game-winning return is his purest underdog triumph.

Cartman discovers "Eavesdropper," a gossip site publishing South Park Elementary's most humiliating secrets — starting with Pete Melman crapping his pants in class. When Mr. Mackey reveals that a similar incident drove a student, Corey Duran, to suicide a year ago after Cartman spread it, the teachers order Cartman to make sure Pete doesn't follow. Cartman's solution is characteristically insane: lace the school's Pizza Hut order with laxatives and horsey sauce so every kid craps themselves at once and nobody can be mocked. Meanwhile Stan learns Eavesdropper has published his private message to Kenny praising a girl's butt crack, and Wendy is mortified. The boys trace the site's IP to the music room — where they find a gerbil typing the articles. The username: "Wikileaks." A spectral "Frog King" appears and explains: Wikileaks is the evil brother of Lemmiwinks the gerbil, and only Lemmiwinks can stop him. The boys spring Lemmiwinks from his cage (belonging to Vernon Trumski) and race back to school — while the teachers, panicking about Eavesdropper's upcoming exposé of their own laxative plot, fake Cartman's suicide, complete with a forged note, and literally throw him under a bus. Back at school, Lemmiwinks and Wikileaks face off in a dance-like duel, and Lemmiwinks emerges victorious, killing his brother. Mr. Mackey deletes the incriminating article. Cartman, run over but alive, demands his promised payment: watching Selena Gomez get beaten up in person.

Featured characters: Cartman, the crisis manager; Stan, Kyle, and the gang; Wikileaks and Lemmiwinks, the warring gerbils; the Frog King and Catatafish, the spirit guides; and Principal Victoria, Mr. Mackey, and Mr. Adler.

Locations: the school, the music room, Vernon's bedroom, the bus, and the faculty restroom.

Key events & continuity: Lemmiwinks returns years after his first adventure, now a mythic hero with a villainous brother; the teachers' conspiracy — drugging students and faking a child's suicide — is covered up without consequence; and Cartman's payment demand is left as a dangling, ominous punchline.

Randy's coworkers let him in on Broadway's open secret: the shows get wives so aroused they spontaneously perform oral sex on their husbands afterward. Randy drags a skeptical Sharon to Wicked, hears nothing but subtext-free singing — until a man at the bar tips him off to listen for the "subtext," at which point every lyric sounds like it's about blowjobs. Sharon proves the theory correct on the drive home. Randy becomes Broadway's biggest fan, seeing Wicked 23 times and writing South Park's own musical — except subtext is lost on him, so he titles it "Splooge-Drenched Blowjob Queen" with lyrics that say the quiet part loud. This draws the wrath of the Broadway establishment — Sondheim, Schwartz, Andrew Lloyd Webber, and Elton John — who warn him that explicitness would expose the entire racket. Randy challenges Sondheim to a "bro-down" in the parking lot; the two earn each other's respect, "bro out" over drinks at Hooters, and the masters help him rework the show into The Woman in White. But when Randy learns Sharon gave Shelley tickets to see Wicked with Larry Feegan — the vegan family's son, who's fallen for Shelley and ditched his life-preserver lifestyle — Randy snaps. He races to Denver, dons a stolen Spider-Man costume, and swings through the theater, wrecking the stage and flooding the building by smashing a water pipe. Larry, who had discarded his life preserver, drowns. Shelley weeps, never knowing her father was the costumed menace. Randy apologizes to Sharon for the manipulation; she admits she enjoyed the shows too, and they agree musicals brought them closer. They wonder what's coming to town next — as an ad for The Book of Mormon plays.

Featured characters: Randy and Sharon Marsh; Shelley and Larry Feegan; the Broadway legends; and Spider-Man (Randy).

Locations: the Wicked theater, the Feegan dinner table, the Hooters bro-out, and the flooded Denver theater.

Key events & continuity: Broadway's "subtext" is confirmed as an in-universe real phenomenon, not just a joke; Larry Feegan's death — by drowning, life preserver discarded for love — is the episode's shocking collateral damage; and the Randy/Sharon marriage gets its most honest moment in ages.

South Park Elementary posts the country's worst Presidential Fitness Test scores, entirely because Cartman's results torpedo the average. Recess becomes PE for four weeks, and the school turns on him. Cartman reframes it as the ninety-nine percent ganging up on the one percent, then takes Craig's taunt literally and goes home to cry to his five stuffed animals — Clyde Frog, Peter Panda, Muscleman Marc, Rumpertumskin, Polly Prissypants — voicing them all as they "blame" President Obama. Inspired, Butters and Jimmy found a real ninety-nine-percent club and protest outside the Colorado fitness council office; police throw a two-square-mile perimeter around two kids while news crews wrongly report they are occupying the Red Robin. Meanwhile Cartman's toys turn up destroyed: Clyde Frog nailed to a tree under the word VENGEANCE gets a full funeral; Peter Panda dies in a bedroom fire. Cartman flees to Tolkien's house with the survivors, reasoning nobody dares criticize Black people. The fifth graders, vowing to make Cartman suffer, stage a rival "eighty-three percent" protest; the demonstrations brawl in what media calls class warfare. At Tolkien's, Kyle, Stan, and Kenny arrive to "help" just as Cartman finds Muscleman Marc and Rumpertumskin wrecked, with Polly Prissypants in an armchair holding a revolver. The fantasy drops: Cartman is voicing her himself as she confesses to every toy "murder" — his friends were right that he needed to grow up, and the deaths at Tolkien's would frame him. When Cartman notes Black people cannot be blamed for anything anymore, her scheme collapses and she talks a weeping Cartman into shooting her. Everyone — Stan, Kyle, Kenny, both mothers, Tolkien's parents — watches the deranged puppet show in horror. Kyle's verdict: they told him to grow up, so he got rid of his stuffed animals. The protests splinter into ever-tinier percentages until reporters chase a crowd "occupying" a Macaroni Grill.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman; his stuffed animals Clyde Frog, Peter Panda, Muscleman Marc, Rumpertumskin, and Polly Prissypants; Butters Stotch; Jimmy Valmer; Craig Tucker; Stan Marsh; Kyle Broflovski; Kenny McCormick; Tolkien Black; Liane Cartman; the fifth-grade ringleaders.

Locations: South Park Elementary and its cafeteria; Cartman's bedroom; Tolkien Black's house; the Colorado Division of the President's Council on Fitness, Sports and Nutrition; the Red Robin; the Macaroni Grill.

Key events & continuity: Cartman effectively "grows up" by destroying — and finally shooting — his own toys, ending their long run as his confidants; the Occupy-style protest framing that starts as a joke in the cafeteria snowballs into competing percentage movements and restaurant "occupations"; Craig's taunt about Cartman crying to his stuffed animals is what sends him down the whole spiral.""

Guest lecturer David "Running Horse" Sawitzky tells the fourth grade that cheerful Thanksgiving stories are written to make the Pilgrims look good, and the boys are assigned a report on the holiday. They cite the laziest source available: a History Channel program claiming the 1621 Thanksgiving was shaped by aliens. Kyle is outvoted three to one. After they turn the reports in, History Channel agents demand their source — and the channel's president treats the boys' homework as vindication, airing their testimonials in a special that credits Stan as a "History Expert" and Kyle as a "Professor of Thanksgiving," even as the footage shows Kyle arguing against it all. An enraged Sawitzky holds Kyle, Stan, and Kenny at gunpoint at Kyle's house over the broadcast. Meanwhile, Captain Miles Standish of Plymouth — a planet in Canis Major populated by people who look exactly like colonial Pilgrims — crashes to Earth. His people's stuffing mines have been raided by their enemies the Indians, and the resulting stuffing shortage sends Cartman into a panic. Standish reaches Kyle's house, kills Sawitzky, and asks for help getting home. With Natalie Portman driving them to a clearing, he unfurls a map of five worlds — Earth, Plymouth, Indi, Colthenheim, Green Lantern World — linked by wormholes shaped like hand-traced turkey drawings. The three-hundred-year treaty between Plymouth and Indi has expired, and Standish warns the Indians will plunder the mines. Kyle reels at the suggestion that the Native Americans' prior claim to the land might be false; Standish tells him not to believe those stories. The agents admit they failed to open the Plymouth wormhole by drawing the turkey symbol at Plymouth Rock — they need Portman, the Keeper of the Portal. After Kyle wines and dines her, she "opens her wormhole," Standish returns home and defeats the Indians, and another History special retells the campaign while adding that the first Thanksgiving was haunted. Kyle is outraged.

Featured characters: Stan Marsh; Kyle Broflovski; Eric Cartman; Kenny McCormick; David "Running Horse" Sawitzky; Captain Miles Standish; Natalie Portman, Keeper of the Portal; the History Channel president and agents.

Locations: South Park Elementary; Kyle's house; the planet Plymouth; Plymouth Rock; the wooded clearing with the wormhole.

Key events & continuity: The History Channel's alien-pseudoscience programming becomes an in-universe force that treats schoolchildren's homework as scholarly validation; Kyle's on-air dissent gets him labeled a "Professor of Thanksgiving" against his will; the wormhole map's turkey-hand-tracing gag ties the cosmic plot back to grade-school crafts.

Kenny McCormick's parents are arrested, and with no one to take him in, Kenny is placed into the foster care system. The one who takes the news hardest is not Kenny's circle of friends but Eric Cartman, who bursts into tears for an entirely self-centered reason: with Kenny gone, Cartman is once again the poorest kid in school. Rather than sit with that, he performs his grief loudly, even turning a "yo mama so poor" joke on his own mother while sobbing about his restored status at the bottom of the school's economic ladder.

Featured characters: Kenny McCormick; Eric Cartman; Stuart and Carol McCormick, whose arrest sets the story in motion.

Locations: South Park Elementary; the McCormick household in the background of the arrest.

Key events & continuity: The McCormicks' arrest puts Kenny in foster care, a rare shake-up of his home life; Cartman's long-running rivalry over who holds the title of poorest kid in school flares up again, with Cartman treating Kenny's misfortune purely as a threat to his own ranking. (The source material for this entry is brief, so this telling stays close to what is established.)

A football game ends when Clyde's mother Betsy storms upstairs shrieking about the toilet seat he left up.
