Cartman declares parents should not rule "toilet time" and spreads an exaggerated version at school; Betsy appears demanding Clyde come home and put the seat down. That afternoon she gets stuck in the toilet; a fireman tells Roger that disconnecting the plumbing would rip out her organs and kill her. Absolving Clyde, Betsy asks only that he put the seat down for his sister's sake — then has the plumbing shut off, killing her. At the funeral, Stephen Stotch hopes her death teaches women to "take the extra second," Linda counters that men should do it, and a mourner declares the blood is on Clyde's penis. Panic spreads: the Toilet Safety Administration belts the Cartmans' toilet, Randy is ticketed for unbelted defecation, IHOP bathrooms clog behind TSA-style security, and a TSA voyeur is caught masturbating to hidden bathroom cameras nationwide. Stan, Kyle, Jimmy, and Clyde hire a lawyer to sue the toilet's inventor, Sir John Harington, via a "sue-ance" — a seance for suing the dead — where the spirit Jimmy Bonds shakes them down for cash across two sessions. Cartman, caught on camera with a baby and a gun, takes a TSA agent hostage and spray-paints the lens; the news cries terrorism, and the public demands a mass sue-ance. The lights die and Betsy's ghost appears: the dead cannot be sued, the lawyer scammed the town, and the death was Clyde's fault — he never put the seat down. Then Harington's ghost interjects that everyone uses his invention wrong: sit facing inward, cistern as a shelf, pants fully off — hence the laundry hole. Cartman spins the ghost story to Kyle by phone, until it emerges he has been talking to Clyde himself, who denounces the exaggerations, finishes on the toilet, and flips the seat up while flipping off his mother.

Featured characters: Clyde Donovan; Betsy Donovan, who dies; Roger Donovan; Eric Cartman; Stan Marsh; Kyle Broflovski; Jimmy Valmer; Randy Marsh; Gerald Broflovski; Stephen and Linda Stotch; the ambulance-chasing lawyer; the spirit Jimmy Bonds; the ghost of Sir John Harington.

Locations: The Donovan bathroom; South Park Elementary; Betsy Donovan's funeral; the Cartman residence; the lawyer's office; IHOP; the TSA-monitored bathrooms.

Key events & continuity: Betsy Donovan's death removes Clyde's mother from the picture, leaving him with his father Roger and his sister — and in the final beat Clyde pointedly leaves the seat up, suggesting the lesson did not stick. The "sue-ance" exposes the lawyer as a con artist preying on grief, and Harington's ghost rewrites the proper way to use a toilet for the whole town.

Visiting Grandpa Marvin at his retirement home, Stan gets a gift: a gold, turquoise, diamond bolo tie Marvin claims cost six thousand dollars. Randy rages at the spending; Marvin is so happy picturing Stan wearing it for picture day that Stan agrees. Cartman mocks it; Kyle suggests Cash For Gold. Offers: fifteen dollars, then eight — nine after Stan invokes King Henry the Fifth — then a Taco Bell/Cash For Gold offers a six-layer burrito, then seven, though it sells no six-layer burritos. Stunned, the boys watch the J&G Shopping Network, where Dean sells wildly overpriced earrings to elderly callers; Cartman diagrams the scam — and then they hear Marvin himself ordering Stan a topaz copper ring. At the home, Marvin admits he can no longer picture his beloved dog's face, and Stan vows to kill the scam. Cartman launches his own Old People's Shopping Network, buying kids' cheap jewelry for pennies — three dollars for Leroy Jenkins' ring — and reselling to seniors. Stan phones Dean and coldly tells him to kill himself; Dean threatens to sue, haggles the suit's price down, Stan persists. Stan, Kyle, and Kenny climb the supply chain — refinery, sign-flippers, melters — everyone blaming the next link until it lands on manufacturers in India. Cartman flies there with Butters to buy direct, finding the other three already berating a child employee. The loop is laid bare: sold, melted, remade, resold, forever. A worker gives Stan a jewel-encrusted gold picture frame; Stan fills it with a photo of Marvin's dog Patches and presents it in the park. Marvin is overjoyed — and, forgetting he bought the tie, calls it "fucking gay as fuck" himself, so Stan retires it. Then three elderly callers in a row tell Dean that Stan was right. A gunshot rings out; blood spatters the carousel.

Featured characters: Stan Marsh; Marvin Marsh; Randy, Sharon, and Shelly Marsh; Eric Cartman; Kyle Broflovski; Kenny McCormick; Butters Stotch; Dean of the J&G Shopping Network; Leroy Jenkins; Patches the dog.

Locations: The retirement home; the bus stop; the Cash For Gold shops and the Taco Bell; the J&G Shopping Network studio; the gold refinery; India Manufacturing Inc.; the park.

Key events & continuity: Marvin's dog Patches is established as the thing he loves most and can no longer picture, and Stan's framed photo becomes the emotional payoff; Marvin's memory is already slipping badly enough that he forgets buying the tie; Cartman's shopping network mirrors the exact scam Stan is fighting, and Dean's on-air suicide closes the loop on Stan's campaign.

The boys treat a Colorado Republican debate as a covert op, and despite a Secret Service lockdown over warnings that someone might "faith hill" the event, Cartman pulls it off. News anchors fret about the first meme death; Professor Lamont lectures the fourth grade on the dangers of memeing with a video on tebowing that leaves Butters too traumatized to participate. Then Craig brings the front page: faith hilling is already outdated, replaced by "Taylor Swifting." The boys film Cartman faith hilling at Café Monet, collide with a rival crew already Taylor Swifting there, and the meme turf war lands the other kids in the hospital. Lamont escalates with a loaded revolver on Butters' desk, forcing the barrel into Butters' mouth to prove memeing is unsafe — until agents drag him out: cats have started "cat breading." Lamont is unfazed; humans have memed since the Egyptians, and memeing cats are evolving toward human intelligence. The boys confront Mr. Kitty, then target the Alcoholics Anonymous building, though Kenny notes faith hilling is pointless now that it is out of style. A new meme, "Oh Long Johnsoning," reportedly kills two people; its cat originator is arrested and interrogated, answering only "Oh Long Johnson" while Lamont threatens war on cats. Stan is caught doing a Taylor Swifting/Oh Long Johnsoning hybrid; Kyle lunges, Kenny defends Stan, Cartman restrains Kyle. Cartman and Kyle faith hill outside Planned Parenthood, endure a hail of insults, and admit the meme is dead. The rival crews unite to watch Cartman perform a Taylor Swifting/Cat Breading/Reporting combo — and at another debate, about to conform, he stops, realizes going along is wrong, and faith hills while singing that it is the only meme he will ever do. Candidates and crowd join in, spellbound. A reporter names the phenomenon "Pandering" — seconds before a train hits him.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman; Stan Marsh; Kyle Broflovski; Kenny McCormick; Butters Stotch; Craig Tucker; Professor Lamont; Mr. Kitty and the memeing cats.

Locations: The Colorado Republican debate; South Park Elementary; Café Monet; the Alcoholics Anonymous building; the Planned Parenthood clinic.

Key events & continuity: The meme life cycle — birth, backlash, obsolescence — plays out at warp speed, with cats evolving through memeing treated as a genuine scientific crisis; Cartman's refusal to abandon faith hilling becomes a statement of individuality that accidentally starts the next big thing.

With Passover falling the same week as Easter, Cartman warns the kids about the "Jewpacabra," a monster that hunts children during Passover — first ambushing Kyle mid-conversation about the holiday. As kids sign up for the Sooper Foods Easter Egg Hunt, Cartman spreads the word; Kyle says only liars or idiots would believe it. A terrified Butters lets Cartman lead him into the forest to lure the beast with anti-Jesus "mating calls." Cartman pressures Sooper Foods to cancel the hunt, backing it with video evidence; president Mr. Billings gives him full capture resources, which Cartman burns on a water-park trip before cryptozoologists solemnly validate the footage — terrifying Cartman himself. Hiding in the church with Butters, Craig, and Tolkien guarding the door, Cartman hears something forcing its way in; his guards flee, and the intruders prove to be Billings and his men, who stuff Cartman into a bunny suit and dump him in the park as a sacrifice to appease the Jewpacabra. Billings informs Kyle; Kyle offers to free Cartman if he admits the creature is fake — but a frightened Cartman insists he truly believes, so Kyle leaves him tied up. The cryptozoologists, watching through binoculars that look like red slanted eyes, mistake bunny-suited Cartman for a "Bunny-man," tranquilize him, and plan an Animal Planet special. That night Cartman dreams himself into Ancient Egypt during the plagues, Kyle beside him; the Pharaoh is Cartman's own father. Cartman fails to talk him into freeing the Jews, watches the slaughter of lambs and children, and vows to become Jewish himself — at which his head explodes. A guilty Kyle frees the real Cartman and carries him home to bed. At the egg hunt, a converted Cartman preaches Judaism to all, wins zero converts, then tells Kyle he finally knows what it feels like to be mocked for his faith. Seeing Cartman has genuinely learned something, Kyle answers with quiet forgiveness as the scene rises toward a sun bearing the Star of David.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman; Kyle Broflovski; Butters Stotch; Craig Tucker; Tolkien Black; Mr. Billings and the Sooper Foods employees; the cryptozoologists; the Pharaoh, who is Cartman's father in the dream.

Locations: The Broflovski home; the forest; Sooper Foods; the South Park Church; the park; Ancient Egypt in Cartman's dream.

Key events & continuity: Cartman's Passover prank collapses into genuine terror and an accidental lesson in empathy, ending with one of his rare sincere moments with Kyle; the cryptozoologists' eagerness to validate the hoax mirrors the town's appetite for sensational claims.

Butters arrives at lunch with a black eye, no lunch, and excuses nobody buys; only Stan presses him, learning a bully took his lunch money, and Kyle's advice to talk to his grandmother proves catastrophic — alone with Butters, she drops her sweet act to slap him, slur him, and call him her "bitch." Anti-bullying spokesman Bucky Bailey bullies the indifferent Mr. Mackey to tears, triggering a mandatory assembly where Stan volunteers to direct an anti-bullying video; Butters begs off, Stan shames him, and Kyle warns the video is really about Stan and that he'll end up "naked and jacking it in San Diego." The grandmother corners Butters in the restroom over a urinal puck and threatens him for "narcing"; Butters later dons a costume to confront her and finds her waiting in one of her own, and she assaults him when he tries to flee. Hollywood's Nick Jabs buys the video, then serves Bucky a cease-and-desist when Bucky claims it; on the Dr. Oz Show, Oz badgers a silent Butters until Butters beats him up, so America brands Butters a violent psychopath, Jabs kills the video, and Jesus menaces Jabs in his bathroom over Hell. That night Butters tells his grandmother's bedside that standing up felt good but left him dark and empty like her, and that one day he'll be a happy adult visiting her deathbed while she dies miserable; next day the school boos Stan, Dr. Oz sues him and the school, and Stan's only recourse is stripping and masturbating on a San Diego street corner.

Featured characters: Butters Stotch and his grandmother; Stan Marsh; Kyle Broflovski; Bucky Bailey; Mr. Mackey; Dr. Oz; Nick Jabs; Jesus.

Locations: South Park Elementary; Butters' home; the Dr. Oz Show studio; San Diego.

Key events & continuity: Butters' grandmother is exposed as his true abuser, and his bedside speech is one of his quietest, most devastating moments; Kyle's throwaway San Diego warning becomes literal; Jesus cameos to menace a Hollywood executive in a bathroom.

entries.n: S16E06 — I Should Have Never Gone Ziplining
entries.t:
On the last day of spring break, the boys settle their what-to-do argument by agreeing on ziplining. Stan's uncle drops them off; after a safety video and a shuttle ride, the ziplining proves crushingly boring — with sixteen more stops to go. They spell HELP in twigs while Cartman, loaded with fast food and Mountain Dew graduating to "Double Dew," farts endlessly and develops full diarrhea. A free lunch of wet sandwiches helps nothing. Their escape excuse: Kenny is bleeding severely from his cold sore — herpes. The staff cannot help from the line but point them to a nearby horse ranch, which turns out to be another slow tour. Stan spots a boat dock; the boat is capped at five miles per hour. Kyle and Cartman resume their feud over whose idea this was; Cartman's diarrhea attracts an attacking beaver swarm; Kenny is revealed to have died of boredom. Finally Stan confesses: it was his idea — three sign-ups earned him a free iPod Nano. Briefly furious, and now sharing Kenny's herpes via the Dew, the boys dissolve into tears. Rescue arrives via Mr. Hankey's "Magical Helicrapter," his "7-turdy-7," and the "Poo-Choo Express." The narrator's coda: Kenny's corpse was left with his family, Cartman and Stan were treated for herpes, and Kyle spent twenty-seven days hospitalized having fecal matter removed from his nose. Recovered, Stan raises ziplining awareness through viral videos — which leads, inevitably, to him masturbating in San Diego. Two weeks later Cartman is back on Diet Double Dew, confident diet soda cannot cause diarrhea.

Featured characters: Stan Marsh; Kyle Broflovski; Eric Cartman; Kenny McCormick, who dies of boredom; Mr. Hankey; the unseen narrator.

Locations: The ziplining course and its shuttle; the horse ranch; the five-mile-per-hour boat; the hospital.

Key events & continuity: Kenny's death-by-boredom is one of his most absurd demises, and his body is simply left with his family; the San Diego gag from "Butterballs" repeats as the coda to Stan's awareness campaign; Mr. Hankey returns as a literal deus ex machina with an entire fleet of fecal transport.
k: i should have never gone ziplining

entries.t:
Butters announces new girl Nichole joined the cheer squad; the boys crowd the gym, and Cartman — noting she is African American — congratulates Tolkien Black, who storms off. Cartman decides Tolkien is shy and plays matchmaker: seated between them in class, pestering Tolkien, telling Bebe and Red that Nichole should make the first move. At Bebe's, the girls play "Living" and Nichole confesses she likes Kyle — which window-spying Cartman takes personally, telling Nichole he and Kyle are a closeted couple; Nichole offers Kyle sympathy, and Kyle concludes she is into him. Cartman escalates: Butters lures Nichole to the boys' locker room with towels, Cartman clears it shouting about the Batmobile, and chain-locks the doors on a still-showering Tolkien. Nichole walks in on towel-wrapped Tolkien; after the panic they find Cartman stocked the room with a deli platter, massage oil, board games, and grape soda. Firemen cut the chain next day; a grateful Nichole suggests lunch, and a tearful Cartman celebrates with Cupid Me, his imaginary cherubic self. When Nichole's father warns against only dating Black people, she calls it coincidence — until she reads the teddy bear's tag: "To my boo" / "'Cuz blacks belong together." She dumps Tolkien the next day; Cartman sobs as Butters comforts him, then beats the invisible Cupid Me with a bat. A laxative commercial inspires Cartman's comeback: he springs Cupid Me from a box, but Nichole is at a basketball game with a "nice white Jewish boy." Cartman hijacks the Megatron screen, declares his "love" for Kyle, duets with Brad Paisley, then shouts the Batmobile is outside; the stampeding arena reunites Tolkien and Nichole, stereotype-blind. Cupid Me celebrates — and reveals he found Cartman someone too: the Halitosis Kidz girl. Horror.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman; Cupid Me; Tolkien Black; Nichole Daniels and her parents; Kyle Broflovski; Butters Stotch; Brad Paisley.

Locations: South Park Elementary and its gym; Bebe's house; the boys' locker room; the basketball arena.

Key events & continuity: Cupid Me, Cartman's imaginary cupid, becomes a recurring fixture; the Cartman-Kyle "couple" lie spreads through the school's assumptions about Kyle; Tolkien and Nichole's romance survives Cartman's sabotage.

Stan mentions that school football has banned kickoffs as too dangerous, and Randy's sarcastic counter-proposal — bras, tin-foil hats, a balloon for a ball, hugging instead of tackling, "sarcastaball" — is taken literally by Mr. Mackey. Randy becomes head coach, then coach of the Denver Broncos, with Butters taking over the school team. Butters has a wet dream and saves the resulting "creamy goo" — semen, though his father has never explained what it is. Asked for coaching help, Butters shares some goo; Cartman drinks it and swears he feels better. Sharon fears Randy's relentless sarcasm means brain damage; the doctor's verdict is permanent: Randy will always be sarcastic. Doctor and patient, both dripping sarcasm, scheme to divert cancer and genetic-disease research money into sarcasm-awareness commercials. Jim Rome soon endorses Butters' Creamy Goo as a sarcastaball supplement, and the whole town is drinking it — until Randy, handed a cup by Stan, tastes it, realizes what it is, and announces to players and crowd that they have all been drinking semen. Butters' parents ground him for two months and a week despite his total innocence; his father will explain "cum" when he is older. That night Butters wakes with an erection and yells for his father, who calls it his "friendly compass," pointing up because Jesus is his friend. Butters thanks him sincerely.

Featured characters: Randy Marsh; Butters Stotch; Eric Cartman; Stan Marsh; Sharon Marsh; Butters' parents; the doctor; Jim Rome.

Locations: The Marsh home; South Park Elementary; the doctor's office; the Denver Broncos.

Key events & continuity: Randy's sarcasm is diagnosed as incurable, locking in a lasting character trait; Butters' sexual innocence — the "creamy goo," the "friendly compass" — remains total, with his father still refusing to explain anything; sarcastaball itself vanishes as quickly as it arrived once the goo's true nature is exposed.

At Wall-Mart, Kyle calls out Cartman's weight; Cartman reflects, admits he is fat — then gains a few more pounds so insurance covers a Rascal mobility scooter. He preaches about the "shame" of being ostracized while milking every handicapped perk, joining scooter users suing property owners over bathroom access; taxpayers retaliate with "Rascal tipping," and the Department of Health spends twenty-five million dollars on self-righting "tip assist" arms. Watching Here Comes Honey Boo Boo, Kyle is stunned that nobody feels shame about anything anymore. Meanwhile James Cameron dives in the USS James Cameron on a literal quest to find "the bar" and raise it, ignoring his crew's pleas that it is a metaphor. Tolkien has Kyle secretly film Cartman's life for a documentary — but edits it into a trashy reality show, "Here Comes Fatty Doo Doo," with a jaunty Randy Newman theme. Tolkien's defense: if a major network can air Honey Boo Boo guilt-free, so can he, and society sets the bar, not individuals. Kyle wavers until Stan reports Honey Boo Boo's heart failure and pig-heart transplant — with her mother utterly unashamed. At fifty thousand feet, Cameron finds Randy Newman already there in a diving suit; Newman, who does not want the bar raised lest nobody hire him, attacks the submersible. Cartman's lawyer fires a cease-and-desist at Tolkien, learning the show aired last night — and lost to Honey Boo Boo in the ratings. Enraged, Cartman wrestles her in "sketti" at Michelle Obama's White House South Lawn event. As Cameron hooks the literal bar with his grappling arm, the crowd — Michelle included — suddenly feels real distaste; Obama halts the spectacle, vows her husband's administration will fight childhood obesity literally, beats up Cartman, and destroys his scooter. Cameron surfaces, declares himself done, and moves on to Avatar 2 — not for his own glory, he insists.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman; Kyle Broflovski; Tolkien Black; James Cameron; Randy Newman; Alana "Honey Boo Boo" Thompson; Michelle Obama; Stan Marsh.

Locations: Wall-Mart; the ocean depths; the USS James Cameron; the White House South Lawn.

Key events & continuity: Cartman's mobility-scooter era ends with Michelle Obama personally destroying the scooter; Tolkien's documentary betrayal shows his willingness to exploit Cartman for ratings; Cameron's literal deep-sea quest satirizes the very idea that one hero can single-handedly restore cultural standards.

Gerald and Sheila role-play in the bedroom — Gerald as a UPS man, per a Cialis commercial — when Ike walks in, fails to recognize his father, and spends the next day in tears. Kyle extracts the story as a stick-figure drawing of a UPS man with Sheila. Kyle confides in the boys; Randy overhears and tells all of South Park's husbands. At Skeeter's, a shady old-timer's tale about a milkman who slept with housewives — "the price to pay for convenience" — ignites paranoia that UPS drivers are sleeping with every wife in town. The men tail the drivers; Randy starts signing for packages himself to keep a driver named Thad from Sharon. Home-security sales boom, but Cartman, disgusted by the useless alarm-response man, tests the system by hiring a real burglar to assault his mother — help arrives far too late. The barroom sage advises them to "kill the milkman"; masked as Bane, they drag the UPS man to a storage facility and beat him bloody. Now there are seven Banes, deepening the fear, and everyone upgrades to "InSecurity," which alarms when fear levels spike. Cartman taunts Kyle about robbing his house until Kyle notes Jewish populations are growing — tripping Cartman's own alarm. The hospitalized driver returns to his route; Stephen blows up his van; and while Kyle pressures Sheila to confess, the terrified driver jumps out a window to his death. Police, summoned by his own InSecurity alarm, find Gerald's UPS uniform in the house; Gerald admits he was just spicing up his sex life, and every alarm in the neighborhood screams at once. Cartman, done with false alarms, confronts the security man in a Bane mask with a gun: he should have respected his "authoritah."

Featured characters: Gerald and Sheila Broflovski; Ike Broflovski; Kyle Broflovski; Randy and Sharon Marsh; Eric Cartman; Stephen Stotch; Thad the UPS man; the shady bar patron; the home-security salesman.

Locations: The Broflovski bedroom; Skeeter's Bar and Cocktails; the Cartman residence; the storage facility; the Broflovskis' neighborhood.

Key events & continuity: The entire panic traces back to Gerald's own role-play costume, a fact that detonates every alarm in town when it surfaces; the UPS man's suicide is one of the darkest punchlines in the town's history of overreaction; Cartman's "respect my authoritah" catchphrase gets a Bane-masked encore.

Butters beats up Scott Malkinson, barricades himself in the school bathroom, screams at Kyle through the door, declares Kenny the only person with dignity, and locks himself back in. Principal Victoria summons the Stotches; Stephen announces an extended leave — a pilgrimage to Butters' birthplace for his Hapa Noa. Butters is a native of "Havaii," Stephen reveals; armed with tradition-book lore and his Mahalo Rewards card, he ships out, with Kenny talked into chaperoning. At the airport, a weeping Butters cannot board — no intoxicated passengers — so Kenny must accompany him. Welcomed at Lihue as a returning native, they tour Kaua'i and meet the Protector and Chief, with Kenny's letter home as narration. At the welcoming ceremony comes the bombshell: the Mahalo Rewards card is being eliminated. The locals prepare to rise against the Haoles and pelt an approaching cruise ship with golf balls; one strikes the captain's eye, he collapses onto the stick, snaps it, and the ship sinks. Obama sends the Coast Guard. Suspicion falls on Kenny; Butters defends him, and Kenny must prove himself Hawaiian via the trial of 'opaekaka — he paddles, falls, drifts down a waterfall, and cracks his head. The locals cheer Butters' speech about tourists ruining everything — until the closed ports mean the chi-chis run out. Kenny crawls into the abandoned Coco Palms, falls through the floor, and meets the ghost of Elvis, who opens a stone wall onto mountains of chi-chi ingredients. The Coast Guard demands surrender; golf balls and bocce balls answer; return fire decimates the locals. The Chief is ready to yield when Butters launches an anti-Ben Affleck tirade — and Kenny arrives with a raft of ingredients. The next letter brings impossible news: the U.S. government has surrendered, Mahalo Rewards is reinstated, the island celebrates. Both earn their Hapa Noa and Mahalo cards; Butters' rage subsides — though he still resents Affleck marrying Jennifer Lopez, until corrected: Jennifer Garner.

Featured characters: Butters Stotch; Kenny McCormick; Stephen and Linda Stotch; the Hawaiian Chief and Protector; the ghost of Elvis Presley.

Locations: South Park Elementary; the airport; Kaua'i and Lihue; the Sheraton Residences; the Coco Palms.

Key events & continuity: Butters' Hawaiian "heritage" gets its fullest expression and his anger finally burns out; Kenny's letters home become the narration device; the Mahalo Rewards card causes the uprising and seals the peace.

entries.n: S16E12 — A Nightmare on Face Time
entries.t:
Randy bursts in with champagne: he bought Blockbuster Video for ten thousand dollars; the family is rich. Stan and Shelly stare at their "MY DAD IS THE OWNER OF BLOCKBUSTER! VIDEO" shirts; Stan notes nobody rents movies anymore. The dilapidated store converts no one; by Friday, Randy and a sullen Shelly work a customer-free counter, and Randy scares off little Filmore Anderson with a DVD pitch. Then the store's age manifests as ghosts: a headbanded woman seeking Turner & Hooch, another telling Emily the war is over. Randy screams at apparitions while Stan and Sharon agree something is wrong with him. Halloween: Butters is a Were-prechaun, Jimmy is Gangnam Style; Cartman and Kenny don Avengers costumes at Kyle's — Thor, Iron Man, the Hulk. Randy drafts the family for a Blockbuster sale, so Kyle improvises: Stan, as Captain America, trick-or-treats via FaceTime, his iPad riding Kyle's iPad on a skateboard. Every house mistakes Cartman for someone else — Bruce Vilanch, Chaz Bono, Harvey Fierstein, Honey Boo Boo — and he blames Stan's costume. At Blockbuster, a deteriorating Randy hallucinates an employee renting RoboCop 2 and the Blade Runner director's cut, urging action against Sharon and Stan for ruining the business; Randy refuses, terrifying Stan. The Avengers stumble onto a Kum & Go robbery, charge in, and the crew shoots the clerk and steals Kyle's iPad — "Stan." The robbers find the Monster Mash invitation on it and dump the iPad in a field to crash the party instead. Randy, now Nicholson-in-The-Shining as Ted plays, confiscates all phones and car keys. A couple takes "Stan" to Hell's Pass Hospital; Officer Peterson goes undercover at the Monster Mash as "Gangnamstein" — Gangnam lower half, iPad head. Randy hijacks Stan's iPad and rampages through town; police fire and kill Peterson through the costume. Stan regains control, the robbers are caught, and Butters must tell Kyle "Stan" is dying — the battery is nearly gone. Kyle tries to save him; Stan says it is okay, tells Kenny to "stay gold," and the screen dies. Meanwhile Shelly solves Blockbuster her way: she burns it down. By morning Sharon reports insurance will cover some losses and asks if Randy wants to "stay frozen" awhile.

Featured characters: Randy, Sharon, Shelly, and Stan Marsh; Kyle Broflovski; Eric Cartman; Kenny McCormick; Butters Stotch; Jimmy Valmer; Officer Peterson.

Locations: The Marsh home; the Blockbuster store; the Monster Mash; the Kum & Go; Hell's Pass Hospital.

Key events & continuity: Randy's Blockbuster investment ends in arson by his own daughter and an insurance payout; Stan's "stay gold" farewell to Kenny echoes through the lore; a dying iPad battery becomes a genuine death scene.

A doping scandal shatters faith in a beloved hero; the Walgreens line to cut off yellow wristbands stretches out the door. Cartman unloads an armful of fad wristbands; Mr. Mackey, who no longer knows what to believe, takes it hardest. Only Stan keeps his "What Would Jesus Do?" bracelet. News breaks: HGH was used by Jesus at the crucifixion — lab footage included — and Pope Benedict XVI says Catholics cannot tolerate a juicing deity. Butters relays a preacher's advice to asterisk "Jesus" in the New Testament; Cartman calls these the Dark Times. Stan will not remove his band; a Charlie Rose interview where he says he simply likes it sparks a brown-wristband craze for individualists. Butters explains Stan was moved by the farmers of Belarus and their "STANd GROUND" video. A Steve Nelson books Stan's Nike commercial about never cutting his wristband — until scientists raid Garrison's class to seize the bracelet: Craig accused Stan of cutting and re-gluing it, and tests confirm he cut it. Kyle confronts him; Stan blames a French scientist. Breaking into the scientist's house, Stan finds Jesus already sneaking inside to dig up dirt. Over the wife's cocoa bread and sausages, both deny everything and agree the real cause is the Belarus farmers — who need bracelets. At the P.F. Pityef Bracelet Factory, the owner explains in Seussian rhyme that Stan wants "Scauses": wrist-worn causes. He manufactures them, then heads to South Park to sell, leaving Stan and Jesus baffled. Butters asks if Stan cut his band to spotlight Belarus; Stan says he may have, and a delighted Butters calls him a "cute, sneaky little butthole." Then, live on air as Jesus pleads the farmers' case, the farmers of Belarus are killed — the orange scauses instantly worthless. The town turns on the factory owner for taking their money. Jesus chugs HGH, hulks out, smashes the factory, and kills the owner in his own machine. Then Jesus addresses South Park: wear causes on T-shirts, not scauses — and launches a Free Pussy Riot protest.

Featured characters: Stan Marsh; Jesus; Eric Cartman; Butters Stotch; Kyle Broflovski; Mr. Mackey; the P.F. Pityef factory owner; the French scientist.

Locations: Walgreens; South Park Elementary; the French scientist's house; the bracelet factory.

Key events & continuity: Jesus returns as an active, HGH-chugging participant in town life; Stan's wristband saga — did he cut it or not — stays deliberately unresolved; the "scause" fad dies with its beneficiaries and Jesus pivots the town to T-shirts.

As the 2012 election ends, Cartman tours the swing states charming elderly poll workers for his own ends. Obama's re-election leaves Ike sobbing; Kyle comforts him with a democracy lesson. Cartman summons Kyle and reveals thousands of stolen ballots that could flip the election — and Kyle's vow to stop him is exactly what Cartman wanted. Obama takes General Tso's call demanding payment for his re-election help; they arrange a secret meeting. Kyle's police search of Cartman's house finds the ballots already moved. Kyle assembles the gang and learns Butters may know something — but the cornered, almond-allergic Butters eats an M&M so he cannot talk. At Red Lobster, Cartman feasts while he and Tso await Obama; Cartman announces he is renegotiating. Obama clears the restaurant: Tso gets the rights to Star Wars for the presidency. At the hospital, Butters' throat is grotesquely swollen; with Kenny translating and Kyle threatening to involve his father, Butters reveals the exchange point: Red Lobster. The boys crash the conspiracy as Morgan Freeman materializes to explain everything. Tso demands the ballots; Cartman withholds them pending a role in the next Star Wars film — then vanishes in smoke. The Duck President gets the FBI briefing. The boys toss Cartman's house until Liane grounds him preemptively; outside, by the Slave 1, they meet a furious Mickey Mouse, who owns Star Wars and wants the ballots. Cartman visits the hospital, feeds Butters another M&M, and names the hiding place: "a place in town people barely even know exists" — Stevenson's Hummer. At Disneyland, Stormtroopers drag a captured Cartman before Mickey, who interrogates, bribes, and — indifferent to Star Wars himself — recruits him. Kyle goes on TV about the missing ballots and, as the millionth "General Tso's Chicken" joker, wins a five-thousand-dollar P.F. Chang's card. Over takeout, Stan and Kyle spot a Stevenson's Hummer commercial and connect the dots. Everyone converges on the dealership — boys, Tso's men, then Cartman riding a tauntaun with the police. The salesman mistakes the mob for a rush; the ballots surface; Freeman explains Tso only wanted Star Wars kept from Disney; Kyle agrees Tso should own it; Stan burns the ballots.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman; Kyle Broflovski; Barack Obama; General Tso; Morgan Freeman; Mickey Mouse; Butters Stotch; Stan Marsh; Liane Cartman.

Locations: The swing states; Cartman's house; Red Lobster; the hospital; Disneyland; Stevenson's Hummer.

Key events & continuity: Morgan Freeman's out-of-nowhere exposition is deployed twice as the signature device; Cartman's heist is about a Star Wars role, not politics; Mickey's claim on Star Wars foreshadows the franchise's corporate fate.

Kyle rants at the bus stop about a speakerphone woman — just as Cartman arrives doing exactly that, loudly discussing his twisted ankle and NSA theories with Lawrence. Kyle calls him a liar; at lunch Cartman films an anti-surveillance video blog; at recess, asked to move along, he warns of an NSA agent at school — which gets Butters thinking. That night Butters "prays" to the government, thanking it and Obama and requesting a puppy. In the computer lab, Cartman plots to infiltrate the NSA and tweet everything; Lawrence pitches "Shitter," an Alec Baldwin-endorsed product posting thoughts straight to the internet — born after Baldwin blamed his thumbs for offensive posts and chopped them off. Cartman adopts it; its only other user is Baldwin. At the DMV, Butters confesses to the government: yelling at a midget, a Jennifer Lawrence photo penis joke. Sentence: sing "Living in America" a thousand times. Butters converts two Jehovah's Witnesses to government worship and DMV confession; they evangelize Craig's house. Posing as Bill Clinton, Cartman talks past the NSA's front desk — Chief Joe waves him in. Agents brief him on vital intel like a pizza guy tweeting about bombing the Lincoln Memorial; they lecture the man on surveillance's necessity. Cartman's real mission: his own file. The NSA's verdict — "fat and unimportant" — devastates him; they refuse to revise it. At the DMV, Barbrady confesses to masturbating to Game of Thrones; the congregation cheers while one clerk fumes at the fun. The panopticon is revealed: they monitor everyone through Santa Claus, wired into a machine. Cartman unmasks and dumps it all online — and next day weeps in his bedroom: nobody cared about "the truth," nobody thinks he is cool. He plans to hide in Russia until Butters preaches DMV confession; Cartman confesses, moving the miserable clerk to hope the DMV could become a place of comfort. The news instead shuts the DMV down for child molestation; confessions move to the post office — shut down likewise — and the anchor declares the news is now in charge, and will be back "in a young boy."

Featured characters: Eric Cartman; Kyle Broflovski; Butters Stotch; Kenny McCormick; Lawrence and Toby; Alec Baldwin; Chief Joe; Santa Claus; Officer Barbrady; the DMV clerks; the Jehovah's Witnesses.

Locations: The bus stop; South Park Elementary; the DMV; NSA headquarters; Cartman's bedroom.

Key events & continuity: The NSA's devastating two-word verdict on Cartman — "fat and unimportant" — becomes the true wound of the story, eclipsing the surveillance exposé; Butters' sincere worship of the government turns the DMV into a confessional movement; Santa Claus is confirmed as a cog in the surveillance state.

Wendy's Syria speech drowns in Cartman's booing, which Garrison ignores before Peter Mullen's report on "Informative Murder Porn" — the spousal-homicide shows all their parents watch, which Peter warns will end with parents killing each other. Stan walks in on his parents watching exactly that mid-lovemaking; they call it a documentary. Then Cartman calls: Aaron Hagen's father has murdered his mother. At the Hagen house, Aaron weeps while his naked, bloody father blames a Black burglar as police drag him off. Kyle convenes the town's children; Butters called the network and was told to spend more time with his parents, which he takes as blame; Kyle's fix: a parental-lock app with a password only a child knows. That night Stan blocks the channel; a baffled Randy cannot answer "How do you tame a horse in Minecraft?," calls the cable company and demands Stan explain; Stan refuses, and Randy insists he would never kill Sharon (too much evidence), has "been thinking about it a lot," and would rather have Jaden Smith as a son. At the Get Cable Company, Stuart declares it useless while a nipple-rubbing employee stonewalls; Stephen knows Corey Lanskin, who will teach parents Minecraft for a hundred ounces of silver. Soon Randy plays all night while Sharon lies exhausted. Jimmy reports the lock is failing; Butters announces he watched his dad kill his mom — in Minecraft. Kyle realizes someone is teaching the parents. At another children's meeting, the kids fume that parents are ruining their Minecraft servers too; Cartman muses the Hagen murder may be unrelated to the shows; Police arrive — for Stephen, who built a castle on the Community Center roof; Randy mocks it with a pickaxe. The boys catch Corey lying by his telltale phrase and find him schooling adults in his basement; he sends them to the cable company. There, the sadistic employee and his supervisor rub each other's nipples while stonewalling — until Stan notes blocking murder porn would bum parents out, and the company spitefully buries the networks in a miserable package tier. After one last family blowup, Randy and Sharon log into Minecraft together and gleefully murder each other's characters on repeat.

Featured characters: Stan, Randy, and Sharon Marsh; Kyle Broflovski; Eric Cartman; Wendy Testaburger; Butters Stotch; Jimmy Valmer; Corey Lanskin; the cable company employees.

Locations: South Park Elementary; the Marsh residence; the Community Center; the Get Cable Company; inside Minecraft.

Key events & continuity: Cartman's reflexive booing of Wendy becomes a running gag; Randy and Sharon's marriage survives by channeling homicidal energy into Minecraft; the cable employees are established as delightedly sadistic bureaucrats.

In class, Cartman dreams he is Gerry, Brad Pitt's World War Z hero, at breakfast when CNN heralds the Trayvon Martin verdict; the radio plays "It's a Beautiful Day," then the bulletin: Zimmerman acquitted. Every Black person on Earth becomes a zombie horde; the family flees to the rooftops, where Tolkien lunges at Gerry. Cartman wakes screaming. Mackey lectures him on the "feud"; a sleepless Cartman tries niceness, and Tolkien hurries away. After another nightmare, Tolkien is summoned so Cartman can read his poem "I Was Not the Bullet": he was not on the jury, stop blaming him. At an assembly, Cartman raps it while Butters beatboxes; Tolkien's furious shout convinces Cartman the apocalypse is here. He grabs a handgun, dresses as Gerry, commandeers Nelly's mom's Tesla to the airport, storms a plane, and orders takeoff; control finds his handmade "survival guide" and panics. Briefing the cabin on their Iceland escape, he finds a Black man in the bathroom, announces "one of them" is aboard; a passenger opens the emergency exit and is sucked out, a flight attendant's shot ricochets and detonates, the plane crashes. Survivors: Cartman, Nelly's mom, a dying pilot who begs Cartman to end the apocalypse. Watching the news, Butters recognizes the "patient zero" sketch: it is Tolkien. At Jimbo's Guns, Cartman learns Florida's "stand your ground" law and realizes he can legally kill the other patient zero: George Zimmerman. He boards another plane, spots another Black passenger — second crash. In Florida, Nelly's mom is hit by a truck. Next morning Zimmerman's routine mirrors Gerry's dream-morning until agents ask him to kill another African American kid "for the country." He spots Cartman in blackface and a hoodie and shoots him; the agents commend it — then realize Cartman is white. Zimmerman is tried, found guilty, sentenced to death, and executed. Channel 4 declares the apocalypse over. Cartman spray-paints a red circle, offers Tolkien a fist bump; Tolkien bumps it, and Cartman shoots him — he was on "his land," standing his ground. Kyle: the ending is the least of it — he is a murderer. In the guidance office, Tolkien in a sling, Mackey forces apologies; Cartman refuses — he was standing his ground. Tolkien explodes: the law only applies when white people need it. 

Featured characters: Eric Cartman; Tolkien Black; Nelly's mom; George Zimmerman; Mr. Mackey; Butters Stotch; Kyle Broflovski.

Locations: The classroom; Cartman's dream-world Florida; the airport and two doomed planes; Jimbo's Guns; the guidance office.

Key events & continuity: Cartman's zombie-apocalypse delusion runs two plane crashes and a blackface encounter; he shoots Tolkien and claims stand-your-ground; Tolkien's sling in the guidance office is the visible aftermath.

entries.n: S17E04 — Goth Kids 3: Dawn of the Posers
entries.t:
The goths recite Poe in Henrietta's room when her parents announce she is going to a camp for emo kids. Michael, Pete, and Firkle learn by text; at Troubled Acres, Henrietta wakes in a white room where a lone ficus rises from the floor and shakes. She returns home emo. The goths report her parents to child protective services for the abuse of calling her emo, and lecture a baffled social worker on the theology: emos are cynical, goths nihilistic; goths think the world is "fucked up," emos think they are "totally fucked up." Michael confronts Henrietta; she warns the emos are rising and converts him — he flees, arranges a Village Inn meetup, and is hauled to Troubled Acres by his parents. Over coffee, Pete's idea: enlist the South Park Vampire Society, the only ones who understand emos. They crash a Vamps meeting, apologize for burning down the Hot Topic, and the Vamps reluctantly agree. After spying on Henrietta's new emo circle, goths and vamps summon Edgar Allan Poe's ghost in the library; he is more goth than all of them, takes no orders, and will help only as "Nightpain." At Troubled Acres, Michael is tied to a chair while an old caretaker, obeying the emo king — a giant ficus — parks a ficus beside him and advises surrender. The rescue team — Pete, Firkle, Mike the Twilight fan, Edgar — walks into Firkle's trap: he has gone emo and levels a gun at them. Bound before ficus plants, Pete contacts Edgar — slipped out to Benny's for coffee — through his coffee's reflection; Edgar returns, shoots the emo king, and reveals the truth: ficus plants from Lowe's in vibrating pots. The old man insists they talk to him — and a TV crew bursts out: he has been on "Yes, I Was Scared" all along, and goths, vamps, and emos are all the same thing. Firkle is shattered: he betrayed his friends for nothing. Pete and Michael tell Henrietta it was an elaborate prank; disbelieving, she gets the lie that they burned the camp down — and snaps back to goth just in time to confront her mother.

Featured characters: Pete, Michael, Firkle, and Henrietta Biggle; the South Park Vampire Society; Edgar Allan Poe's ghost; Mike the Twilight fan; the Troubled Acres caretaker.

Locations: Henrietta's bedroom; Troubled Acres camp; the Village Inn; the school library; Hot Topic.

Key events & continuity: The goth-emo-vampire taxonomy gets its definitive theological statement; Firkle's betrayal for a reality show is the emotional core; Henrietta's return to goth resets the faction status quo.
k: goth kids 3: dawn of the posers

entries.t:
Mackey demos the school's new IntelliLink system — barely functional — and pulls up Ike's discussion-board post: Kyle with a "whooping crane" on his forehead. The crane is a penis. Kyle's mother preaches tolerance: Ike is hitting puberty. Kyle bonds with Ike over Yo Gabba Gabba!, but Ike only wants to "tame Foofa's strange." Mackey prescribes a joint lesson in Canadian puberty: a Canadian health video explains babies come from a man farting on a woman, who queefs in his face. Told this is false, the instructor is crushed — his wife lied. Kyle cannot fathom why it stayed in the cut; Ike storms off. Kyle's attempt to book principal permission for Friday's Yo Gabba Gabba! concert dies in an IntelliLink glitch; Ike challenges him to a fight. Mackey upgrades to Silver. They attend anyway; for the "cool, cool trick" segment, Ike strips and grinds on Foofa onstage. A backstage scolding from Plex ends with Ike convincing Foofa to expand beyond children's audiences — she leaves with him. Mackey bullies the faculty into the Gold upgrade. E! News covers Foofa's drug use, partying, and raunchy VMA set — with Ike as her manager. Home becomes torment: Ike introduces Kyle as his little brother; the cast stages a "Don't Show Your Strange" intervention with Sinéad O'Connor. The instructor phones Kyle, mistaking him for Ike, and mentions Ike's medication supplier. Kyle confronts the Canadian official: a catastrophic mix-up — Ike got hormones instead of his laxative prescription; Tom Brady got the laxatives and soiled himself mid-game. The official grasps his wife's queef at last: proof no computer should run Canadian health care. Mackey unveils the "Centurion" package: physically removing IntelliLink; the technician thanks him and shoots himself. At the VMAs, Ike realizes he should have let puberty happen naturally; Foofa performs raunchily anyway. The instructor reconciles with his wife: the fix is the Gold package. Next morning Ike is his giggly old self; they watch Dora — until Ike muses he "wouldn't mind hitting that hot Puerto Rican strange."

Featured characters: Kyle and Ike Broflovski; Mr. Mackey; Foofa, Plex, and the Yo Gabba Gabba! gang; the Canadian Department of Health instructor and his wife; the Canadian health official; Tom Brady; Sinéad O'Connor.

Locations: South Park Elementary; the Broflovski residence; the Yo Gabba Gabba! concert; the MTV Video Music Awards; Canada.

Key events & continuity: Ike's premature puberty is traced to a Canadian prescription mix-up — hormones instead of laxatives — and resolves the moment the dosing stops; IntelliLink's "upgrades" satirize tech support all the way to the system being physically ripped out; the Canadian fart-based conception lesson joins the canon of gloriously wrong Canadian health guidance.

At lunch, Cartman grandly apologizes to Kyle for mocking his claim that animals could be ginger — he has seen a red cow himself. Produced on demand, the cow is plainly costumed; only Kyle sees through it. But the story escapes: global news reports the ginger cow, and believers, convinced the red heifer ends times, kill themselves en masse. In the principal's office, two rabbis — whom Victoria and Mackey absurdly ask Kyle to translate, though they speak English — declare the red heifer means Armageddon; Kyle's attempts to expose the prank fail. The leaders of Islam, Christianity, and Judaism convene to haggle apocalypse protocol until a Muslim cleric proposes the heifer might mean the end of Middle East violence instead of destruction. They agree; the cow is sacrificed in Israel via helicopter drop onto a building. Peace breaks out. Watching on TV, Kyle is aghast; Cartman says he should confess — Kyle begs him not to, and Cartman sells his silence for an insult to his mother, which Kyle delivers. To keep the secret buried, Kyle becomes Cartman's servant, even asking Cartman to fart in his mouth — repeatedly, including in Mackey's office, where Kyle professes his love of Cartman's farts. In Jerusalem, the faiths merge their symbols into the Van Halen logo, inaugurating ten prophesied years of Van Halen. Stan finds Kyle's devotion unconvincing and recruits Kenny to investigate. Kyle hallucinates a glowing orb commanding him to shave his head and be at peace; he complies. He keeps taking the farts "for the greater good" as Stan and Butters plead with him to stop; Stan advises enjoying it without sanctimony. In Israel, Stan moves to expose the prank; Kyle stops him, and Stan improvises a cover story about the heifer descending from the sky. The Hebrew scholars demolish it with the actual prophecy: a fat kid with a small penis would make a cow look ginger — rendering Kyle's degradation pointless. Cartman denies the anatomy, contra established lore. Peace destroyed, Cartman serves Kyle a fart "dessert" of whipped cream and cherry, smeared across his face. Kyle stares at the floor, dejected.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman; Kyle Broflovski; Stan Marsh; Kenny McCormick; Butters Stotch; Craig Tucker; Mr. Mackey; Principal Victoria; the two rabbis; the Muslim, Christian, and Jewish leaders.

Locations: The school cafeteria and principal's office; Israel and Jerusalem.

Key events & continuity: The ginger-cow hoax — a callback to Cartman's original "Ginger Kids" hatred — accidentally brokers Middle East peace and then destroys it; Kyle's humiliation is rendered meaningless by the prophecy's fine print, a classic Cartman victory; the "fat kid with a small penis" clause ties back to earlier-established lore about Cartman.

At the mall, security is briefed on Black Friday's horrors: eighty percent off for the first thirty shoppers. Randy is among the guards, there for holiday cash. Wizard-robed Cartman summons "Lady McCormick" to a great-hall meeting: the boys must beat the crowds to the mall, and training begins. Randy and a fellow guard remember last year's horrors and their fallen oldest officer. The alliance fractures over Xbox One versus PlayStation 4; Stan and Kyle split, genuinely upsetting Kyle. Sharon learns Randy took the job for gifts. Cartman doubles his Xbox army with the Star Trek kids and needles Kyle over Stan's indecision. Then the "Stop Touching Me Elmo" announcement sends parents camping early. Stan, Jimmy, and Craig fail to recruit the Goth Kids — who declare for PS4 but will not fight. Kenny and Cartman game out Kyle's betrayal odds in the Garden of Betrayal until the owner ejects them for trespassing. Randy shops guiltily while Captain Officer Krum praises his selflessness, troubling him. Sony's president, fearing an Xbox sell-through embarrasses Sony, counters with the "Brack Friday Bunduru": four controllers, a Japan map, a hundred-dollar rebate, a Metal Gear Solid V preorder. Wristbands for line-holding spark a brawl; the Captain is fatally stabbed. Cradling him, Randy confesses his selfish motives; the Captain peels off his prosthetic scar, presses it onto Randy — he is the Captain now, mall protector. Transformed, Randy rallies the guards. The Bunduru swells the PS4 ranks; Stan rallies his army around a new leader guaranteeing victory: Lady McCormick, defected from Xbox, now hailed as "Princess Kenny."

Featured characters: Eric Cartman; Randy and Sharon Marsh; Stan Marsh; Kyle Broflovski; Kenny McCormick, a.k.a. Lady McCormick and Princess Kenny; Jimmy Valmer; Craig Tucker; the Goth Kids; the Star Trek kids; Captain Officer Krum; the president of Sony; the Garden of Betrayal's owner.

Locations: The South Park Mall; Cartman's house, the great hall; the McCormick residence; the Garden of Betrayal.

Key events & continuity: Part one of the Black Friday trilogy — the console war is framed as a Game of Thrones-style epic, with Kenny's cross-dressing "Princess Kenny" persona as its turning point; Randy inherits the Captain's scar and his sacred duty to the mall; the Garden of Betrayal becomes the saga's recurring stage for treachery.

entries.n: S17E08 — A Song of Ass and Fire
entries.t:
Lady McCormick narrates the coming storm. At Cartman's, Butters and Scott Malkinson spar under his disgusted eye; Kyle reports the PS4 army's gains, and Cartman blames Kenny. Cartman warns Microsoft; the CEO calls the war ridiculous and refuses marketing's pleas. Niles Lawson reports another guard death and ten percent more off. The guards hold a ceremony while scar-wearing Randy holds the line. In the Garden of Betrayal, Cartman manipulates Butters into visiting George R. R. Martin with Scott to ask about dragons; the owner grills Cartman on his endless betrayal talks. At Microsoft HQ, Bill Gates has the CEO murdered: one winner only; coexistence is over. At Martin's, the author's penis tangents trap the boys — Scott, diabetic, desperately needs food. Cartman tries to get Kyle to ground Stan; Kyle refuses until Cartman mentions Randy's mall job. The owner warns Kyle he is being manipulated. Anchors Tom and Tammy Thompson are in bed when Niles barges in: Gates promises a bloodier war for spiking a story; Tom resists, and Niles threatens to expose the siblings' incest. Gates and Niles discuss arming the Xbox faithful. The Xbox army demands the PS4 army's surrender at Kenny's; refused. At Martin's, Scott is fading and George has not reached the dragons. In the garden, Gates turns Cartman's own manipulation tactics on him; the owner laughs. At Sony HQ, Niles — fresh from sleeping with Sony's president — asks how Sony evens the odds; the president shows him something astonishing in a box. Butters gives up on Martin as Scott nears collapse — but explaining their quest moves Martin to make calls. Sony's executives give Kenny a medallion making her a true princess. Niles announces Black Friday and Thanksgiving are pushed back a week: ninety-six percent off for the first hundred inside, Martin's proposal. Shoppers brawl; Niles warns of a bloodbath.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman; Kyle Broflovski; Butters Stotch; Scott Malkinson; Kenny McCormick, a.k.a. Princess Kenny; Bill Gates; George R. R. Martin; Niles Lawson; Tom and Tammy Thompson; the president of Sony; Randy Marsh; the Garden of Betrayal's owner.

Locations: Cartman's house; the South Park Mall; Microsoft and Sony headquarters; George R. R. Martin's house; the Garden of Betrayal; Kenny's house.

Key events & continuity: Part two of the Black Friday trilogy — Bill Gates murders Microsoft's CEO to take personal command of the Xbox war effort; George R. R. Martin's dragon lore keeps getting derailed by his own digressions while Scott Malkinson's diabetes becomes a ticking clock; the Garden of Betrayal's owner openly mocks Cartman's scheming to his face.
k: a song of ass and fire

entries.t:
Sony's president briefs Princess Kenny on Microsoft's PS4 shipping blockades. At Cartman's, Clyde reports Kenny is winning for Sony; Kyle hatches a plan. At the PS4 base, Stan, Jimmy, and Craig plan to seize the Red Robin for a back entrance; Pete arrives: the Xbox army wants to defect. Cartman begs; Stan refuses — until Cartman reveals the Red Robin entry via a "Red Robin Wedding." Stan makes Kyle swear off the Xbox One forever; Kyle crosses his fingers, and the Xbox army is absorbed. At Sony HQ, Kenny gets Cartman's wedding invite and jumps out the window — and survives the bloody landing. Stan walks out; Cartman confirms it was Kyle's idea and threatens to defecate in the garden. Black Friday dawns; Martin rides horseback toward South Park with Butters and Scott to cut the ribbon. At the Red Robin, both armies decorate for the "wedding" of Tom Hanks and Beyoncé, per Cartman. Kyle learns Cartman got Stan grounded — for defecating in the old man's garden, Sharon confirms — and that Stan never knew about Randy's mall job. At the mall, Randy's pep talk collapses as shoppers smash the windows; a fleeing guard is arrowed dead by Randy, who screams about being liked. Martin arrives and speechifies about his penis instead of cutting the ribbon. At the Red Robin, Kyle and the PS4 army turn on the Xbox army — Kyle is getting Stan a PS4; the war is over. Bill Gates and Sony's president arrive unplanned; Stan locks the doors and declares the war is Microsoft versus Sony — they should fight it themselves. They do. Outside, a shopper severs Martin's penis, then cuts the ribbon: Black Friday begins. Guards are trampled, shoppers murder each other, Randy battles toward the Red Robin as Sharon reports Stan snuck out. Inside, Gates beats Sony's president to death as Randy unlocks the doors. The kids wander the corpse-strewn mall and quietly buy Xbox Ones. Channel 4 News names the true winners: Channel 4 News. At Cartman's, the Xbox One feels barely different from the 360; haunted by Gates' skull-bashing, Cartman proposes they play outside instead — all they ever needed was a stick. They swear off gaming as a Stick of Truth ad plays.

Featured characters: Stan, Kyle, Cartman, and Kenny; Butters; Randy Marsh; Bill Gates; the Sony president; Martin; Scott Malkinson.

Locations: The Red Robin; the South Park Mall; the Garden of Betrayal; Sony HQ; Cartman's house.

Key events & continuity: The console-war trilogy concludes with the kids buying Xbox Ones after all; Randy works mall security and accidentally kills a guard; the final swing to a stick outside is the saga's punchline.

At cheer practice, Lisa Berger introduces herself as "the fat, ugly cheerleader." Captain Wendy defends her from the squad's sneers and urges confidence — but Red and Heidi note Wendy only cares because Lisa crushes on Butters. Wendy's prescription: ask Butters out. Lisa does; Butters rejects her as "too fat." Clyde and Craig howl; Cartman corrects them — mock her for ugly, not fat. Wendy confronts Butters; he doubles down, preferring slimmer women like Kim Kardashian. Wendy retorts that Kim has "the body of a hobbit" and only looks that way via Photoshop, which is why average girls feel awful. Kanye West lectures Garrison's class that Kim is not a hobbit, torpedoing his own case and repeatedly phoning Kim mid-argument to ask why not. Wendy lures a wary Butters into the computer lab and Photoshops Lisa into impossible glamour to prove how the illusion works. It backfires: Butters falls for the doctored image as her true face and resolves to ask her out — learning she is already with Clyde. At the Time Person of the Year ceremony, as Pope Francis accepts, Kanye storms the stage — and learns live from Kim that her new film actually is The Hobbit, which he spins as based on Keeping Up With the Kardashians. At the gym, only Lisa gets cheers; the squad begs Wendy for Photoshops; she refuses. Then Lisa appears scantily dressed preaching "working out" — and at "the gym" the girls learn Photoshop, not exercise, uploading their fakes for the school. Boys ogle them on the playground; Stan is crushed no photo is Wendy's, and asking about it gets him shamed before a gathering crowd; Bebe calls her a "hater," Mackey summons her again. Practice inverts: Wendy is the meek one, Lisa advises confidence via asking out Butters, Wendy snaps that they believe their own "bullshit" and vows that if society will not fight Photoshop, she will. That night Kanye slips into her bedroom and reads a weepy bedtime story about a poor ugly hobbit saved by Photoshop's magic from an evil "Jelly Monster." Guilt-stricken, Wendy admits she has been "jelly" and a "hater." Next day she Photoshops herself into conventional beauty, mass-emails it to everyone through tears, and walks out as the credits roll in silence.

Featured characters: Wendy Testaburger; Lisa Berger; Butters Stotch; Kanye West and Kim Kardashian; Mr. Mackey; Stan Marsh; Pope Francis.

Locations: The school gym; the computer lab; Garrison's classroom; Wendy's bedroom; the Time Person of the Year ceremony.

Key events & continuity: Wendy's Photoshop crusade collapses into self-defeat — her final mass-email is the payoff; "jelly" becomes the season's weaponized word; Kanye's defense of Kim keeps backfiring, hobbit-style.

The boys and Butters found a do-nothing startup; after a day of raunchy brainstorming, the Law Office rejects every name but "Furry Balls Plopped Menacingly on the Table, Inc." Their Kickstarter launches at Stan's to universal disappointment — until Cartman races in: they will be "The Washington Redskins." Kyle's legal worries are waved off. Funding floods in; Dan Snyder begs Cartman to stop using his team's name; Cartman refuses, and Snyder spirals. The company gets so big even ISIS endorses it. Six days before funds go liquid, Kyle and Stan quit — a company should do something — and crawl back to Furry Balls. Snyder pleads to the Goodell-bot, which breaks; he Skypes the NFL owners, who vote to change the Redskins' logo. Cartman's press-conference unveiling: the logo with breasts and a penis added. Kyle and Stan's argument over their company's name ends with Stan walking out. That night the real Washington Redskins storm Kickstarter HQ and destroy the company — killing both startups at once. Next day the trio found a Kickstarter clone, "Go Fund Yourself," its logo two breasted-penised Redskins logos in congress. At the Cowboys game, the demoralized real Redskins will not play; Snyder takes the field alone, is tackled repeatedly, and is nearly killed. Backlash is total — even ISIS turns — the company dies, and it is back to school. The fallout bleeds into the next story: the boys return universally despised after telling everyone to "go fuck themselves," Wendy dumps Stan over the startup, and Butters is barred for burning down the gym.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman; Stan Marsh; Kyle Broflovski; Butters Stotch; Dan Snyder; the Goodell-bot; the NFL owners.

Locations: The Law Office; Stan's and Kyle's houses; the boys' company headquarters; Kickstarter headquarters; the football stadium.

Key events & continuity: The fallout carries directly into the next story — the boys return to school universally despised after telling everyone to "go fuck themselves" on their way out, Wendy dumps Stan over the startup, and Butters is barred from school for burning down the gym; the mangled Redskins logo becomes the season's visual signature.

The boys slink back to school universally hated — they told the whole town to "go fuck themselves" on the way out. Wendy is furious at Stan for dumping her over the startup; Butters is barred entirely for burning down the gym. At the meeting on his fate, Mackey cannot stop gloating about his gluten-free diet. For redemption, Cartman proposes a party with a cause: Scott Malkinson's diabetes. The radio announcement draws complaints about non-gluten-free food. At the Community Center, scientist John Garner extracts pure gluten from wheat dough onstage to debunk the panic; Mackey baits him into drinking the concentrate — Garner melts, sparks, and his penis launches like a rocket. Terror erupts. The Marshes purge gluten; Kyle budgets while Cartman panics — the town is burning gluten foods, so no party. The military torches the wheat farm; the USDA flails; the FDA mobilizes. Cartman takes to his sickbed; Kyle clings to "we still have Lorde," but Stan has not asked his father about the singer, supposedly a coworker's niece. USDA agents find wheat-based Pabst Blue Ribbon at the Marsh house; Randy is quarantined at Papa John's with a stranger and Garrison, living on toppings, while military men drag Stan off before he gets answers. Cartman dreams of Aunt Jemima as Mother Abigail from The Stand: "the pyramid is upside down." At Papa John's, a resident risks the dough — seems fine, then his penis rockets off. On air, the boys (minus Cartman) cancel the party and lecture on gluten; Wendy corners Stan, who cracks: no Lorde, no food plan. Cartman raves to Kyle about the dream, then phones the USDA: the pyramid is upside down. The scientists flip it — grains to the top, fats to the bottom — and it magically fixes everything. The party happens with Scott as waiter; grounded Butters cannot attend. Cartman waves at a smiling distant Aunt Jemima. "Lorde" performs; Stan and Wendy reconcile.

Featured characters: Stan Marsh; Kyle Broflovski; Eric Cartman; Wendy Testaburger; Butters Stotch; Scott Malkinson; Randy and Sharon Marsh; Mr. Mackey; Mr. Garrison; John Garner; Aunt Jemima; Lorde.

Locations: South Park Elementary; the Community Center; the Marsh residence; Papa John's; the USDA headquarters; the wheat farm; the radio station.

Key events & continuity: The gluten panic is resolved by literally inverting the food pyramid on the strength of Cartman's dream; Lorde performs at the party, deepening the mystery of the singer's identity that the next story resolves; Stan and Wendy get back together, and Butters' gym arson keeps him grounded and out of the celebration.

At recess, finding the boys' stalls taken, Cartman executes his plan: bow on head, into the girls' bathroom past a horrified Wendy, Bebe, and Red, announcing he is "transginger" — transgender. Victoria cannot punish him; Garrison calls it a "royal flush" — refuse him and the media descends. SPIN reporter Brandon Carlile questions Gerald about Lorde's party performance; Gerald covers: a coworker's niece. Sharon finds fishnets in Randy's jeans. Cartman fouls the girls' bathroom on purpose and is awarded a private one in the janitor's closet; Wendy cries foul. In his garage, Randy tries to quit his secret to his producer, who refuses — then tells fixer Ron that Lorde is Randy, and to silence anyone close. Randy keeps writing, nearly caught by Sharon. At Skeeter's, Brandon gets Randy's coworker Peter Nelson drunk enough to crack: Lorde is a geologist covering for Randy's double life. Wendy escalates, declaring herself transgender — "Wendyl" — enraging Cartman, who brands Stan a girl and a homosexual for dating a girl who likes girls. Stan seeks Randy's advice; Randy mistakes it for a Lorde question and confesses all: he became Lorde to be in the girls' bathroom, demonstrating his song-making to a disbelieving Stan. Stan uses the transgender bathroom; Cartman is livid. At the USGS, Randy-as-Lorde wins a private bathroom — which depresses him. The school brands Stan a "cissy." Sharon gives Randy the speech that sends him back to music; his released song moves everyone. Lorde's boss scraps the private bathroom; the SPIN reporter kills the tell-all. The school's new policy: anyone may use any bathroom — except cissies. Outed, Stan takes his assigned bathroom and sings his own version of Randy's song.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman; Stan Marsh; Randy Marsh, a.k.a. Lorde; Wendy Testaburger, a.k.a. Wendyl; Sharon Marsh; Gerald Broflovski; Brandon Carlile; Peter Nelson; Principal Victoria; Mr. Mackey; Mr. Garrison; Bebe Stevens; Red; Craig Tucker; Kyle Broflovski; Ron the fixer.

Locations: South Park Elementary and its bathrooms; the Cartman and Marsh residences; Randy's garage; the U.S. Geological Survey; Skeeter's Bar and Cocktails.

Key events & continuity: Randy is revealed as the pop star Lorde — the secret behind the previous story's concert — with his double life as a geologist covering for his recording sessions; Cartman's "transginger" gambit backfires into a school-wide bathroom free-for-all; Stan ends the story branded a "cissy," singing alone in his assigned bathroom.

The Stotches and Broflovskis leave the Bijou; the Stotches are using Timmy's Handicar, a cut-rate taxi service, and Gerald downloads the app on the spot. A Russian cab driver watches his fares vanish; the Hummer salesman loses sale after sale to Timmy's pickups. At the funding meeting, Timmy has raised a fortune for summer camp — which Nathan despises: the singing, the competitions, Jimmy getting the girls. When Mimsy cackles about Nathan's shark rape in "Crippled Summer," Nathan recruits him to kill Handicar. At the Community Center, cabbies and the Hummer salesman conspire, Nathan whipping them up. They break into the Burch home and "break" Timmy's legs — Handicar rolls on; Nathan rages at their incompetence. Nathan then advises Timmy to hire extra drivers, gets hired himself, and tries harassing a passenger into a scandal — but she turns out to be a transvestite who assaults him. The fleet only grows. At a Tesla conference, a besieged Elon Musk fields Handicar questions while Nathan proposes a race: Timmy versus Elon. CNN heralds another Wacky Races; South Park stockpiles milk and cereal. The grid: Lyft, Zipcar, taxi, Hummer, Tesla D, the queef-powered Queef, the Handi Car, a Japanese self-driver, and Dick Dastardly and Muttley. The Tesla leads; Nathan has Elon slow so the passenger can be stolen — Lyft grabs her, the Hummer salesman steals her for a test-drive pitch, Elon destroys the Hummer, the taxi takes her, the Queef runs dry, Dastardly fells a tree wrecking the taxi and the Japanese car — but the Handicar sails through and collects her. Swarmed by Handicars, the Tesla falters; Nathan detonates what he thinks is the Handicar's bomb — it is the Zipcar's. It explodes; driver Matthew McConaughey is sucked into a wormhole; the Handicar wins. Timmy donates 2.3 billion dollars. With camp inevitable, Nathan begs his mother to let him stay home; she pretends not to understand, then tells his father Nathan said he did not want camp — but she will be damned if he ruins their Italy trip.

Featured characters: Timmy Burch; Nathan; Mimsy; Jimmy Valmer; Elon Musk; Gerald Broflovski; Stephen and Linda Stotch; the cab drivers; the Hummer salesman; Dick Dastardly and Muttley; Matthew McConaughey.

Locations: The Bijou Cinema; the car dealership; the Park County Community Center; the Burch residence; the Tesla conference; the Wacky Races course.

Key events & continuity: Timmy's Handicar empire funds the summer camp Nathan dreads, setting up their eternal rivalry; every sabotage attempt — broken legs, harassment, a misplaced bomb — only makes Handicar stronger; Nathan's shark trauma from "Crippled Summer" is still raw.

Bored, Cartman visits Butters, learns his father owns a drone, and takes it despite the ban — meet after dark. That night, with Kenny looped in, they film Craig's mother Laura undressing, nude, while Cartman marvels at her pubic hair on the audio. Thomas Tucker spots the drone and screams at Stephen Stotch, who proves his drone never left the garage; Thomas storms off unconvinced, and Stephen grows paranoid, quizzing a visibly winded just-landed-it Butters. At the bus stop, Cartman swears Kenny to secrecy, then instantly asks Stan and Kyle if they want to see Craig's mom's "bush"; Kyle is disgusted, Stan suspicious — Cartman lies he downloaded it and posts it online. Butters confronts Cartman in the school bathroom; Kyle overhears from a stall. The Neighborhood Watch meets: members insult Laura's pubic hair while each insisting he never watched, then vote to deploy watch drones. Kyle confronts the duo; Cartman reverse-blames Kyle for spying. At the Hobby Enthusiast, Stephen insists the drone flies itself while the owner eyes Butters. Re-buzzed by a Watch drone, the Tuckers go to the police. That night Randy's Watch drone is shot down by a police drone — right after spying on Peter Nelson mid-coitus. The Watch drones hold a candlelight vigil; police drones break it up over the fire hazard. Stephen asks Randy point-blank if he spied on Nelson; Randy's denial deepens Stephen's certainty the drones are sentient. Drone riots engulf the town; the governor sends the National Guard — with Guard drones. On 20/20, the interviewer pretends he never saw the video while insulting Laura to her face; Stephen hacks the feed to declare the drones sentient, citing the video nobody admits watching — three hundred thousand views and counting. Butters begs Cartman to apologize to Laura; Cartman has a plan. Stephen builds a drone-killing weapon; the drone is gone — Cartman has paired it with a life-size blowup doll sporting an enormous bush, luring every drone out of South Park pied-piper style. The town celebrates Laura and her bush with a minstrel's song, apparently believing she was the doll; the real Laura is still devastated, leaving Butters miserable — until he decides to thank Cartman for making it all work out.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman; Butters Stotch; Kenny McCormick; Laura and Thomas Tucker; Stephen Stotch; Randy Marsh; Kyle Broflovski.

Locations: The Stotch garage; the school bathroom; the Neighborhood Watch meeting; the Hobby Enthusiast; the 20/20 studio.

Key events & continuity: Cartman's drone video of Laura Tucker becomes the town's shared open secret nobody admits watching; Stephen's sentience theory spreads to full drone-on-drone warfare; Laura never gets real closure — the town celebrates a decoy.

Jimmy pushes the new Terrance and Phillip mobile game on Kyle, who tries it with Butters: crushingly boring, Cartman and Kenny agree. In Canada, Terrance and Phillip storm the Department of Mobile Gaming: the game uses their likenesses unconsulted. The Minister and the Prince bluff; the duo sees through it — low-quality games plus micro-transactions equals free money. Stan is grounded for spending $489; Randy blames Marvin's gambling demons, Sharon names Randy's alcohol, Randy denies — he quit; only PBR and wine now. The Minister's philosophy: barely fun, so players pay to make it fun. Stan's habit becomes addiction; he skips school, and Kyle, Cartman, and Kenny learn Jimmy put him onto it. Cornered, Jimmy admits he is a paid pusher who has never played. In Canada, Terrance and Phillip balk at freemium's toll on players; the Minister counters with the alcohol industry's "Drink Responsibly" playbook. At the Three Feathers casino, Randy parades Stan past Marvin's ruin, then hauls both home; Marvin throws Randy's drinking back; Stan and Marvin vow to quit together. Jimmy confesses he needed pusher money for his own freemium habit — by design. That night push notifications break Stan; he spends $26,000. Randy's scolding stings: being Lorde does not license it. At Kyle's, Jimmy advises asking a higher power while the others trace Canada's pusher network — Cartman just tweets it, and it trends. Livid, Terrance and Phillip confront the Minister about farming addicts; he drops the mask: a tiny fraction pays, they are the addicts, and it is all funding his micro-payment New Canada — revealing himself as Beelzaboot, the Canadian Devil. Stan's prayer summons Satan, who lectures on dopamine, evolution, and inherited demons — then diagnoses the truth: addictive things must be fun; this is "blatant skinnerbox manipulation," a cruelty only the Canadian Devil's nuance-free mind could ship. Satan borrows Stan's soul, possesses him, marches on Canada, and blows Beelzaboot's complex into Hell. Stan rises by the basketball courts, fine. Terrance, Phillip, and the Prince announce: no more freemium, no more addict money — Canada stays an ethical, respected, "shitty" tundra. Stan and Marvin play board games to stay clean; Randy joins and asks if they want to bet on it.

Featured characters: Stan and Randy Marsh; Marvin Marsh; Terrance and Phillip; Jimmy Valmer; the Canadian Minister (Beelzaboot); Satan; Kyle Broflovski.

Locations: Canada and the Department of Mobile Gaming; the Three Feathers casino; Kyle's house; the basketball courts.

Key events & continuity: Randy's Lorde identity is invoked as a scolding point; Stan and Marvin share a vow of sobriety — from games and drink; Satan distinguishes mere addiction from engineered cruelty, and Canada renounces freemium.

Butters insists he is wearing an Oculus Rift, living in VR. He is not — Cartman just told him so. Removing the "headset" would expose the prank (he has been touching the real Stan), so Cartman sends him to his bedroom "access point," where Butters theatrically "exits." That night Butters goes "back in": shoveling real snow for VR cash while Stan eye-rolls from his window. Defying the access-point order, Butters goes home, punches his father in the testicles, rampages, is stabbed by a prostitute, and wakes grounded in Hells Pass Hospital. Cartman convinces him he is still in VR and that mentioning it means death. At the bus stop Kyle scolds Cartman — until Steve from Oculus support calls: the headset had a "problem"; Cartman himself is stuck in VR, comatose in his bedroom. Cartman denies it; at home, Liane brings her motionless son a sandwich. A rattled Cartman visits grounded Butters with a new theory: grounded in VR means grounded in real life. Stan and Kyle find Cartman truly comatose; Steve explains a total headset recall and begs Kyle to rate him well — someone must enter VR to save Cartman. "Awake," Cartman refuses belief; Kyle comes to rescue him, and Cartman reverses it: maybe Kyle is the comatose one. They phone Best Buy about who bought a headset and land back with Steve. Stan stays on with Steve while Kenny enters VR; Kyle and Cartman emerge baffled — everything was real; Kyle theorizes they have been taking turns. Cartman insists he is a program being watched. Asked who first called support: Butters. Then Steve gets a call from himself — another Steve: a VR-trapped customer called support, creating a customer-feedback loop. A vindaloop. At Butters', barred from visitors, Butters explains: he called when they first got the Oculus, forgot he was in VR, got grounded, then grounded again for real. Is this the real world? Butters says yes; Cartman still believes he is code. Everyone vanishes. Stan hurries to the access point — Cartman's room — sits at the computer, and removes the headset. The truth: the four were just trying the Oculus in real life. The graphics suck, Stan concludes. Butters bursts in: he is not grounded after all.

Featured characters: Eric Cartman; Butters Stotch; Stan Marsh; Kyle Broflovski; Kenny McCormick; Steve from Oculus support; Liane Cartman.

Locations: Cartman's bedroom (the "access point"); Butters' home; Hells Pass Hospital; the school bus stop.

Key events & continuity: The vindaloop — a customer-feedback paradox — is the episode's signature gag; Cartman's refusal to believe he isn't code persists past the reveal; Steve's desperation for a good support rating drives the entire rescue.

The volleyball team's fliers cannot compete with tonight's event: Kenny versus Slaughterhouse. The "fight" is Magic: The Gathering, watched in suspense by half the town — Kenny dismantles him expertly. Next day the boys savor the "carnage"; Wendy mentions volleyball, Stan brushes her off, and the janitor tempts them with "real man shit" and an address. It leads to City Wok's basement: Tuong Lu Kim charges five dollars for "Cock Magic" — roosters playing Magic while the crowd bets. Kenny doubts the birds' happiness; the boys buy a young chicken, name him "McNuggets," and train him in Kenny's image. Yates investigates at the McCormick door; Stuart knows nothing. Randy lectures the boys, having concluded "Cock Magic" means penis tricks — and demonstrates, horrifying them. At City Wok, McNuggets wins his debut; a businessman slips them the "big leagues" address. Randy takes his act to a kindergartner's birthday, cuts his penis mid-trick, and traumatizes the kids.
